author: HomiLabs

stem: FrostyCream asked 400 people outside one shopping mall in Lahore which new ice-cream flavour they would buy. 92 chose mango, 140 chose pistachio, 108 chose chocolate fudge and 60 chose none of these.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of people asked who chose mango.

parts.label: b
parts.text: FrostyCream estimates that 25,000 people in its target market will buy a new flavour. Using the results for pistachio, estimate how many of them would choose pistachio.
parts.answer: 8,750 people

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the results of this survey may not be reliable.
parts.answer: 1. Sample from one mall only: shoppers there may be wealthier or younger than the whole target market, so results are biased. 2. People may say they would buy a flavour but not actually buy it, or answer quickly to get away. (Also: sample size small relative to market; leading questions; time of day/season.)
parts.working: For each reason: 1 mark identify + 1 mark explain linked to FrostyCream.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bolan Travels runs coaches between Quetta and Karachi. It plans to start a premium service with reclining seats and Wi-Fi. The marketing manager must choose between an online survey sent to 2,000 past customers by email and a focus group of 10 regular passengers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two problems Bolan Travels might have in making sure its market research is accurate.
parts.answer: 1. The sample may not represent the target market: past customers who gave an email address may be younger or richer than other passengers, so the results could overstate demand for the premium service. 2. Questions may be badly written or leading, or people may not answer honestly about how much extra they would pay, so the firm could set the wrong fare. (Also: low response rates; out-of-date data; researcher bias.)
parts.working: For each problem (max 4 each): 1 mark identify; 1 mark apply to Bolan Travels' premium coach service; 2 marks explain the consequence for its decision.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recommend which research method Bolan Travels should use. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Online survey: cheap, quick and gives numerical data from many people, so the firm can estimate how many would pay more; but response rates may be low and answers are short. Focus group: gives detailed opinions on seats and Wi-Fi and why people value them, but only 10 people, so may not represent all passengers. Recommendation: the online survey, because the key question is how many customers would pay the higher fare; a focus group could follow to refine features.
parts.working: Content: online survey of 2,000 — cheap, quick, numerical data on how many would pay more, but low response rate and short answers; focus group of 10 — detailed opinions on seats and Wi-Fi and why, but small and may not represent all passengers; the key question is how many would pay the higher fare; a focus group could follow. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Bolan Travels, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Bolan Travels, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Leila wants to open a bookshop and café in Muscat, Oman. She has limited money for research and plans to rely only on secondary research.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two pieces of information secondary research could give Leila.
parts.answer: e.g. population/age structure of the area; average incomes; number and locations of competing bookshops/cafés; trends in reading or café spending; rents in the area.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two relevant pieces of information.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think secondary research alone is enough for Leila? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Secondary research is cheap and quick and shows market size, incomes and competitors. But it was collected for other purposes, may be out of date and will not tell her what local customers want from a bookshop-café (e.g. Arabic or English books, prices, opening hours). As a new business with limited money, a mistake would be costly, so a small amount of cheap primary research (e.g. a short questionnaire to people in the area or a social-media poll) is worthwhile. Judgement: not enough on its own.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks knowledge, up to 2 marks analysis (developed consequences), up to 2 marks evaluation (justified judgement that weighs both sides for this business).

author: HomiLabs

stem: HealthyBite plans to sell a new protein bar. An online survey of 1,200 gym members found that 60% would buy the bar at Rs 150 and 25% would buy it at Rs 200. Each bar costs Rs 90 to make.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Should HealthyBite rely on these survey results to choose the price of its protein bar? Justify your answer using suitable calculations (for example, the expected profit per 1,000 gym members at each price).
parts.answer: Calculations: Rs 150: Rs 36,000; Rs 200: Rs 27,500. The results suggest Rs 150 gives more profit (Rs 36,000 v Rs 27,500 per 1,000 members) and more customers. But only gym members who use the internet were asked, so the sample excludes other possible buyers; people often say they will buy but do not; answers for one bar per person ignore how often people buy; competitors' prices are not considered. Judgement: use the results as a guide (Rs 150 looks better) but test-market in a few gyms before deciding.
parts.working: Calculations: Rs 150: 600 buyers × (150 − 90) = Rs 36,000. Rs 200: 250 buyers × (200 − 90) = Rs 27,500. Content: per 1,000 gym members, Rs 150 → 600 buyers × Rs 60 = Rs 36,000; Rs 200 → 250 buyers × Rs 110 = Rs 27,500; limitations — only online gym members sampled, stated v actual behaviour, frequency of purchase ignored, competitors' prices not considered; test marketing. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to HealthyBite, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to HealthyBite, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Pixel Print is a small business in Kampala, Uganda, that prints T-shirts. It wants to find out what designs young customers prefer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages of using an online questionnaire for this research.
parts.answer: Any two: cheap; quick to reach many people; young people use social media so it reaches the target market; results are easy to analyse automatically; can include pictures of designs.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two disadvantages of using an online questionnaire for this research.
parts.answer: Any two: low response rate; people who answer may not be representative; cannot ask follow-up questions; people may give careless answers; some people may answer more than once.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Cool Breeze sells air coolers in Pakistan. Last year its sales were Rs 360 million and total market sales of air coolers were Rs 2,400 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Cool Breeze's market share.
parts.working: Market share = firm's sales ÷ total market sales × 100 (M1) = 360 ÷ 2,400 × 100 = 15% (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'market segment'.
parts.answer: An identifiable sub-group of a whole market in which consumers have similar characteristics or needs.
parts.working: 1 mark: part/sub-group of a market; 1 mark: customers with similar characteristics (e.g. age, income, location).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Velocity Sportswear sells trainers and sports clothing in Pakistan and the UAE.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'niche market'.
parts.answer: A small, specialised segment of a larger market with particular needs.
parts.working: 1 mark: small part/segment of the market; 1 mark: specialised/particular needs (e.g. running shoes for marathon runners).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways Velocity Sportswear could segment its market.
parts.answer: 1. By age: different ranges for children and adults, so designs and prices can match each group and advertising can be aimed at them. 2. By use/lifestyle (activity): football boots, running shoes, gym wear; customers needing specialist products will pay more. (Also: income, gender, location/region, e.g. lighter fabrics for the UAE climate.)
parts.working: For each way: 1 mark identify, 1 mark application to sportswear, 1 mark explanation of the benefit (better targeting, higher sales).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Desi Chips Ltd sells potato crisps. The managing director is pleased that sales have increased. Appendix (Rs million):
Year | Desi Chips sales | Total market sales
Year 1 | 4.2 | 30
Year 2 | 4.6 | 40
Two new foreign crisp brands entered the market in Year 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Desi Chips' market share in each year. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the managing director should be concerned, and explain one way Desi Chips could respond to the new competition.
parts.answer: Sales rose by about 9.5% but the market grew by a third, so market share fell from 14.0% to 11.5%; rivals, including the new foreign brands, are growing faster and Desi Chips may lose bargaining power with shops. Response: e.g. launch new local flavours (e.g. chatpata masala) that foreign brands do not offer, and promote them, to attract customers and win back share; or improve distribution to small shops in rural areas.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks: concern explained using data (sales up but share down, market growing faster, new entrants). Up to 3 marks: one response identified, applied and developed.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Laptop Lane is a computer shop in Rawalpindi. Customers now compare prices online, and two large electronics stores have opened nearby.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways Laptop Lane could keep its customers despite the stronger competition. Which way is likely to be the most important? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: 1. Better customer service: expert advice, installing software and fast repairs that big stores and online sellers do not offer; customers who value help will stay loyal. 2. Loyalty scheme / after-sales care, e.g. discounts on repairs for returning customers. Judgement: customer service is most important, because a small shop cannot match large stores on price, but personal service gives a reason to pay slightly more and creates loyalty and recommendations.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks knowledge (two ways, e.g. service, loyalty scheme, price matching, after-sales service, online presence). Up to 2 marks analysis applied to Laptop Lane. Up to 2 marks evaluation choosing one with a reason why it beats the other.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why customer spending patterns may change.
parts.answer: Any two: changes in income; changes in tastes/fashion; new technology (e.g. online shopping); population/age changes; changes in prices of substitutes; advertising.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Rang Fashions sells shalwar kameez in Pakistan and wants to start selling in the UK.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two problems Rang Fashions may face when entering a foreign market.
parts.answer: Any two: lack of knowledge of the market/customers; different tastes or culture; strong local competitors; different laws and regulations; exchange-rate changes; transport costs; language barriers; import taxes.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'licensing' as a way of entering a foreign market.
parts.answer: Allowing a business in another country to make or sell a product using the firm's brand or design in return for a fee or royalty.
parts.working: 1 mark: permission given to a foreign business to make/sell using the brand/design; 1 mark: in return for a payment/royalty.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Masala Munch Ltd makes spicy snacks in Karachi. It wants to sell in Malaysia and is considering a joint venture with a Malaysian food company.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to Masala Munch Ltd of a joint venture with the Malaysian company.
parts.answer: Advantage: the Malaysian partner knows local tastes, laws and has distribution links to shops, so the snacks can reach customers faster with less risk; costs and risks are shared. Disadvantage: profits must be shared and the partners may disagree, e.g. about recipes, prices or how halal certification is promoted, which could slow decisions or damage the brand.
parts.working: Advantage: 1 identify, 1 application, 1 development. Disadvantage: 1 identify, 1 application, 1 development.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Sukoon Herbal Teas makes herbal tea in Pakistan. Its advertisements say the tea "cures headaches and stress". It wants to sell in the European Union, where advertising and labelling laws are strict. Option 1: open its own shops in Germany. Option 2: license a German tea company to pack and sell the tea under the Sukoon name.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways laws may control Sukoon Herbal Teas' marketing in the European Union.
parts.answer: 1. Laws against misleading advertising: Sukoon cannot claim the tea 'cures' headaches unless this is proved, so its adverts must change, which may weaken its main selling point. 2. Labelling and food-safety laws: packs must show ingredients, weight and allergy information correctly, which may need new packaging and testing and raises costs. (Also: rules on product safety, weights and measures, consumer rights to refunds.)
parts.working: For each way (max 4 each): 1 mark identify the legal control; 1 mark apply to Sukoon's tea or its 'cures' claim; 2 marks explain the effect on Sukoon's marketing or costs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recommend which option Sukoon Herbal Teas should choose to enter the German market. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Licensing: low cost and risk; the German company already knows EU labelling laws and has distribution to shops, and Sukoon receives royalties. But it loses control of quality and receives only a share of the profit. Own shops: full control and all the profit, but very expensive, slow, and Sukoon lacks local knowledge. Recommendation: licensing at first, with strict quality terms in the contract, because it reduces legal and financial risk in an unfamiliar market.
parts.working: Content: licensing — low cost and risk, German partner knows EU labelling laws and has distribution, royalties, but less control of quality and only a share of profit; own shops — full control and all the profit, but very expensive, slow and lacks local knowledge; strict quality terms in a licence contract. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Sukoon Herbal Teas, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Sukoon Herbal Teas, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
stem: Golden Crust is a bakery in Hyderabad that makes bread and cakes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'fixed costs'.
parts.answer: Costs that do not change with the level of output in the short run, e.g. rent.
parts.working: 1 mark: do not vary with output; 1 mark: short run / example such as rent, salaries, insurance (must be linked).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two variable costs for Golden Crust.
parts.answer: Any two: flour, sugar, eggs, butter, packaging, electricity/gas for ovens (if per batch), wages paid per item.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept rent or managers' salaries.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
stem: Kite Masters makes kites for the spring festival season. Fixed costs are $18,000 per season. Each kite sells for $12 and has variable costs of $7. It expects to sell 5,000 kites.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the break-even level of output.
parts.answer: 3,600 kites
parts.working: Contribution per kite = 12 − 7 = $5 (M1). Break-even = 18,000 ÷ 5 = 3,600 kites (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the margin of safety.
parts.answer: 1,400 kites
parts.working: Margin of safety = expected sales − break-even output (M1) = 5,000 − 3,600 = 1,400 kites (A1).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
stem: Coastal Nets makes fishing nets in Gwadar. Its fixed costs are $50,000 a year and its variable cost is $20 per net. It makes 5,000 nets a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average cost per net.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline two economies of scale Coastal Nets could gain if it grew larger.
parts.answer: 1. Purchasing economies: buying nylon thread in bulk gives discounts, lowering cost per net. 2. Technical economies: it can afford faster net-making machines that produce more nets per hour. (Also: financial economies – cheaper loans; marketing economies – advertising cost spread over more nets; managerial economies – specialist managers.)
parts.working: For each of two economies: 1 mark identify + 1 mark outline applied to Coastal Nets.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
stem: Desert Rose makes scented candles in Bahawalpur. Each candle sells for Rs 450 and has variable costs of Rs 270. Fixed costs are Rs 900,000 a year. Next year it expects to sell 7,000 candles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected profit next year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the break-even level of output.
parts.answer: 5,000 candles

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one limitation of break-even analysis for Desert Rose.
parts.answer: It assumes all candles made are sold at the same price, but Desert Rose may have unsold candles or give discounts, so actual break-even could be higher.
parts.working: 1 mark: limitation (assumes all output sold / constant price / costs stay constant / straight-line costs / only as good as forecast data). 1 mark: explanation applied to Desert Rose.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
stem: Threadline Ltd is a garment exporter in Faisalabad. In three years it has grown from 80 to 900 workers and opened two more factories.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two diseconomies of scale Threadline Ltd might experience.
parts.answer: 1. Poor communication: with 900 workers across three factories, messages pass through many levels and arrive late or distorted, so mistakes in orders for foreign buyers increase and costs rise. 2. Low worker motivation: workers feel unimportant in a large firm and managers rarely see them, so absenteeism and labour turnover rise and productivity falls. (Also: weak coordination between factories / slow decision-making.)
parts.working: For each: 1 mark identify, 1 mark application to Threadline, 1 mark development showing average costs rise.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
stem: Sun Shade makes garden umbrellas. It sells each umbrella for $80; variable cost is $50 per umbrella and fixed costs are $120,000 a year. It expects to sell 6,000 umbrellas. The manager is considering raising the price to $90, which market research suggests would reduce sales to 5,200 umbrellas.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Should Sun Shade raise its price to $90? Justify your answer using suitable calculations (for example, the break-even output and expected profit at each price).
parts.answer: Calculations: At $80: break-even 4,000, profit $60,000. At $90: break-even 3,000, profit $88,000. Yes, probably: profit rises from $60,000 to $88,000, break-even falls from 4,000 to 3,000 and the margin of safety rises from 2,000 to 2,200. But the forecast fall in sales may be wrong; if rivals keep lower prices, sales could fall more, and lower sales could cost market share in the long term. Judgement: raise the price if the research is reliable, and monitor sales.
parts.working: Calculations: $80: 120,000 ÷ 30 = 4,000; 30 × 6,000 − 120,000 = $60,000. $90: 120,000 ÷ 40 = 3,000; 40 × 5,200 − 120,000 = $88,000. Content: $80: break-even 4,000, profit $60,000, margin of safety 2,000; $90: break-even 3,000, profit $88,000, margin of safety 2,200; reliability of the market-research forecast; rivals' prices; market share in the long term. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Sun Shade, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Sun Shade, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
stem: Pure Pour bottles mineral water in Murree and sells each case for $25. It must choose a new bottling machine. Machine A: fixed costs $200,000 a year, variable cost $15 per case. Machine B (more automated): fixed costs $320,000 a year, variable cost $9 per case. Expected sales are 30,000 cases a year, but sales vary a lot with the weather.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Recommend which bottling machine Pure Pour should buy. Justify your answer using suitable calculations (for example, the break-even output and expected annual profit for each machine).
parts.answer: Calculations: A: break-even 20,000 cases, profit $100,000. B: break-even 20,000 cases, profit $160,000. Both break even at 20,000 cases, but above that B earns $16 per case instead of $10, so at 30,000 cases B gives $60,000 more profit. Risk: below 20,000 cases B makes bigger losses (higher fixed costs), and sales depend on weather. Unless sales are likely to fall below 20,000, choose B; it may also need fewer workers, though breakdowns of an automated machine could stop production.
parts.working: Calculations: A: 200,000 ÷ (25 − 15) = 20,000; 10 × 30,000 − 200,000 = $100,000. B: 320,000 ÷ (25 − 9) = 20,000; 16 × 30,000 − 320,000 = $160,000. Content: both break even at 20,000 cases; profit A $100,000, B $160,000 at 30,000 cases; contribution $10 v $16 per case; B's higher fixed costs mean bigger losses below break-even; weather makes sales uncertain; automation — fewer workers, breakdown risk. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Pure Pour, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Pure Pour, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
stem:
Aroma Kitchenware can make only one new product next year. Appendix:
Item | Rice cooker liner (X) | Pressure cooker (Y)
Selling price ($) | 15 | 40
Variable cost per unit ($) | 9 | 22
Fixed costs ($) | 48,000 | 135,000
Forecast sales (units) | 12,000 | 9,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the appendix, recommend which product Aroma Kitchenware should make. Justify your answer using suitable calculations (for example, break-even output, margin of safety and expected profit for each product).
parts.answer: Calculations: X: break-even 8,000, margin of safety 4,000, profit $24,000. Y: break-even 7,500, margin of safety 1,500, profit $27,000. Y gives slightly more profit ($27,000 v $24,000), but its margin of safety is only 1,500 units (17% of forecast) compared with 4,000 (33%) for X. If sales are 20% below forecast, X still makes a profit (9,600 units → $9,600) but Y makes a loss (7,200 units → −$5,400). X is the safer choice unless the forecast for Y is very reliable; the extra $3,000 profit from Y is small for the extra risk.
parts.working: Calculations: X: contribution $6; 48,000 ÷ 6 = 8,000; 12,000 − 8,000 = 4,000; 6 × 12,000 − 48,000 = $24,000. Y: contribution $18; 135,000 ÷ 18 = 7,500; 9,000 − 7,500 = 1,500; 18 × 9,000 − 135,000 = $27,000. Content: X break-even 8,000, margin of safety 4,000 (33%), profit $24,000; Y break-even 7,500, margin of safety 1,500 (17%), profit $27,000; if sales are 20% below forecast X still profits, Y makes a loss; reliability of forecasts; fit with existing range. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Aroma Kitchenware, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Aroma Kitchenware, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
stem: Sara is opening a small café in Gilgit. Her weekly fixed costs are Rs 42,000. Each meal sells for Rs 600 and costs Rs 250 in ingredients and packaging.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many meals Sara must sell each week to break even.
parts.answer: 120 meals

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think a break-even chart would be useful to Sara when she opens her café? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Useful: shows how many meals she needs to sell (120 a week) and the profit or loss at different sales levels; helps her see the effect of changing prices or costs, and supports a loan application. Limitations: assumes all food prepared is sold and every meal sells at the same price, but cafés waste food and offer different meals; costs (e.g. ingredient prices) change; tourist demand in Gilgit is seasonal, so weekly sales vary. Judgement: useful as a planning guide for a new business, but she should update it and not rely on it alone.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks knowledge, up to 2 marks analysis (developed consequences), up to 2 marks evaluation (justified judgement that weighs both sides for this business).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
stem: Oak & Pine makes wooden chairs in Nairobi, Kenya.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether each of these costs is fixed or variable: (i) rent of the workshop, (ii) wood for each chair, (iii) insurance, (iv) paint for each chair.
parts.answer: (i) fixed (ii) variable (iii) fixed (iv) variable
parts.working: 2 marks for all four correct; 1 mark for two or three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Monthly fixed costs are $15,000 and the variable cost is $35 per chair. Calculate the total cost of making 600 chairs in a month.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
stem: FreshMart has grown from one supermarket to a chain of 40 supermarkets across Pakistan. In its central bakery, output rose from 10,000 loaves a week (total cost Rs 400,000) to 25,000 loaves a week (total cost Rs 750,000).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'economies of scale'.
parts.answer: The factors that cause average (unit) costs to fall as a business increases its scale of production.
parts.working: 1 mark: average/unit costs fall; 1 mark: as output/size of the business increases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average cost per loaf before and after the increase in output.
parts.answer: Before Rs 40; after Rs 30

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why FreshMart may be able to charge lower prices than a small corner shop.
parts.answer: FreshMart buys in bulk for 40 stores, so suppliers give large discounts (purchasing economies); it can borrow more cheaply and spread advertising over many stores. Lower average costs mean it can charge lower prices and still make a profit, whereas a corner shop buys in small quantities at higher unit cost.
parts.working: 1 mark per relevant economy identified (up to 2) + up to 2 marks for explaining the link from lower average cost to lower prices, with application.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Saba Ceramics makes floor tiles. Last month 40 workers produced 12,000 boxes of tiles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'productivity'.
parts.answer: A measure of the efficiency of inputs: output per unit of input, e.g. output per worker in a time period.
parts.working: 1 mark: output compared with inputs; 1 mark: e.g. output per worker per period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate labour productivity for last month.
parts.answer: 300 boxes per worker
parts.working: Labour productivity = output ÷ number of workers (M1) = 12,000 ÷ 40 = 300 boxes per worker per month (A1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Three businesses in Lahore use different methods of production.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the most suitable method of production (job, batch or flow) for each business: (i) a tailor making wedding dresses to each customer's design; (ii) a bakery making 200 loaves of brown bread, then 200 loaves of white bread; (iii) a factory filling soft-drink bottles 24 hours a day.
parts.answer: (i) job (ii) batch (iii) flow
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one disadvantage of flow production.
parts.answer: e.g. Very high cost of machinery: the business needs large, steady demand to cover it; or boring, repetitive work lowers worker motivation; or a breakdown at one stage stops the whole line; or products are standardised.
parts.working: 1 mark identify + 1 mark outline.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Rehman Rice Mills processes and packs rice in Gujranwala. Its manager wants to increase productivity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline two ways Rehman Rice Mills could increase productivity.
parts.answer: 1. Train workers so they operate the husking and packing machines faster with fewer mistakes. 2. Buy more automated packing machines, so more bags are packed per worker per hour. (Also: improve motivation, e.g. bonuses; better organisation/lean production; reduce machine breakdowns with maintenance.)
parts.working: For each of two ways: 1 mark identify + 1 mark outline applied to the rice mill.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Sahil Motors assembles cars in Karachi. It is thinking of introducing just-in-time (JIT) inventory control, so that parts arrive from suppliers only when needed on the assembly line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'lean production'.
parts.answer: Techniques used to reduce waste of all kinds (e.g. time, materials, inventory) in production and so increase efficiency.
parts.working: 1 mark: reducing waste; 1 mark: to improve efficiency / lower costs (or examples JIT, kaizen).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of JIT for Sahil Motors.
parts.answer: Advantage: little money is tied up in inventory of parts and less warehouse space is needed, so costs fall and cash is available for other uses. Disadvantage: if a supplier delivers late (e.g. imported parts delayed at the port or by strikes), the assembly line stops, cars are not finished and customers wait, so sales are lost.
parts.working: Advantage: 1 identify, 1 application, 1 development. Disadvantage: 1 identify, 1 application, 1 development.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Chenab Bicycles makes bicycle frames. In Year 1, 60 workers produced 48,000 frames. In Year 2, after new welding equipment was installed, 65 workers produced 54,600 frames.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate labour productivity in each year.
parts.answer: Year 1: 800 frames per worker; Year 2: 840 frames per worker

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in labour productivity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why higher productivity is important for Chenab Bicycles.
parts.answer: More frames per worker means lower labour cost per frame (average costs fall). Chenab can then cut prices to compete with imported bicycles, or keep prices and earn a higher profit margin; it may also afford higher wages, improving motivation.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower average/unit costs. 1 mark application. Up to 2 marks development: more competitive prices, higher profit, higher wages, faster delivery to customers.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Golden Biscuits Ltd makes biscuits using batch production: one oven line makes one type for a few hours, then is cleaned and changed to another type. Demand for its best-selling biscuit has grown so much that the line runs that type nearly all the time. The directors are considering a new flow-production line for this biscuit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two benefits to Golden Biscuits Ltd of using flow production for its best-selling biscuit.
parts.answer: 1. Lower average costs: machines run continuously without stopping for cleaning and changeover, and ingredients can be bought in bulk, so each biscuit costs less and prices can be competitive. 2. Higher output and consistent quality: an automated line makes identical biscuits quickly, so the firm can meet growing demand without losing sales.
parts.working: For each benefit (max 4 each): 1 mark identify; 1 mark apply to the biscuit factory (changeovers, high demand); 2 marks develop the consequence (costs, profit, meeting demand).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recommend whether Golden Biscuits Ltd should introduce flow production for this biscuit. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Yes, if demand stays high: the line already runs this biscuit almost constantly, so flow production uses the equipment fully and cuts unit costs. Risks: high cost of the new line; if tastes change, a dedicated line is inflexible; workers may find tasks repetitive. Because demand is large and stable, the cost savings and output are likely to outweigh the risk; keep batch production for the other types.
parts.working: Content: line already runs this biscuit almost constantly, so flow uses equipment fully and cuts unit costs; high cost of the new line; inflexible if tastes change; repetitive work and motivation; keep batch production for other types; level and stability of demand. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Golden Biscuits Ltd, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Golden Biscuits Ltd, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Pak Packaging Ltd makes cardboard boxes. It is considering buying an automated cutting machine costing $500,000. The machine would reduce the number of production workers from 50 to 30. Each worker is paid $12,000 a year. The factory is the main employer in a small town.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual saving in wages and the number of years of wage savings needed to cover the cost of the machine. Give the number of years to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Saving $240,000 a year; 2.1 years

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think Pak Packaging Ltd should buy the automated machine? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: wage costs fall by $240,000 a year, so the machine pays for itself in about 2.1 years; cutting is faster and more accurate, so quality and output improve. Against: 20 workers lose their jobs in a town where the firm is the main employer – bad publicity, lower morale among remaining workers, possible union action; redundancy pay; machine needs maintenance and skilled operators. Judgement: buy it, since the payback is short, but reduce the impact by retraining some workers to operate and maintain the machine or by natural wastage.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks knowledge, up to 2 marks analysis (developed consequences), up to 2 marks evaluation (justified judgement that weighs both sides for this business).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Al-Noor Pharmacy controls its inventory of a common painkiller. The maximum inventory level is 900 packs, the reorder level is 400 packs and the buffer inventory is 200 packs. It sells 100 packs a day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the lead time (the number of days between placing an order and receiving it) if the order arrives just as inventory falls to the buffer level.
parts.answer: 2 days
parts.working: Inventory used during lead time = 400 − 200 = 200 packs (M1). 200 ÷ 100 = 2 days (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many packs should be ordered each time so that inventory returns to the maximum level when the order arrives.
parts.answer: 700 packs
parts.working: Order quantity = maximum − buffer (M1) = 900 − 200 = 700 packs (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one problem for Al-Noor Pharmacy of holding too much inventory and one problem of holding too little.
parts.answer: Too much: cash is tied up and medicines may pass their expiry date and have to be thrown away; storage costs rise. Too little: the pharmacy may run out, so patients go to another pharmacy and it loses sales and goodwill.
parts.working: Too much: 1 identify + 1 explain (opportunity cost of cash, expiry/waste, storage, theft). Too little: 1 identify + 1 explain (stock-outs, lost sales/customers, cannot meet sudden demand).

author: HomiLabs

stem: City Care Hospital's pharmacy often has long queues, and staff spend time searching for medicines on badly organised shelves. The manager wants to introduce kaizen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'kaizen'.
parts.answer: Continuous improvement through many small changes, usually suggested by workers themselves.
parts.working: 1 mark: continuous improvement; 1 mark: small changes / ideas from workers (teams).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think kaizen will improve the efficiency of the hospital pharmacy? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Likely yes: staff know the problems best and can suggest small changes, e.g. reorganising shelves so common medicines are near the counter, labelling, or a separate queue for collecting repeat prescriptions; queues and wasted time fall at little cost, and staff feel valued. But it takes time and needs managers to listen and staff to be willing; it will not solve major problems such as too few pharmacists. Judgement: it should improve efficiency if managers support it and act on suggestions.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks knowledge, up to 2 marks analysis (developed consequences), up to 2 marks evaluation (justified judgement that weighs both sides for this business).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Chiniot Furniture makes hand-carved beds using many skilled craftsmen. Lahore Steel makes steel sheets using large automated rolling machines and few workers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between labour-intensive and capital-intensive production, using these two businesses as examples.
parts.answer: Labour-intensive production uses a large amount of labour relative to capital (Chiniot Furniture – skilled carvers, few machines). Capital-intensive production uses a large amount of machinery relative to labour (Lahore Steel – automated rolling machines, few workers).
parts.working: 1 mark each definition (2) + 1 mark each correctly linked example (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline two benefits to Lahore Steel of using technology in production.
parts.answer: 1. Higher productivity: machines produce more sheets per hour than workers could, lowering average costs. 2. Consistent quality: computer-controlled machines give the same thickness every time, reducing waste and rejected sheets. (Also: lower labour costs; can operate 24 hours; safer for workers.)
parts.working: For each of two benefits: 1 mark identify + 1 mark outline applied to Lahore Steel.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two businesses are choosing where to locate: a clothing shop and a brick-making factory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two factors that affect the location of the clothing shop.
parts.answer: Any two: footfall/number of customers passing; nearness to competitors or other shops; rent; parking/transport access; security; visibility.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline two factors that affect the location of the brick-making factory.
parts.answer: 1. Nearness to raw materials: clay is heavy and costly to transport, so a site near clay deposits cuts costs. 2. Availability and cost of land: brick kilns need large areas and are best away from homes because of smoke. (Also: transport links to building sites; supply of labour; planning rules; energy supply.)
parts.working: For each of two factors: 1 mark identify + 1 mark outline applied to brick-making.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Thread World Ltd makes T-shirts in a factory in the UK. Its directors are thinking of moving production to Bangladesh.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Thread World Ltd might relocate its factory to Bangladesh.
parts.answer: 1. Lower wage costs: garment workers in Bangladesh earn much less than in the UK, so labour cost per T-shirt falls and the firm can cut prices or raise profit. 2. Closer to raw materials and suppliers: cotton fabric and garment suppliers are nearby, lowering transport costs and delivery times. (Also: government incentives/export zones; large workforce with garment skills; avoid UK rules or costs; access to Asian markets.)
parts.working: For each reason: 1 mark identify, 1 mark application, 1 mark development.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Fresh Pack Ltd packs dried fruit for export through Karachi port. It needs a new warehouse with 40 workers. Appendix: annual costs (Rs).
Item | Site A (Hub, inland) | Site B (near Karachi port)
Rent | 1,800,000 | 1,200,000
Wage per worker | 420,000 | 480,000
Transport costs | 2,400,000 | 900,000
Other information: Site A is close to fruit farms in Balochistan; Site B is in a busy industrial area with many skilled workers but traffic congestion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the appendix, recommend which site Fresh Pack Ltd should choose for its new warehouse. Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Calculations: Site A: Rs 21,000,000; Site B: Rs 21,300,000. The costs are very close (A is Rs 300,000 cheaper, about 1.4%), so other factors decide. Site A is near the fruit farms, so fresh supplies arrive quickly and wages are lower, but it is further from the port and transport costs are much higher, and fuel price rises would hurt. Site B is near the port, has skilled workers and lower transport costs, but congestion may delay shipments. Recommendation: either with justification, e.g. B, because export deadlines and skilled packing workers matter more than a 1.4% cost difference, and transport costs are the most likely to rise.
parts.working: Calculations: A: 1,800,000 + 40 × 420,000 + 2,400,000 = Rs 21,000,000. B: 1,200,000 + 40 × 480,000 + 900,000 = Rs 21,300,000. Content: total annual cost A Rs 21.0 m, B Rs 21.3 m (difference Rs 300,000, about 1.4%); A near fruit farms with lower wages and rent v higher transport costs; B near the port with skilled workers and low transport costs v congestion delays; export deadlines; fuel price risk. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Fresh Pack Ltd, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Fresh Pack Ltd, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
SolarWave plc makes solar panels in Germany and wants to build a factory in Asia employing 200 workers. Appendix:
Factor | Country P | Country Q
Average monthly wage ($) | 310 | 460
Import tariff on solar panels in that country | 0% | 25%
Government grant for new factories | none | $500,000
Size of local solar market | small | large and growing
Political stability | some unrest | stable

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the appendix, recommend which country SolarWave plc should choose for its new factory. Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Calculations: $360,000 a year (Q is more expensive). Country Q: although wages cost $360,000 a year more, the grant of $500,000 covers well over one year of the difference; the large, growing market means panels can be sold locally, and making them inside the country avoids the 25% tariff that imported panels would face. Political stability reduces the risk of disruption. Country P has lower wages and no tariff barrier to worry about, but a small market and unrest. Recommendation: Q, because market access and stability outweigh the higher wage bill.
parts.working: Calculations: Difference per worker per month = 460 − 310 = $150; 150 × 12 × 200 = $360,000. Content: wage bill difference $360,000 a year (Q dearer); $500,000 grant in Q covers more than one year of the difference; 25% tariff in Q protects panels made inside Q; large, growing market in Q v small market in P; political stability v unrest. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to SolarWave plc, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to SolarWave plc, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

author: HomiLabs

stem: BrightCall Ltd plans to open a call centre that answers customer enquiries for banks. It is choosing between a large city and a smaller town where the government offers a tax break to new employers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two factors BrightCall Ltd should consider when choosing the location. Which factor is likely to be the most important? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: 1. Availability of skilled labour: staff need good communication and IT skills; a large city has more graduates, but wages are higher. 2. Government incentives: the tax break in the smaller town lowers costs and raises profit. (Also: reliable internet/electricity, rent.) Judgement: labour is most important, because a call centre's service quality depends on its staff; a tax break is of little use if it cannot recruit enough skilled workers, though if the town has a college the incentive could tip the decision.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks knowledge of two factors; up to 2 marks analysis applied to a call centre; up to 2 marks evaluation choosing one with a reason why it beats the other.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways a government might influence location decisions.
parts.answer: Any two: grants or subsidies; tax breaks; planning permission/refusing permission; building infrastructure (roads, internet); special economic zones; laws restricting location (e.g. pollution).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Swat Honey Co. collects, filters and bottles honey for sale in supermarkets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'quality assurance'.
parts.answer: A system of checking quality at every stage of production, so that standards are met and faults are prevented rather than found at the end.
parts.working: 1 mark: checking at every stage of production; 1 mark: to prevent faults/meet agreed standards (involves all workers).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two benefits to Swat Honey Co. of producing high-quality products.
parts.answer: Any two: good reputation/brand image; customer loyalty and repeat sales; can charge higher prices; fewer complaints/returns; less waste; supermarkets more willing to stock it.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: MediLab Pharmaceuticals makes tablets. At present inspectors test samples at the end of production. Last week 4,800 boxes were made and 120 boxes were rejected.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of boxes rejected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between quality control and quality assurance. Do you think MediLab should change to quality assurance? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Quality control: inspectors check finished products (or samples) at the end and remove faulty ones. Quality assurance: every worker checks quality at each stage, preventing faults. For MediLab, faulty medicines are dangerous; 2.5% rejects is costly waste, and sampling may miss faults that reach patients. QA cuts waste and risk, but needs training and time. Judgement: yes, because for medicines safety and reputation are critical; keep some final testing too.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks: correct difference (end inspection v at every stage/prevention). Up to 2 marks: analysis applied to medicines and the reject rate. Up to 2 marks: justified judgement.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The Pearl Hotel in Gwadar has received many online complaints about slow room service, dirty rooms and rude staff.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two benefits to The Pearl Hotel of introducing total quality management (TQM).
parts.answer: 1. Every member of staff, from cleaners to receptionists, becomes responsible for quality and treats other staff and guests as customers, so problems such as dirty rooms are fixed before guests see them; complaints fall. 2. Better reputation: improved online reviews attract more guests, raising occupancy and allowing higher room rates. (Also: less waste/costs of putting things right; staff more motivated by involvement.)
parts.working: For each benefit: 1 mark identify, 1 mark application to the hotel, 1 mark development.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hamza Garments makes 25,000 shirts a month. 3.2% of shirts are faulty and must be thrown away; each faulty shirt costs Rs 650 to make. A quality-training course for all workers costs Rs 250,000. The training company says it will reduce the fault rate to 1.4%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Should Hamza Garments pay for the training course? Justify your answer using suitable calculations (for example, the number of faulty shirts before and after training and the monthly saving).
parts.answer: Calculations: Before 800; after 350; saving Rs 292,500 per month. Yes: the monthly saving of Rs 292,500 is more than the one-off cost of Rs 250,000, so the training pays for itself in under a month; fewer faults also improve reputation with buyers, and trained workers may feel more valued. But the fault rate of 1.4% is only the training company's claim; workers may forget the training or leave; production time is lost during the course. Judgement: pay for it, as even a much smaller improvement would cover the cost, but monitor fault rates afterwards.
parts.working: Calculations: 3.2% × 25,000 = 800; 1.4% × 25,000 = 350; (800 − 350) × 650 = Rs 292,500. Content: faulty shirts 800 → 350 a month; saving Rs 292,500 a month v one-off cost Rs 250,000 (pays back in under a month); reputation with buyers, motivation; reliability of the training company's claim, staff turnover, lost production time; monitoring fault rates. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Hamza Garments, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Hamza Garments, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Marvi Bank is opening a new branch in Hyderabad and has just hired 14 new customer service staff.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'induction training'.
parts.answer: Training given to new employees when they start a job to introduce them to the business, its people, rules and procedures.
parts.working: 1 mark: training for new employees. 1 mark: introduces the business, e.g. layout, colleagues, health and safety, policies.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two benefits to Marvi Bank of giving induction training to the new staff.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. new staff become productive more quickly; they make fewer mistakes with customers; they feel welcome so are less likely to leave; they learn safety and security rules.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid benefits.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Shalimar Grand Hotel in Karachi needs to recruit a new receptionist. The HR manager is preparing a job description and a person specification.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two items that would be included in the job description for the receptionist.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. job title; main duties and tasks (checking guests in and out, answering phone calls); hours of work; who the receptionist reports to; place of work.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two items. Do not accept qualities of the person (they belong in the person specification).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two items that would be included in the person specification for the receptionist.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. qualifications required; experience needed; skills such as good spoken English and Urdu; personal qualities such as being polite and well presented.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two items describing the ideal candidate.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Crust & Crumb is a bakery in Rawalpindi. It employs 4 part-time sales assistants who each work 25 hours a week. Each is paid PKR 450 per hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the bakery's total weekly wage cost for the part-time sales assistants. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two methods the bakery could use to recruit new part-time sales assistants, and explain why each is suitable for a small bakery.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) A notice in the shop window: costs almost nothing and is seen by local people, such as students and parents, who may want part-time hours nearby. 2) Word of mouth / recommendation by current staff: free and quick, and current staff can suggest reliable people. Other: local social media group or community page (cheap, reaches local people); local newspaper (wider reach but costs more).
parts.working: For each of two methods: 1 mark for a suitable method, 1 mark for explaining why it suits a small local bakery (e.g. low cost, reaches local applicants). Do not credit expensive methods such as recruitment agencies or national newspapers unless justified.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Al-Noor Textiles has closed one of its weaving sheds because demand for its cloth has fallen. It has also sacked one worker who was repeatedly late.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'dismissal'.
parts.answer: When an employee is made to leave their job because of their own fault, such as poor behaviour, breaking rules or poor performance.
parts.working: 1 mark: employment ended by the employer. 1 mark: because of the employee's conduct or performance (not because the job is no longer needed).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two reasons why a business might make workers redundant.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. fall in demand for the product; a factory or branch closes; machines/automation replace workers; the business relocates; a merger creates duplicate jobs.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two reasons where the job itself is no longer needed.

author: HomiLabs

stem: FreshMart is a supermarket chain with 18 stores in Islamabad and Rawalpindi. It needs a new store manager for its largest branch. The HR director wants to promote one of the current assistant managers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two methods FreshMart could use to recruit externally.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. job advertisements in newspapers; online job websites; recruitment agencies; university job fairs; social media.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two advantages to FreshMart of recruiting the store manager internally.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) The assistant manager already knows FreshMart's systems, suppliers and customers, so needs little induction and can run the busy branch quickly, keeping sales high. 2) Promotion opportunities motivate other assistant managers across the 18 stores, which may reduce labour turnover and recruitment costs. Other: cheaper and quicker than advertising; the business already knows the candidate's ability and reliability.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point). Application must refer to FreshMart, e.g. 18 stores, largest branch, supermarket.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Spice Route is a busy restaurant in Dubai. It is open from 11:00 to 23:00, and most customers come at lunchtime and in the evening. The owner is deciding whether to replace three full-time waiters with six part-time waiters.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'part-time employee'.
parts.answer: An employee who works fewer hours per week than a full-time employee (for example fewer than about 30–35 hours).
parts.working: 1 mark: works for the business. 1 mark: fewer hours than full-time / a normal working week.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to Spice Route of employing part-time waiters.
parts.answer: Advantage: part-time waiters can be scheduled only at the lunch and evening peaks, so the restaurant does not pay staff during the quiet afternoon, lowering wage costs per meal. Disadvantage: six part-time waiters may be less committed and need more training and supervision, so service quality may fall and customers may not return.
parts.working: Advantage: 1 identify, 1 apply, 1 develop. Disadvantage: 1 identify, 1 apply, 1 develop. Other disadvantages: harder to communicate with more staff; more recruitment cost; staff may leave for full-time work.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Pak Packaging Ltd employs 25 workers who are all paid the minimum wage. The government has announced that the monthly minimum wage will rise from PKR 37,000 to PKR 40,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the increase in Pak Packaging's monthly wage bill for these 25 workers. Show your working.
parts.answer: PKR 75,000 per month

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two other legal controls over employment that affect businesses.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. health and safety at work laws; laws against discrimination (for example by gender or religion); laws on maximum working hours; rules on unfair dismissal; employment contract requirements.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two ways the rise in the minimum wage could affect Pak Packaging.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Higher costs: the wage bill rises by PKR 75,000 a month, which reduces profit unless the firm raises the prices of its boxes. 2) Motivation: workers may feel better rewarded, so they may work harder and fewer may leave, which reduces recruitment costs.
parts.working: For each of two points: 1 mark for the effect, 1 mark for development in context. Other: may replace workers with machines; may recruit fewer staff.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Sindh Snacks makes crisps in a factory in Hyderabad. It needs a production supervisor for a shift of 30 workers. Appendix 1 shows the two shortlisted applicants.
Appendix 1
Applicant A – Amina: internal applicant; machine operator at Sindh Snacks for 8 years; no supervisory experience; has led the factory's safety committee; Intermediate certificate; expected salary PKR 95,000 per month.
Applicant B – Bilal: external applicant; BSc Food Science; 3 years as a shift supervisor at a soft-drinks company; would need to move from Multan; expected salary PKR 120,000 per month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which applicant should Sindh Snacks choose as production supervisor? Justify your answer using suitable calculations and Appendix 1.
parts.answer: Calculations: PKR 300,000 per year (Bilal costs more). Amina: knows the machines, workers and procedures; cheaper by PKR 300,000 a year; safety committee shows leadership; promotion motivates other operators. But no supervisory experience and fewer qualifications; may find it hard to manage former colleagues. Bilal: has 3 years of supervisory experience and food science knowledge which may improve quality; brings new ideas. But costs more, needs induction, may not stay if relocation fails. Judgement e.g. Amina, because she knows the factory and the shift workers, and the saving can pay for supervisory training, which reduces the main risk.
parts.working: Calculations: (120,000 − 95,000) = 25,000 per month. 25,000 × 12 = PKR 300,000. Content: Bilal costs PKR 300,000 a year more; Amina — internal, knows machines and workers, safety committee leadership, motivates others, but no supervisory experience and may struggle to manage former colleagues; Bilal — 3 years' supervisory experience and food-science degree, new ideas, but dearer, needs induction and relocation. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Sindh Snacks, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Sindh Snacks, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
CodeNest is a software company in Bengaluru, India. It has hired 12 new junior developers. It is considering two ways to train them in its programming systems.
Option A – off-the-job course at a training institute: fee $850 per person, and each developer misses 5 working days. The company values a developer's lost working day at $120.
Option B – on-the-job training by a senior developer: the senior developer is paid an extra $1,500 in total, and the company estimates that the senior developer's own lost output is worth $2,400.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Option B costs $3,900. Which option should CodeNest choose to train its new developers? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Calculations: $17,400. Option B is $13,500 cheaper and the training is directly related to CodeNest's own systems and projects; developers keep producing while learning. However, the senior developer's bad habits may be passed on, and his own work suffers. Option A gives expert, structured training and possibly recognised qualifications, but costs more and developers are away for 5 days. Judgement, e.g. Option B because CodeNest's systems are specific to the company, so an outside course may not cover them, and the saving of $13,500 is large.
parts.working: Calculations: cost per person = 850 + 5 × 120 = $1,450. 12 × 1,450 = $17,400. Content: Option A costs 12 × (850 + 5 × 120) = $17,400, so B is $13,500 cheaper; B uses CodeNest's own systems and developers keep working, but the senior developer's output falls and bad habits may pass on; A gives expert, structured training and possibly qualifications, but costs more and developers miss 5 days. author: HomiLabs

stem: Medicare Pharmacies has 40 branches in Pakistan. When a branch manager leaves, head office always advertises the job externally.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two stages of the recruitment and selection process after a vacancy has been advertised.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. receiving application forms/CVs; shortlisting applicants; interviewing; testing (skills or aptitude tests); checking references; offering the job/contract of employment.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think Medicare Pharmacies should always recruit branch managers externally? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: brings new ideas and experience from other retailers; wider choice of applicants, e.g. qualified pharmacists; avoids jealousy between internal candidates. Against: more expensive and slower (advertising, interviews); new manager needs induction and does not know the 40-branch systems; existing staff are demotivated if they never get promotion, so good pharmacists may leave. Judgement, e.g. no – recruit internally where a suitable assistant manager exists, and only go external when no one has the skills, because promotion chances keep experienced staff.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Chenab Weaving in Faisalabad plans to buy automated looms costing PKR 30 million. The new looms would replace 40 workers. Each worker earns PKR 45,000 per month, and each would receive a redundancy payment equal to 3 months' pay. The new looms would cost PKR 9 million a year to run and maintain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Should Chenab Weaving buy the automated looms? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Calculations: PKR 5,400,000. Annual wage saving = 40 × 45,000 × 12 = PKR 21.6 million; net saving after running costs = 21.6 − 9 = PKR 12.6 million a year, so the PKR 35.4 million total cost (30 m looms + 5.4 m redundancy) is covered in under 3 years. Looms may also improve quality and output. Against: large outlay may need a loan; remaining workers may be demotivated or strike; bad publicity locally; staff need training to use looms. Judgement with reasoning, e.g. buy, because the cost is recovered in about 2.8 years, but communicate with workers and the union first.
parts.working: Calculations: 3 × 45,000 = 135,000 per worker. 135,000 × 40 = PKR 5,400,000. Content: redundancy pay PKR 5.4 m; wage saving 40 × 45,000 × 12 = PKR 21.6 m a year; net saving PKR 12.6 m a year after running costs; total outlay PKR 35.4 m recovered in about 2.8 years; quality and output; loan finance; morale, union action, local reputation, training. stem: BrightAds is a small advertising agency in Lahore with 15 creative staff who design advertising campaigns. Its manager currently uses an autocratic style.

stem: StarLink Contact Centre in Manila, Philippines, has many staff leaving within a year. Staff say the work is repetitive and boring, although the pay is above average.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using Herzberg's theory, explain why the above-average pay is not stopping staff from leaving.
parts.answer: Pay is a hygiene factor: good pay prevents dissatisfaction but does not motivate; staff need motivators such as interesting work, recognition and responsibility.
parts.working: 1 mark: pay is a hygiene factor. 1 mark: hygiene factors only remove dissatisfaction / motivators are missing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two non-financial methods StarLink could use to motivate staff. Which method is most likely to reduce the number of staff leaving? Justify your answer.

Job enrichment: staff are given more responsibility, e.g. solving complaints themselves, which gives a sense of achievement (a Herzberg motivator), but needs training. Other: teamworking, training and promotion opportunities, recognition schemes. Judgement, e.g. job enrichment, because the problem is boring work and enrichment adds the motivators Herzberg says are missing, whereas rotation only varies equally simple tasks.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for each method (knowledge + analysis). 2 marks for a justified choice that explains why the other method is less effective.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A government is deciding whether to build a new international airport outside a city. The following effects have been identified:
1 Construction cost paid by the airport company
2 Noise for families living nearby
3 New jobs for local people in hotels and taxis
4 Wages paid by the airport company to its own staff
5 Loss of farmland and wildlife habitat
6 Shorter journey times for business travellers from the whole region

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each of the six effects as a private cost, an external cost, or an external benefit.
parts.answer: Private costs: 1 and 4. External costs: 2 and 5. External benefits: 3 and 6.
parts.working: 4 marks for all six correct; 3 marks for five; 2 marks for four; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the government might approve the airport even though it creates external costs.
parts.answer: The government considers the total social costs and benefits; if the external benefits (jobs, faster travel, growth) plus private benefits are greater than all the costs, society as a whole gains.
parts.working: 1 mark: compare social benefits with social costs. 1 mark: development, e.g. benefits outweigh costs so society gains.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Green Leaf Tea Company buys tea from farmers in Sri Lanka. It pays farmers above the market price and uses only recyclable packaging. Its shareholders want higher profits.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one way ethical behaviour could increase Green Leaf's sales.
parts.answer: e.g. Customers who care about fair treatment of farmers may choose Green Leaf over rival brands, increasing sales and allowing a higher price.
parts.working: 1 mark for the point, 1 mark for development in context.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think acting ethically will reduce Green Leaf's profits? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Reduce: paying above market prices and recyclable packaging raise costs; if prices cannot rise, profit margins fall; price-sensitive customers may buy cheaper tea. Not reduce: stronger brand image and loyalty; can charge a premium price; reliable supply from loyal farmers; avoids bad publicity. Judgement, e.g. in the short run profit may fall, but in the long run it may rise if customers value ethical tea; it depends on how many customers will pay more.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for knowledge/analysis of points for, up to 2 for points against, 2 marks for a justified judgement that explains why one side outweighs the other in this context.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bean There is a chain of coffee shops in Karachi. It buys 20,000 kg of coffee beans a year from Supplier X at $4.50 per kg. Supplier X has been accused of paying workers very low wages. Supplier Y is a certified fair-trade supplier that charges 12% more per kg. Bean There's customers are mostly young professionals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Should Bean There switch to Supplier Y? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Calculations: $10,800. Switch: protects reputation; fair-trade logo can be used in promotion and may attract young professionals who care about ethics; may justify slightly higher prices; avoids risk of boycott. Stay: extra $10,800 a year raises costs and reduces profit; customers may not notice or pay more; Supplier X may improve. Judgement, e.g. switch, because the extra cost is small compared with the risk to the brand and could be covered by a very small price rise per cup.
parts.working: Calculations: 20,000 × 4.50 = $90,000. 12% × 90,000 = $10,800. Content: extra cost 12% × 20,000 × 4.50 = $10,800 a year; fair-trade logo in promotion, appeal to ethically minded young professionals, reputation and boycott risk, possible small price rise per cup; higher costs and lower profit, customers may not notice or pay more. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Bean There, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Bean There, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Kohinoor Spinning Mills pays PKR 2.1 million a month for electricity from the national grid. It could install solar panels on its roof for PKR 18 million. The panels would reduce its electricity bill by PKR 450,000 a month. The mills would need a bank loan to buy the panels.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Should Kohinoor Spinning Mills install the solar panels? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Calculations: 40 months. For: saves PKR 5.4 m a year; cost recovered in 40 months (about 3 years 4 months) and panels last much longer; less pollution so better image with buyers; protects against rising grid prices and power cuts. Against: PKR 18 m loan means interest costs; savings may be less on cloudy days; money cannot be used for new machinery (opportunity cost). Judgement, e.g. install, because savings repay the cost in just over 3 years while panels last far longer, as long as loan interest is affordable.
parts.working: Calculations: 18,000,000 ÷ 450,000. 40 months. Content: payback 18,000,000 ÷ 450,000 = 40 months; saving PKR 5.4 m a year; panels last much longer than the payback; protection from grid price rises and power cuts; image with buyers; loan interest; lower output on cloudy days; opportunity cost (machinery). Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Kohinoor Spinning Mills, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Kohinoor Spinning Mills, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

author: HomiLabs

stem: AutoPak assembles cars in Karachi. The government and customers are increasingly concerned about the environment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ways AutoPak could make its cars more environmentally friendly.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. produce hybrid or electric cars; improve fuel efficiency; use recycled materials; reduce weight; fit cleaner engines meeting emission standards.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two environmental issues AutoPak faces. Which is likely to be the most important to AutoPak? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Air pollution from cars and the factory: stricter emission laws may force costly redesigns and fines. Waste and resource use: disposal of old parts and use of steel and plastics raises costs and attracts criticism. Other: energy use in the factory; pressure groups. Judgement, e.g. air pollution, because government emission rules affect whether AutoPak can legally sell its cars, so it directly affects sales.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for each issue (knowledge + analysis). 2 marks for a justified choice explaining why the other issue is less important.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Many Pakistani consumers now buy products made in China, the USA and Europe.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'globalisation'.
parts.answer: The increasing freedom of movement of goods, services, capital and people between countries, so that the world acts more like one market.
parts.working: 1 mark: growing trade/links between countries. 1 mark: movement of goods, capital or people / world becoming one market.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons for the growth of globalisation.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. fewer trade barriers due to free trade agreements; cheaper and faster transport (container ships, air freight); improved communications and the internet; growth of multinational companies; industrialisation of developing countries.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A Japanese motorcycle company has opened a factory in Pakistan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'multinational company'.
parts.answer: A business that has factories, production or service operations in more than one country.
parts.working: 1 mark: business operating/producing. 1 mark: in more than one country (not just selling there).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two benefits to Pakistan of the multinational opening the factory.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. creates jobs; workers gain new skills; government receives more tax revenue; increases exports; brings new technology; more choice of products for consumers.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The government of a country wants to protect its local shoe makers from cheap imported shoes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'import tariff'.
parts.answer: A tax placed on goods brought into a country.
parts.working: 1 mark: tax. 1 mark: on imported goods.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'import quota'.
parts.answer: A limit on the quantity (number or volume) of a good that can be imported into a country.
parts.working: 1 mark: limit/restriction. 1 mark: on the physical quantity of imports.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Sialkot Sports makes footballs that it exports to the USA. It charges PKR 3,360 per football. The exchange rate is $1 = PKR 280.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price of one football in US dollars at this exchange rate. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The exchange rate changes to $1 = PKR 260 and Sialkot Sports keeps its price at PKR 3,360. Calculate the new price in US dollars, correct to 2 decimal places, and state whether the rupee has appreciated or depreciated.
parts.answer: $12.92; the rupee has appreciated
parts.working: B1: 3,360 ÷ 260 = $12.92. B1: appreciated (fewer rupees are needed to buy $1).

author: HomiLabs
