stem: Pak Auto Assemblers in Karachi imports steel at $650 per tonne. The government has put a 15% tariff on imported steel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the tariff paid on each tonne of imported steel. Show your working.
parts.answer: $97.50 per tonne

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways the tariff could affect Pak Auto Assemblers.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Higher costs: steel costs $747.50 a tonne, raising the cost of each car; either price rises (fewer sales) or profit per car falls. 2) Change of supplier: it may buy steel from local mills instead, which could be cheaper now but may be lower quality or slower to deliver. Other: may need more working capital; competitiveness against imported cars may fall.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Surgimed exports surgical instruments from Sialkot to the USA. A set of instruments is priced at PKR 8,700. The exchange rate changes from $1 = PKR 250 to $1 = PKR 290.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price in US dollars of a set before and after the exchange rate change. Show your working.
parts.answer: Before $34.80; after $30.00

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two effects of the change in the exchange rate on Surgimed.
parts.answer: The rupee has depreciated. 1) Exports become cheaper for US buyers ($34.80 → $30.00), so Surgimed may sell more sets and gain market share. 2) Imported inputs such as special steel or machinery cost more in rupees, raising production costs and possibly reducing profit margins. Other: Surgimed could instead keep the dollar price and earn more rupees per set.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A large Chinese electronics multinational plans to build a television factory in Kenya.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two reasons why the multinational might want to produce in Kenya.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. lower labour costs; to be closer to African markets and cut transport costs; to avoid import tariffs; government incentives/grants; access to raw materials.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two possible disadvantages to Kenya of the multinational building the factory.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Local TV makers may not be able to compete with the multinational's economies of scale and may close, so some local jobs are lost. 2) Profits may be sent back to China rather than reinvested in Kenya. Other: senior jobs filled by foreign managers; environmental damage; multinational may leave suddenly; may pressure the government for tax breaks.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Chiniot Craft makes hand-carved wooden furniture and sells it in Pakistan. It is worried about globalisation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one threat and one opportunity that globalisation creates for Chiniot Craft.
parts.answer: Threat: cheaper factory-made furniture imported from abroad may take customers, so Chiniot Craft's sales and profit fall unless it cuts costs or stresses its hand-made quality. Opportunity: it can sell online to customers abroad, for example in the Gulf or UK where buyers value hand-carved furniture, increasing sales and allowing higher prices.
parts.working: Threat: 1 identify, 1 apply, 1 develop. Opportunity: 1 identify, 1 apply, 1 develop. Other opportunities: import cheaper tools or materials; set up abroad.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one way Chiniot Craft could respond to more foreign competition.
parts.answer: e.g. focus on unique hand-carved designs and branding to differentiate from mass-produced imports.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid response, 1 mark for brief development.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Several multinational fast-food and drinks companies have opened outlets in Pakistan over the last 20 years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one reason why a multinational company may be welcomed by the government of the host country.
parts.answer: e.g. It creates jobs, which reduces unemployment and increases income tax and spending in the economy.
parts.working: 1 mark for the reason, 1 mark for development.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think multinational companies are good for a country such as Pakistan? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Good: jobs, training and new skills; tax revenue; new technology; investment in infrastructure; more choice and better quality for consumers; may increase exports. Bad: local firms may close; profits sent abroad; may use resources and cause pollution; may have power over government; senior jobs may go to foreigners. Judgement, e.g. good overall if the government regulates them and they use local suppliers, because the jobs and investment benefits are large; depends on how much profit stays in the country.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for knowledge/analysis of points for, up to 2 for points against, 2 marks for a justified judgement that explains why one side outweighs the other in this context.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Lahore Lights imports LED components from China. It must pay its Chinese supplier CNY 500,000 (Chinese yuan) for the next order. The current exchange rate is 1 CNY = PKR 39. Lahore Lights could pay now, or pay in three months' time when the order arrives. Its bank forecasts that the exchange rate in three months will be 1 CNY = PKR 41.50. Paying now would use most of the company's cash.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Should Lahore Lights pay its Chinese supplier now or in three months? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Calculations: PKR 1,250,000 more. Pay now: avoids the forecast extra PKR 1.25 m cost; certainty about cost for pricing. But uses most cash, so cash-flow problems (cannot pay wages or other suppliers); risk if goods arrive late or faulty. Pay later: keeps cash; forecast may be wrong and the rupee could strengthen. Judgement, e.g. pay now only if an overdraft can cover short-term needs, because the saving (about 6% of the order) is large; otherwise protect cash flow.
parts.working: Calculations: now 500,000 × 39 = PKR 19.5 m; later 500,000 × 41.5 = PKR 20.75 m. difference PKR 1.25 m. Content: now PKR 19.5 m, later PKR 20.75 m at the forecast rate (PKR 1.25 m, about 6% more); certainty for pricing; paying now uses most cash — cash-flow risk, risk if goods are late or faulty; forecast may be wrong; overdraft option. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Lahore Lights, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Lahore Lights, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Threadline, a European clothing company, wants to open a garment factory employing 800 workers in Asia. Appendix 2 shows information it has collected about two possible countries.
Appendix 2
Country A: average monthly wage $300; good roads and ports; workers experienced with high-quality fabrics; low tariffs on exports to Europe.
Country B: average monthly wage $160; frequent power cuts; long delays at the port; government offers a 5-year tax holiday to new foreign factories.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which country should Threadline choose for its new garment factory? Justify your answer using suitable calculations and Appendix 2.
parts.answer: Calculations: $1,344,000 a year (Country B is cheaper). Country B: labour about $1.34 m a year cheaper; 5-year tax holiday increases profit. But power cuts stop production and port delays mean late deliveries to European shops, which matters for fashion. Country A: higher wages but reliable infrastructure, skilled workers for quality, low export tariffs to Europe. Judgement, e.g. Country A if Threadline sells quality fashion where speed matters; Country B if it competes on low price and can buy generators.
parts.working: Calculations: A: 800 × 300 × 12 = $2,880,000; B: 800 × 160 × 12 = $1,536,000. difference $1,344,000. Content: labour cost A $2.88 m, B $1.536 m a year (B $1,344,000 cheaper); B's 5-year tax holiday v power cuts and port delays (late deliveries to European shops); A's reliable infrastructure, skilled workers for quality fabrics, low export tariffs to Europe; fit with Threadline's market (quality fashion v low price). Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Threadline, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Threadline, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Economists say the country may enter a recession next year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'recession'.
parts.answer: A period when a country's GDP (total output) falls, usually for six months or more.
parts.working: 1 mark: fall in GDP/output. 1 mark: for a period, e.g. two quarters / six months.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two likely effects of a recession on businesses.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. lower sales as incomes fall; lower profits; workers made redundant; some businesses close; less investment; more bad debts.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A country's economy goes through the business cycle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the four stages of the business cycle.
parts.answer: Growth; boom; recession; slump (in order of the cycle: growth, boom, recession, slump, then growth again).
parts.working: 1 mark each for growth, boom, recession, slump.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two features of a boom.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. high consumer spending; low unemployment; rising inflation/prices; skills shortages and rising wages; high business profits.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Prime Autos is a car dealership in Lahore. It has a bank loan of PKR 5 million to finance its stock of cars. The central bank has raised interest rates, and the loan's interest rate rises from 18% to 22% per year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the increase in Prime Autos' annual interest payments. Show your working.
parts.answer: PKR 200,000 per year

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two other ways the rise in interest rates could affect Prime Autos.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Fewer car sales: many customers buy cars with loans/car financing; higher interest makes monthly payments larger, so demand falls. 2) Less expansion: borrowing to open a new showroom becomes more expensive, so Prime Autos may delay investment. Other: customers may save rather than spend.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Tasty Karahi is a restaurant in Islamabad. The country has high inflation. The price Tasty Karahi pays for chicken has risen from PKR 1,250 per kg to PKR 1,400 per kg in one year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the price of chicken. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two effects of high inflation on Tasty Karahi.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Rising costs: chicken is 12% dearer, so the cost of each karahi rises; if menu prices are not raised, profit margins fall. 2) Falling demand: customers' real incomes fall, so eating out (a non-essential) may be cut back and sales fall. Other: workers demand higher wages; frequent menu price changes cost money.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Last year a country's GDP was $340 billion. This year it is $357 billion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage growth in GDP. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two government economic objectives other than economic growth.
parts.answer: Any two: low unemployment; low and stable inflation (price stability); balance of payments stability (exports and imports balanced).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Outline two benefits to a construction company of economic growth.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Rising incomes mean more people can afford new houses, so the company gets more orders. 2) Government may receive more tax and spend more on roads and schools, giving the company more contracts.
parts.working: For each: 1 mark for the benefit, 1 mark for linking it to a construction company.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The government has increased income tax rates. Luxe Motors sells expensive imported cars. Daily Needs is a grocery store selling rice, flour and cooking oil.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two other ways the government could use fiscal policy to influence the economy.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. change sales tax/GST; change corporation tax on profits; change government spending (e.g. on infrastructure); change import duties.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think the increase in income tax will affect Luxe Motors more than Daily Needs? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Higher income tax reduces disposable income. Luxe Motors sells luxury goods that people can delay buying, so demand is likely to fall significantly; buyers may switch to cheaper cars. Daily Needs sells necessities that people must still buy, so demand changes little, though customers may switch to cheaper brands. However, very rich customers of Luxe Motors may be little affected, while Daily Needs' low-income customers feel the tax more. Judgement, e.g. yes, Luxe Motors is affected more, because its products are not essential.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for knowledge/analysis of points for, up to 2 for points against, 2 marks for a justified judgement that explains why one side outweighs the other in this context.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which option should Comfort Home Furniture choose? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Calculations: PKR 96,750,000. Option 1: revenue falls from PKR 100 m to PKR 96.75 m even though more items are sold, and the forecast may be optimistic in a recession; but it keeps staff and customers. Option 2: saves 8 × 60,000 × 12 = PKR 5.76 m a year; but customer service may fall, remaining staff demotivated, redundancy payments, and staff are lost for when the economy recovers. Note: revenue is not profit – selling 150 more items also adds to costs, so Option 1's effect on profit is worse than the PKR 3.25 m revenue fall suggests. Judgement, e.g. Option 2, because Option 1 reduces revenue by PKR 3.25 m while Option 2 cuts costs by PKR 5.76 m; or a justified alternative.
parts.working: Calculations: new price 50,000 × 0.9 = PKR 45,000. 2,150 × 45,000 = PKR 96,750,000. Content: Option 1 revenue 2,150 × 45,000 = PKR 96.75 m v PKR 100 m now (fall of PKR 3.25 m, and extra items add costs); Option 2 saves 8 × 60,000 × 12 = PKR 5.76 m a year; reliability of the sales forecast in a recession; customer service, morale, redundancy pay, losing staff before recovery. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Comfort Home Furniture, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Comfort Home Furniture, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ayesha wants to start a mobile app business in Karachi that helps families book home tutors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two characteristics of a successful entrepreneur.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. willing to take risks; creative/innovative; hard-working; self-confident; good communicator; determined/resilient; able to plan and organise.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two items Ayesha should include in her business plan.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. description of the business idea and objectives; market research findings and target market; marketing plan (price, promotion); finance needed and sources; cash-flow forecast and forecast profit; details of the owner and staff; location.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Business size can be measured in several ways.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two methods of measuring the size of a business, other than the number of employees.
parts.answer: Any two: value of output; capital employed; market share; sales revenue (value of sales).
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'internal growth'.
parts.answer: When a business expands its existing operations, for example by opening new branches or increasing output, using its own resources rather than joining with other businesses.
parts.working: 1 mark: expanding existing operations. 1 mark: not by merger or takeover / organic growth.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The following decisions have been made by different businesses:
1 A flour mill buys a chain of bakeries.
2 A clothing retailer merges with another clothing retailer.
3 A dairy company buys the farms that supply its milk.
4 A cement company buys a chain of hotels.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of integration shown in each of the four decisions.
parts.answer: 1 Forward vertical integration; 2 Horizontal integration; 3 Backward vertical integration; 4 Conglomerate integration (diversification).
parts.working: 1 mark each. For 1 and 3, accept 'vertical' for the mark only if forward/backward is correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one advantage to the dairy company of decision 3.
parts.answer: e.g. secure supply of milk, so it can control the quality and cost of milk and is not affected by supplier shortages.
parts.working: 1 mark for the advantage, 1 mark for development.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The table shows information about two businesses.
Business A (a call centre): 120 employees; capital employed PKR 80 million
Business B (a chemical plant): 45 employees; capital employed PKR 150 million

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the capital employed per employee for each business, correct to the nearest PKR 1,000. Show your working.
parts.answer: Business A: PKR 667,000; Business B: PKR 3,333,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it can be misleading to compare these two businesses using only the number of employees.
parts.answer: Business A looks larger by employees, but Business B is capital-intensive (uses expensive machinery) and is larger by capital employed; different industries use different mixes of labour and capital.
parts.working: 1 mark: B is larger by capital employed / capital-intensive. 1 mark: industries differ in labour intensity.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bilal opened a café in Islamabad six months ago. Sales have been lower than he expected and he is worried that the business might fail.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two sources of support available to people starting a business.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. government grants or low-interest loans; business advice and training schemes; business incubators/business parks; banks' small-business advisers; mentoring from experienced entrepreneurs.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why new businesses such as Bilal's café often fail.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Lack of market research: Bilal may have chosen a location or menu that customers do not want, so sales are too low to cover rent. 2) Poor cash-flow management: he may run out of cash to pay suppliers and staff even if the café could become profitable. Other: strong competition from established cafés; lack of management experience; too little capital; changes in the market.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Gul Khan runs a tailoring shop in Peshawar with two employees. He has run the business for 15 years and has no plans to expand.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Gul Khan's business may stay small.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Owner's objectives: Gul Khan may be happy with his income and want to keep control and avoid stress, so he chooses not to grow. 2) Small market: tailored clothing is a personal service and customers want individual attention from a local tailor, so demand is limited to his area. Other: lack of finance for expansion; a skilled personal service is difficult to scale.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two advantages to customers of buying from a small business.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. personal service; flexibility to meet individual needs; owner knows customers; local and convenient.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Nadia wants to borrow PKR 3 million from a bank to open a beauty salon in Faisalabad. The bank has asked her for a business plan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'business plan'.
parts.answer: A written document that describes a business, its objectives and how it will achieve them, including marketing, production and financial plans.
parts.working: 1 mark: written document. 1 mark: sets out the business's objectives/strategies and forecasts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits to Nadia of writing a business plan.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Easier to get finance: the bank can see forecast revenue and how Nadia will repay the PKR 3 million, so it is more likely to lend. 2) Reduces risk of failure: planning makes Nadia research customers, competitors and costs before she spends money, so she can spot problems early. Other: gives clear aims to measure progress against; helps her to persuade suppliers or partners.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two mobile network companies in the same country have merged to form one large company.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a merger and a takeover.
parts.answer: A merger is when two businesses agree to join together to form one business; a takeover is when one business buys enough shares to gain control of another.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct description.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two problems the merged company might face.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Different cultures: managers and staff from the two companies may have different ways of working, causing conflict and lower productivity. 2) Redundancies: duplicate shops and offices are closed, causing poor morale and possibly strikes. Other: diseconomies of scale – communication is slower in a much larger organisation; customers may lose choice and complain to the government; integrating IT networks is costly.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Pak Biscuits Ltd makes biscuits. It plans to grow by buying one of its rival biscuit manufacturers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two benefits to a business of growth.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. economies of scale (lower average costs); larger market share; higher profits; more power over suppliers; less risk of being taken over.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think horizontal integration is the best way for Pak Biscuits Ltd to grow? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: quick increase in market share and fewer competitors; economies of scale in buying flour, sugar and packaging; gains the rival's brands and factory. Against: costly to buy the rival; cultural clashes; may need redundancies; competition authorities may object; risk is concentrated in one product. Alternatives: internal growth (cheaper, less risky but slow); vertical integration (secures supply of flour). Judgement, e.g. yes, because it quickly gains market share and lower costs, provided the price paid is not too high.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for knowledge/analysis of points for, up to 2 for points against, 2 marks for a justified judgement that explains why one side outweighs the other in this context.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Bread Basket owns 8 bakeries in Lahore and wants to expand. It is considering two options.
Option 1 – internal growth: open 3 new bakeries, costing PKR 25 million each. Forecast annual profit: PKR 6 million per new bakery.
Option 2 – take over Golden Oven, a rival with 5 bakeries, for PKR 110 million. Golden Oven's annual profit is PKR 20 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which option should Bread Basket choose? Justify your answer using suitable calculations (for example, forecast annual profit as a percentage of the cost of each option).
parts.answer: Calculations: Option 1: 24.0%; Option 2: 18.2%. Option 1: higher return (24.0%), cheaper (PKR 75 m), keeps Bread Basket's own culture and quality, but slower and the forecast profit for new bakeries is uncertain. Option 2: lower return (18.2%) and costs PKR 110 m, but gains 5 bakeries at once with a known profit record, removes a competitor and gives more market share; may bring integration problems. Judgement, e.g. Option 1, because it gives a higher return for less money, unless Bread Basket needs to grow quickly to block competitors.
parts.working: Calculations: Option 1: (3 × 6) ÷ (3 × 25) × 100 = 18 ÷ 75 × 100 = 24.0%. Option 2: 20 ÷ 110 × 100 = 18.2%. Content: Option 1 = 18 ÷ 75 × 100 = 24.0%; Option 2 = 20 ÷ 110 × 100 = 18.2%; internal growth cheaper and keeps culture/quality but slower and forecast uncertain; takeover gives 5 bakeries at once with a known profit record, removes a rival, more market share, but integration problems and higher cost. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Bread Basket, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Bread Basket, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Zain plans to open a juice bar in Multan and wants a bank loan of PKR 6 million. His business plan contains these monthly forecasts:
Juices sold: 300 per day, 26 days a month; price PKR 350 per juice
Ingredient cost: PKR 120 per juice
Rent PKR 250,000; wages PKR 400,000; other fixed costs PKR 144,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Do you think the bank should lend Zain the PKR 6 million? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Calculations: PKR 1,000,000. For: forecast profit of PKR 1 m a month (PKR 12 m a year) would easily cover repayments; plan shows he has thought about costs. Against: forecasts may be optimistic – 300 juices every day may be unrealistic for a new business, especially in winter; no evidence of market research or competitors; Zain's experience unknown; the loan is large and he may have no collateral. Judgement, e.g. lend only if Zain shows market research supporting the sales forecast and offers security, because profit is very sensitive to the number of juices sold.
parts.working: Calculations: revenue 300 × 26 × 350 = 2,730,000; ingredients 300 × 26 × 120 = 936,000; fixed costs 794,000. 2,730,000 − 936,000 − 794,000 = PKR 1,000,000. Content: revenue PKR 2.73 m, ingredients PKR 0.936 m, fixed costs PKR 0.794 m, forecast profit PKR 1 m a month (PKR 12 m a year); repayments easily covered if forecasts are right; but 300 juices a day may be optimistic (new business, winter), no market research or competitor evidence, experience and collateral unknown; profit very sensitive to sales. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to the bank's decision about Zain, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to the bank's decision about Zain, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Saleem is a sole trader who runs a mobile phone repair shop in Quetta.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'unlimited liability'.
parts.answer: The owner is personally responsible for all the debts of the business, so personal possessions can be taken to pay them if the business fails.
parts.working: 1 mark: owner responsible for all business debts. 1 mark: personal assets at risk.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two advantages to Saleem of being a sole trader.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. easy and cheap to set up; Saleem keeps all the profit; he has full control and makes decisions quickly; financial information stays private; flexible working.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Many businesses in Pakistan are organised as companies or franchises.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'franchise'.
parts.answer: A business arrangement where the franchisor gives the franchisee the right to use its brand name, logo and business methods in return for a fee and/or a share of sales (royalty).
parts.working: 1 mark: right to use another business's name/brand/methods. 1 mark: in return for a fee or royalty.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two features of a public limited company.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. shares can be sold to the general public, e.g. on the stock exchange; shareholders have limited liability; separate legal identity; must publish its accounts; owned by shareholders and run by directors.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Dr Farah and Dr Imran are dentists. They plan to set up a dental clinic together in Lahore as a partnership.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'partnership agreement'.
parts.answer: A written legal document setting out the terms of a partnership, such as how much capital each partner invests, how profits are shared and what happens if a partner leaves.
parts.working: 1 mark: written/legal agreement between partners. 1 mark: an example of what it contains.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two advantages to the dentists of forming a partnership instead of each operating as a sole trader.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) More capital: both dentists invest, so they can afford expensive dental chairs and X-ray equipment. 2) Shared workload and skills: they can cover each other's patients during holidays or illness, and one could specialise in children's dentistry, attracting more patients. Other: shared decision-making; losses shared.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Rizwan runs a successful furniture shop in Islamabad as a sole trader. He plans to borrow money to open a large showroom and is thinking of forming a private limited company with his brother.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two advantages to Rizwan of forming a private limited company.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Limited liability: if the large showroom fails, Rizwan would only lose the money he invested, not his house or savings. 2) More capital: he can sell shares to his brother (and other family or friends) to raise finance for the showroom. Other: separate legal identity, so the company continues if an owner dies; may appear more creditworthy to suppliers and banks.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one disadvantage of a private limited company compared with a sole trader.
parts.answer: e.g. more legal formalities and costs to set up and run; accounts must be filed and are less private; profits shared with other shareholders; Rizwan loses some control.
parts.working: 1 mark for the disadvantage, 1 mark for brief development.

author: HomiLabs

stem: QuickBite is a burger chain with 30 outlets run by franchisees. Each franchisee pays QuickBite a royalty of 6% of sales revenue. One franchisee in Rawalpindi had sales revenue of PKR 24 million last year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the royalty paid to QuickBite by the Rawalpindi franchisee. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits to QuickBite (the franchisor) of growing by franchising.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Low-cost growth: franchisees pay to open their outlets, so QuickBite can expand to 30 outlets without raising large amounts of capital. 2) Regular income: QuickBite receives royalties (e.g. PKR 1.44 m from one outlet) with less risk than running the outlets itself. Other: franchisees are motivated owners, so outlets are well run; brand awareness grows.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point). Answers about benefits to the franchisee gain no marks.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hassan Foods Ltd is a family-owned private limited company that makes cooking oil. The directors are considering becoming a public limited company to raise finance for a new refinery.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one reason why a public limited company can usually raise more capital than a private limited company.
parts.answer: It can sell shares to the general public on the stock exchange, so many more investors can buy shares.
parts.working: 1 mark: sells shares to the public. 1 mark: on the stock exchange / much larger pool of investors.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think Hassan Foods Ltd should become a public limited company? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: raises large amounts of capital for the refinery without interest payments; higher status helps with suppliers and banks; shares easy to sell. Against: the family may lose control if outsiders buy many shares, including risk of takeover; costly and complicated to convert; must publish detailed accounts; shareholders may want short-term dividends. Judgement, e.g. yes if the family keeps more than half of the shares and the refinery cannot be financed by loans; otherwise use a bank loan to keep control.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for knowledge/analysis of points for, up to 2 for points against, 2 marks for a justified judgement that explains why one side outweighs the other in this context.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Omar wants to open a fried-chicken restaurant in Karachi. He could open it under his own brand, or buy a franchise from an international chain. The franchise would cost an initial fee of $40,000 plus a royalty of 5% of sales each year. Omar forecasts first-year sales of $300,000. He has never run a restaurant before.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Should Omar buy the franchise or open under his own brand? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Calculations: $55,000. Franchise: well-known brand attracts customers from the first day; training and support useful as Omar has no restaurant experience; proven menu and suppliers; banks may lend more readily. But costs $55,000 in year 1 and royalties every year; less control over menu, prices and decor; must follow franchisor rules. Own brand: keeps all profit and full control, but higher risk of failure and must build customer awareness. Judgement, e.g. franchise, because Omar's lack of experience makes failure likely without support, and the brand reduces risk despite the $55,000 cost.
parts.working: Calculations: royalty 5% × 300,000 = $15,000. 40,000 + 15,000 = $55,000. Content: first-year payment 40,000 + 5% × 300,000 = $55,000; franchise — known brand, training and support for an inexperienced owner, proven menu and suppliers, easier bank loans, but fees every year and less control; own brand — keeps all profit and control, but higher risk of failure and must build awareness. Mark bands (12; knowledge 2, application 2, analysis 4, evaluation 4): Level 3 (9–12): developed analysis of both sides / all options applied to Omar, using the data, and a justified decision that explains why the rejected option(s) are weaker. Level 2 (5–8): advantages and disadvantages analysed and applied to Omar, with a decision that is only partly justified or one-sided. Level 1 (1–4): relevant knowledge with little application or analysis; a decision with no reasoning earns no evaluation marks. Correct calculations count towards application and analysis; follow through an earlier calculation error.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Mehran Motors is a private sector car parts manufacturer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two objectives that a private sector business might have.
parts.answer: Any two: survival; profit; growth; increasing market share; social/ethical objectives (e.g. helping the community).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'stakeholder'.
parts.answer: Any person or group with an interest in the activities and performance of a business.
parts.working: 1 mark: person or group. 1 mark: with an interest in/affected by the business.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The following groups have an interest in Faisal Textiles:
employees; customers; shareholders; the local community; managers; the government

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each of the six groups as an internal or an external stakeholder.
parts.answer: Internal: employees, shareholders (owners), managers. External: customers, the local community, the government.
parts.working: 4 marks for all six correct; 3 for five; 2 for four; 1 for two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one objective that customers of Faisal Textiles might have.
parts.answer: e.g. good-quality cloth at reasonable prices / reliable delivery / good after-sales service.
parts.working: 2 marks for a clear objective; 1 mark for a vague one.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Sapphire Paints plans to extend its factory near a residential area in Gujranwala. The extension will double output and create 80 new jobs, but will increase lorry traffic and fumes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two stakeholder groups that would support the factory extension.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. shareholders (higher profit); managers (business growth); unemployed local people/workers (more jobs); government (more tax, jobs); suppliers (more orders).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two conflicts between stakeholder objectives that the extension might cause.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Shareholders vs local community: shareholders want higher profits from doubled output, but residents want clean air and quiet roads, so they may protest and delay planning permission. 2) Workers vs shareholders: new jobs are welcome, but workers may want higher wages from the increased profits while shareholders want higher dividends. Other: customers want low prices vs owners want high profit; government wants jobs but also environmental protection.
parts.working: For each conflict: 1 mark for the two groups/objectives, 1 mark for application, 1 mark for development.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Roshni Solar is a social enterprise in Sindh. It sells low-cost solar lamps to villages without electricity and trains local women to sell and repair them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'social enterprise'.
parts.answer: A business that has social objectives, such as helping people or the environment, as well as making a profit, and uses most of its profit to meet those social aims.
parts.working: 1 mark: business with social/environmental objectives. 1 mark: also needs profit / reinvests profit in its aims.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two objectives Roshni Solar is likely to have.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Social: provide light to homes without electricity so children can study at night and families stop using dangerous kerosene lamps. 2) Economic: make enough profit to survive and expand to more villages, and provide income for the local women it trains. 3) Environmental: reduce pollution by replacing kerosene with solar power.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Fizz Up is a new soft-drinks business. In its first year it had sales of PKR 4.2 million in a market where total sales were PKR 35 million. It made a small loss.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Fizz Up's market share. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think profit should be the most important objective for Fizz Up at this stage? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For profit: needs profit for long-term survival and to repay loans; owners want a return. Against: as a new business, survival is more important – it must build cash flow and customers first; increasing market share (already 12%) and brand awareness may require low prices and heavy advertising that reduce short-term profit; profit becomes more important later. Judgement, e.g. no – survival and market share matter more now, because a new drinks brand must win customers from established brands before it can earn profit; objectives change as the business grows.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for knowledge/analysis of points for, up to 2 for points against, 2 marks for a justified judgement that explains why one side outweighs the other in this context.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Sana makes celebration cakes at home in Lahore. The ingredients and box for one cake cost PKR 750, and she sells the cake for PKR 1,800.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'added value'.
parts.answer: The difference between the selling price of a product and the cost of the bought-in materials and components used to make it.
parts.working: 1 mark: selling price minus. 1 mark: cost of bought-in materials/components.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the added value of one cake. Show your working.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Al-Haq Motors assembles cars on a production line where each worker does one task, such as fitting doors or installing seats.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'specialisation'.
parts.answer: When people, businesses, regions or countries concentrate on what they are best at producing, for example workers concentrating on one task (division of labour).
parts.working: 1 mark: concentrating on one task/product. 1 mark: what they are best at / division of labour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to Al-Haq Motors of specialisation on its production line.
parts.answer: Advantage: each worker becomes skilled and quick at one task, so more cars are assembled per day and the cost per car falls. Disadvantage: the work is repetitive and boring, so workers may be demotivated, make mistakes or leave; also, if one worker is absent, the whole line may stop.
parts.working: Advantage: 1 identify, 1 apply, 1 develop. Disadvantage: 1 identify, 1 apply, 1 develop.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hill Valley Tea buys loose tea for PKR 1,100 per kg. It packs it into branded 250 g packs which sell for PKR 520 each. The packaging for each pack costs PKR 40.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the added value per kg of tea. Show your working.
parts.answer: PKR 820 per kg
parts.working: M1: 4 packs per kg: selling price 4 × 520 = PKR 2,080; bought-in costs 1,100 + 4 × 40 = PKR 1,260. A1: 2,080 − 1,260 = PKR 820.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways Hill Valley Tea could increase its added value.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Stronger branding and advertising, e.g. stressing that the tea comes from hill gardens, so customers will pay a higher price per pack without costs rising much. 2) Attractive or premium packaging, e.g. gift tins, which allows a much higher price than the extra packaging cost. Other: add flavours (cardamom, green tea) to create premium products; reduce the cost of bought-in materials by buying in bulk; sell directly online at a higher price.
parts.working: For each of the two points: 1 mark for identifying the point, 1 mark for applying it to the business, 1 mark for developing the consequence (max 3 per point).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Print Pro, a printing business in Karachi, has PKR 10 million to invest. It can either buy a new digital printing machine, expected to add PKR 2.2 million to profit each year, or buy two delivery vans, expected to save PKR 1.6 million a year in courier costs. It can afford only one.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'opportunity cost'.
parts.answer: The next best alternative that is given up when a choice is made.
parts.working: 1 mark: next best alternative. 1 mark: given up/forgone.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Print Pro chooses the printing machine. State the opportunity cost of this decision and explain why opportunity cost is important when Print Pro makes decisions.
parts.answer: Opportunity cost: the two delivery vans (and the PKR 1.6 million a year saving they would have brought). It is important because resources are scarce; comparing the benefit given up helps Print Pro choose the option with the greatest benefit (here PKR 2.2 m is more than PKR 1.6 m), although it should also consider risk and non-financial factors such as reliable delivery.
parts.working: 1 mark: vans/the saving forgone. Up to 3 marks for explanation: scarce resources (1); compare benefits of alternatives (1); development using the figures or a non-financial factor (1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Businesses can be classified into three sectors of economic activity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'primary sector'.
parts.answer: The sector of the economy that extracts natural resources, such as farming, fishing, mining and forestry.
parts.working: 1 mark: extracting/using natural resources. 1 mark: example(s).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the sector for each of these businesses: a fish farm in Thatta; a bank in Islamabad; a fertiliser factory in Multan; a coal mine in Balochistan.
parts.answer: Fish farm – primary; bank – tertiary; fertiliser factory – secondary; coal mine – primary.
parts.working: 2 marks for all four correct; 1 mark for two or three correct.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
The table shows the number of workers (in millions) in each sector in Country Z.
2005: primary 18; secondary 6; tertiary 6
2025: primary 15; secondary 10; tertiary 15

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of workers employed in the primary sector in 2005 and in 2025. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the importance of the tertiary sector has grown in Country Z.
parts.answer: e.g. 1) Rising incomes: as people become richer they spend more on services such as restaurants, banking, education and tourism, creating more service jobs. 2) Mechanisation of farming: fewer workers are needed in agriculture, so people move to towns to work in services. Other: growth of IT and telecoms; tourism; global outsourcing of call centres.
parts.working: For each reason: 1 mark for the reason, 1 mark for development.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The government of a country owns the national railway. It is losing money, and some politicians want to sell it to private sector businesses (privatisation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between the public sector and the private sector.
parts.answer: Public sector businesses are owned and controlled by the government; private sector businesses are owned by private individuals or shareholders.
parts.working: 1 mark for each sector correctly described. Do not accept 'private limited company' as a definition of the private sector.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think the railway should be privatised? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: private owners aim for profit, so may cut waste and improve efficiency; may invest more in new trains; government stops paying for losses and receives money from the sale. Against: private owners may close unprofitable routes that villages depend on; fares may rise; safety may be reduced to cut costs; the railway is a strategic service that benefits society (external benefits such as less road congestion). Judgement, e.g. privatise only with government rules on fares, safety and keeping essential routes, because efficiency gains are useful but the social service must be protected.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for knowledge/analysis of points for, up to 2 for points against, 2 marks for a justified judgement that explains why one side outweighs the other in this context.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bukit Accessories is a wholesaler in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, that sells phone cases and chargers to small shops. Last year its profit for the year was RM 90,000 and its capital employed was RM 600,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'capital employed'.
parts.answer: The total long-term finance invested in the business: total equity plus non-current liabilities.
parts.working: 1 mark: long-term finance / money invested in the business; 1 mark: shareholders' equity + non-current liabilities (or total assets − current liabilities).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the return on capital employed (ROCE) of Bukit Accessories. Show your working.
parts.working: ROCE = profit for the year ÷ capital employed × 100 (M1) = 90,000 ÷ 600,000 × 100 = 15% (A1).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Tools Point is a hardware shop in Sukkur. Its accountant has calculated these ratios.
Ratio | Year 1 | Year 2
Current ratio | 1.8 | 1.2
Acid test ratio | 0.9 | 0.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'liquidity'.
parts.answer: The ability of a business to pay its short-term debts (current liabilities) as they fall due.
parts.working: 1 mark: ability to pay debts / turn assets into cash; 1 mark: short-term debts / current liabilities when they are due.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the liquidity of Tools Point improved or worsened between Year 1 and Year 2. Use one ratio as evidence.
parts.answer: Worsened: e.g. the current ratio fell from 1.8 to 1.2 (or the acid test ratio fell from 0.9 to 0.5).
parts.working: 1 mark: worsened; 1 mark: correct evidence from either ratio with both figures.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Rapid Coaches and Hilltop Travels both run intercity bus services. Last year Rapid Coaches had revenue of $3,200,000 and profit for the year of $256,000. Hilltop Travels had revenue of $1,500,000 and profit for the year of $165,000. An investor wants to buy shares in the business that performs better.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit margin of each business. Show your working.
parts.answer: Rapid Coaches 8%; Hilltop Travels 11%

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why comparing these profit margins alone may not show which bus company is the better investment.
parts.answer: e.g. (1) Rapid Coaches is larger and earns more total profit ($256,000 v $165,000), so a lower margin does not mean it is weaker; (2) ratios use past data from one year only and say nothing about future plans, safety record, customer loyalty or liquidity.
parts.working: Points: different sizes / absolute profit differs; accounts may cover different dates or use different methods; one year's data may include one-off events; ratios ignore non-financial factors (reputation, quality of buses, managers); margin says nothing about liquidity or ROCE. For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Green Valley Fertilisers Ltd sells fertiliser to farmers in Punjab. Many farmers buy on credit and pay after the harvest. Green Valley buys from three large manufacturers on 60 days' credit.
Appendix: extract from statements of financial position (Rs 000)
Item | Year 1 | Year 2
Current assets | 540 | 600
of which inventory | 200 | 390
Current liabilities | 300 | 400

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the appendix, explain two reasons why the manufacturers that supply Green Valley Fertilisers might be worried about its liquidity.
parts.answer: Current ratio fell from 1.8 to 1.5; acid test ratio fell from about 1.13 to about 0.53 (0.525). (1) Without selling inventory it can pay only about half its current liabilities, so suppliers may not be paid on time. (2) Inventory almost doubled (200 → 390) – fertiliser may be unsold until the next season, so cash is tied up and the debts to suppliers have also risen (300 → 400).
parts.working: Calculations: CR Y1 540 ÷ 300 = 1.8, Y2 600 ÷ 400 = 1.5; acid test Y1 (540 − 200) ÷ 300 = 1.13, Y2 (600 − 390) ÷ 400 = 0.53. Credit for using figures as application. For each of two points: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to the case, 2 marks developed analysis. Developed analysis: late payment → suppliers may stop trade credit / ask for cash on delivery.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Saffron Sweets has two shops in Rawalpindi. The owner wants to close one shop and use the money to open a shop in Islamabad. The lease on the Saddar shop ends in 6 months and the landlord wants 30% more rent. A large rival sweet shop will open next to the Gulberg shop next year.
Appendix: last year's results (Rs)
Item | Saddar shop | Gulberg shop
Revenue | 4,000,000 | 2,500,000
Gross profit | 1,600,000 | 1,125,000
Profit for the year | 360,000 | 300,000
Capital employed | 3,000,000 | 1,500,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which shop should Saffron Sweets close? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Saddar: GPM 40%, profit margin 9%, ROCE 12%. Gulberg: GPM 45%, profit margin 12%, ROCE 20%. Gulberg uses its capital far more efficiently and the Saddar rent rise will cut its profit further, so closing Saddar is the stronger choice – unless the new rival is expected to take a large share of Gulberg's sales; Saddar does earn more total profit (Rs 360,000 v 300,000).
parts.working: Calculations: GPM 1.6m ÷ 4.0m = 40%, 1.125m ÷ 2.5m = 45%; PM 360k ÷ 4.0m = 9%, 300k ÷ 2.5m = 12%; ROCE 360k ÷ 3.0m = 12%, 300k ÷ 1.5m = 20%. Either decision acceptable if justified; must weigh higher absolute profit/revenue at Saddar against better ratios at Gulberg, the rent rise and the rival. Levels: L3 (9–12) a justified recommendation that weighs the options against each other, uses the case data (and calculations where asked) and explains why the rejected option is weaker; L2 (5–8) developed analysis of the options applied to the business, decision only partly supported; L1 (1–4) relevant knowledge with limited application, or a bare decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Indus Knitwear makes woollen sweaters in Lahore and exports them to Canada. Its customers pay 90 days after delivery, but Indus Knitwear must pay for wool and wages straight away.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two reasons why a business needs finance.
parts.answer: Any two: to start up the business; to buy non-current assets such as machinery; to expand; to pay day-to-day costs (working capital) such as wages and materials; to survive a cash shortage.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'trade credit'.
parts.answer: An agreement under which a supplier allows the business to pay for goods some time (e.g. 30–90 days) after they are delivered.
parts.working: 1 mark: supplier lets the business buy now; 1 mark: pay later / after an agreed period.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Coastline Seafood Ltd freezes and packs fish in Gwadar. It is considering these sources of finance: retained profit; bank overdraft; sale of an unused warehouse; issue of new shares.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each of the four sources as an internal or an external source of finance.
parts.answer: Internal: retained profit, sale of an unused warehouse. External: bank overdraft, issue of new shares.
parts.working: 2 marks all four correct; 1 mark two or three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two disadvantages to Coastline Seafood Ltd of using retained profit.
parts.answer: Any two: shareholders receive lower dividends; the amount may be too small; it is not available to a loss-making business; the money can no longer be used for other projects (opportunity cost).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Arif owns a car repair workshop in Sargodha. He borrows Rs 1,200,000 from a bank to buy new equipment. He will repay the loan plus Rs 300,000 interest in 24 equal monthly instalments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Arif's monthly repayment. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two things the bank might ask Arif for before agreeing to the loan.
parts.answer: Any two: a business plan; a cash-flow forecast; collateral / security; the accounts of the workshop; evidence of his credit history.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Sky Line Coaches runs buses between Peshawar and Islamabad. It needs Rs 9 million to buy two new air-conditioned buses. It plans to raise the money by selling three of its oldest buses instead of taking a bank loan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'internal source of finance'.
parts.answer: Finance raised from within the business itself, e.g. retained profit or the sale of existing assets.
parts.working: 1 mark: from inside the business / its own resources; 1 mark: example or 'not from outsiders'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to Sky Line Coaches of selling its old buses rather than taking a bank loan.
parts.answer: Advantage: no interest or repayments, so its cash flow is not burdened and there is no risk of defaulting. Disadvantage: it loses three buses, so it can run fewer journeys and earn less revenue; old buses may sell for less than Rs 9 million so it may still be short of money.
parts.working: Advantage points: no interest; no collateral needed; no repayments. Disadvantage points: lose capacity / revenue; may not raise enough; takes time to find buyers. For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Mehak Electronics is a shop in Hyderabad. The owner has listed four things she needs money for:
(i) a new delivery truck
(ii) paying wages in a slow month
(iii) building a warehouse extension
(iv) buying extra stock of fans before summer

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which two of the four needs are long-term finance needs.
parts.answer: (i) the delivery truck and (iii) the warehouse extension.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one suitable source of finance for need (ii) and one suitable source for need (iii). Give a reason for each.
parts.answer: (ii) bank overdraft – flexible, short-term, only pay interest on the amount used for a few weeks. (iii) long-term bank loan (or retained profit / mortgage) – a large amount repaid over several years to match the long life of the building.
parts.working: For each need: 1 mark suitable source, 1 mark reason linked to the time period or amount. Trade credit is acceptable only for (iv), not (ii).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Karachi Marine Ltd repairs fishing boats at its own dock. It wants a 7-year bank loan of Rs 40 million to build a covered repair shed. Profit for the year has risen in each of the last three years, to Rs 11 million last year. It already repays an older loan of Rs 6 million a year. The dock and land are valued at Rs 120 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two factors the bank would consider before lending to Karachi Marine Ltd.
parts.answer: e.g. (1) Ability to repay: rising profit of Rs 11 million a year, but Rs 6 million already goes on the old loan, so the bank will check the cash flow can cover both. (2) Security: the dock and land worth Rs 120 million could be offered as collateral, reducing the bank's risk. Others: purpose of loan / business plan, existing debt, track record of the managers.
parts.working: Factors: profitability and cash flow; existing borrowing; collateral; business plan / purpose; size and age of the business; interest rates and the risk of the fishing industry. For each of two points: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to the case, 2 marks developed analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: SunDrop Energy is a new business in Nairobi, Kenya, that installs solar water heaters. It needs $80,000 for equipment. A bank offers a 4-year loan at 9% simple interest per year. The government runs a grant scheme for green businesses, but decisions take about 8 months and only one in four applicants succeeds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total amount SunDrop Energy would repay on the bank loan. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think SunDrop Energy should wait to apply for the government grant instead of taking the bank loan? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Grant: does not need to be repaid, saving $28,800 interest, but the 8-month wait and 25% success rate mean the business may lose customers or be unable to start. Loan: money now, but repayments of $27,200 a year strain a new business's cash flow. Reasonable judgement: take the loan now (or a smaller loan) and still apply for the grant to repay early – start-up timing matters more.
parts.working: Annual repayment 108,800 ÷ 4 = 27,200 can be used in analysis. Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
CodeCraft (Private) Limited is a software company in Lahore owned by two founders. It needs Rs 20 million to build a new product. Forecast profit before interest is Rs 9 million a year.
Option 1: a 5-year bank loan of Rs 20 million at 16% interest a year; Rs 4 million of the loan is repaid each year (interest is charged on Rs 20 million in the first year).
Option 2: sell 30% of the company's shares to a private investor for Rs 20 million. The investor will receive 30% of profit and wants a seat on the board.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which option should CodeCraft choose? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Loan: first-year interest Rs 3.2 million, so the founders keep Rs 5.8 million profit, but cash out in year 1 is Rs 7.2 million (3.2m interest + 4m repayment) against Rs 9 million profit – risky if the forecast is missed. Shares: no repayments; founders keep 70% × 9m = Rs 6.3 million, investor gets Rs 2.7 million, but founders lose 30% ownership and some control. Either answer if justified; e.g. shares are better because the forecast is uncertain for a new product and the investor may bring expertise.
parts.working: Calculations: 20m × 16% = 3.2m; 9m − 3.2m = 5.8m; 3.2m + 4m = 7.2m; 70% × 9m = 6.3m; 30% × 9m = 2.7m. Levels: L3 (9–12) a justified recommendation that weighs the options against each other, uses the case data (and calculations where asked) and explains why the rejected option is weaker; L2 (5–8) developed analysis of the options applied to the business, decision only partly supported; L1 (1–4) relevant knowledge with limited application, or a bare decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Spotless is a dry-cleaning business in Doha, Qatar. Its owner is reading the business's first income statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'revenue'.
parts.answer: The income a business earns from selling its goods or services: selling price × quantity sold.
parts.working: 1 mark: income/money from sales; 1 mark: price × quantity (or 'before any costs are taken away').

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'cost of sales'.
parts.answer: The cost of the goods or materials used directly to make or buy the products that were sold in the period.
parts.working: 1 mark: direct costs; 1 mark: of the goods/services actually sold.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Page Turner is a bookshop in Accra, Ghana. Part of its income statement is missing.
Revenue $500,000
Cost of sales ?
Gross profit $180,000
Expenses ?
Profit for the year $45,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of sales. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the expenses. Show your working.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Golden Oven is a bakery in Abbottabad. Its accountant must decide where to put these costs in the income statement: flour; rent of the shop; eggs for the cakes; salary of the part-time accountant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each of the four costs as part of cost of sales or as an expense.
parts.answer: Cost of sales: flour, eggs. Expenses: rent of the shop, salary of the accountant.
parts.working: 2 marks all four correct; 1 mark two or three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'gross profit'.
parts.answer: Revenue minus cost of sales – the profit made before expenses (overheads) are taken away.
parts.working: 1 mark: revenue − cost of sales; 1 mark: before expenses/overheads are deducted.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Nile Tours organises boat trips in Luxor, Egypt. Last year: revenue $640,000; cost of sales $256,000; expenses $310,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit and the profit for the year. Show your working.
parts.answer: Gross profit $384,000; profit for the year $74,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways the income statement could help the managers of Nile Tours make decisions.
parts.answer: e.g. (1) Comparing expenses with last year shows which costs (such as fuel for boats) are rising, so managers can decide where to cut costs. (2) The profit figure shows whether the business can afford to buy another boat or must borrow; it can also be shown to a bank to support a loan application.
parts.working: Points: identify costs to control; compare with previous years / competitors; decide prices; decide whether to expand; show to banks/investors; decide how much profit to retain. For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Rehman Electric sells air conditioners in Lahore.
Item (Rs 000) | Year 1 | Year 2
Revenue | 2,400 | 3,000
Cost of sales | 1,200 | 1,650
Expenses | 800 | 1,050

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the profit for the year in each year. Show your working.
parts.answer: Year 1 Rs 400,000; Year 2 Rs 300,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: The owner says, "Revenue rose by 25%, so the business is more successful." Using the data, explain two reasons why he may be wrong.
parts.answer: (1) Profit fell from Rs 400,000 to Rs 300,000 because costs grew faster than revenue. (2) Cost of sales rose by 37.5% (1,200 → 1,650), so each air conditioner earns less gross profit – perhaps prices were cut or suppliers charged more; expenses also rose 31.25%.
parts.working: 2 × (1 mark point from data + 1 mark explanation). Revenue rise: (3,000 − 2,400) ÷ 2,400 = 25%.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Mehran Tiles plc made a profit before tax of Rs 8 million last year. Tax is charged at 29% of profit before tax. The directors will pay Rs 3 million in dividends to shareholders.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the retained profit for the year. Show your working.
parts.answer: Rs 2.68 million (Rs 2,680,000)
parts.working: Tax = 8m × 29% = 2.32m; profit after tax = 5.68m (M1); retained = 5.68m − 3m = Rs 2.68m (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline two ways Mehran Tiles plc could use its retained profit.
parts.answer: e.g. buy a new kiln to increase output; build up reserves to cover a future fall in sales; repay part of a loan; pay for market research for new tile designs.
parts.working: For each: 1 mark use, 1 mark linked to tile business.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Highway Diner is a café at a motorway service area. Its owner is unhappy with last year's profit.
Appendix: income statement (Rs 000)
Revenue 9,600
Cost of sales 4,800
Gross profit 4,800
Expenses: wages 2,400; rent 1,200; electricity 900; other 200
Profit for the year 100

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the appendix, explain two ways Highway Diner could increase its profit for the year.
parts.answer: e.g. (1) Cut expenses: wages are about half of all expenses (2,400 of 4,700) – use fewer staff at quiet times; electricity of 900 could fall with energy-saving fridges/lights. (2) Raise gross profit: cost of sales is 50% of revenue – buy ingredients in bulk or raise prices slightly; travellers at a motorway have few alternatives, so demand may not fall much.
parts.working: Total expenses 2,400 + 1,200 + 900 + 200 = 4,700; profit 4,800 − 4,700 = 100; profit margin about 1%. For each of two points: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to the case, 2 marks developed analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Polar Bottles sells reusable water bottles in Cape Town, South Africa. Last year it sold 20,000 bottles at $15 each. Cost of sales is $6 per bottle and expenses were $110,000. The manager believes that if the price is cut to $13, sales will rise to 26,000 bottles. Expenses would not change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gross profit and the profit for the year at the current price and at the new price. Show your working.
parts.answer: Current: gross profit $180,000, profit $70,000. New: gross profit $182,000, profit $72,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think Polar Bottles should cut its price to $13? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Profit rises only $2,000 (about 3%) while the business must make and sell 6,000 more bottles; the sales forecast is only an estimate – if sales reach only 25,000, gross profit falls to $175,000 and profit to $65,000. Benefits: higher market share, more customers who may buy again. Judgement e.g.: not worth it unless the manager has good research, because the gain is small and the risk large.
parts.working: Credit use of break-even style reasoning: at $13 it needs 25,715 bottles just to match current gross profit. Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
FixIt Hub repairs mobile phones in five shopping malls. The directors say, "We are doing better because revenue grew by 25%."
Appendix: income statements (Rs 000)
Item | Year 1 | Year 2
Revenue | 1,600 | 2,000
Cost of sales | 640 | 900
Expenses | 720 | 880

parts.label: a
parts.text: Do you agree with the directors? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Gross profit 960 → 1,100 (GPM 60% → 55%); profit 240 → 220 (profit margin 15% → 11%). Revenue and gross profit rose, but parts cost more per repair and expenses rose 22%, so profit fell by Rs 20,000. Disagree overall – the business is bigger but less efficient; it may recover if the new shops' costs are one-off start-up costs.
parts.working: Calculations: 1,600 − 640 = 960; 2,000 − 900 = 1,100; 960 − 720 = 240; 1,100 − 880 = 220; 960 ÷ 1,600 = 60%; 1,100 ÷ 2,000 = 55%; 240 ÷ 1,600 = 15%; 220 ÷ 2,000 = 11%. Levels: L3 (9–12) a justified recommendation that weighs the options against each other, uses the case data (and calculations where asked) and explains why the rejected option is weaker; L2 (5–8) developed analysis of the options applied to the business, decision only partly supported; L1 (1–4) relevant knowledge with limited application, or a bare decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ravi Foods plc has 2,000,000 shares. This year its profit after tax is Rs 4,200,000 and the directors will pay a dividend of Rs 1.50 per share. Last year the retained profit was Rs 2,500,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate this year's retained profit. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think the shareholders of Ravi Foods plc should be concerned that retained profit has fallen? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Not necessarily: they receive Rs 3 million in dividends now. But lower retained profit means less internal finance for new factories or products, so the company may have to borrow (interest) or issue shares (diluting ownership), which could reduce future dividends and share value. Judgement depends on whether profit after tax itself fell and on future investment plans.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Metro Cabs runs a fleet of 30 taxis in Karachi.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'working capital'.
parts.answer: Current assets minus current liabilities – the money available to pay day-to-day costs.
parts.working: 1 mark: current assets − current liabilities; 1 mark: used for day-to-day running.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two cash outflows for Metro Cabs.
parts.answer: Any two: fuel; drivers' wages; repairs and servicing; insurance; vehicle licence fees; loan repayments.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Himalaya Gifts is a souvenir shop in Kathmandu, Nepal. For next month its forecast shows: opening balance $15,000; total cash inflows $42,000; total cash outflows $50,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net cash flow and the closing balance for next month. Show your working.
parts.answer: Net cash flow −$8,000; closing balance $7,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two reasons why the cash-flow forecast for Himalaya Gifts may be inaccurate.
parts.answer: Any two: fewer tourists than expected; suppliers raise prices; unexpected costs such as repairs; exchange-rate changes; customers' spending changes.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Oakwood Furniture is a new business in Gujranwala. It sells dining tables to hotels on 60 days' credit. It made a profit last month but had almost no cash in the bank.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between cash and profit.
parts.answer: Profit is revenue minus all costs over a period; cash is the money the business actually holds. A credit sale counts as revenue (profit) before the cash is received.
parts.working: 1 mark each correct description, or 1 + 1 for the credit-sale link.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two causes of cash-flow problems.
parts.answer: Any two: giving customers too long credit; holding too much inventory; overtrading / expanding too fast; buying non-current assets with cash; poor planning; unexpected fall in sales.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Swat Apple Orchards sells most of its apples in August and September. Cash-flow forecast (Rs 000):
Item | June | July | August | September
Opening balance | 5 | ? | ? | ?
Cash inflows | 2 | 3 | 30 | 40
Cash outflows | 9 | 9 | 12 | 12

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the closing balance for each month.
parts.answer: June −2; July −8; August 10; September 38 (Rs 000)
parts.working: Net flows −7, −6, 18, 28; closing 5 − 7 = −2, −2 − 6 = −8, −8 + 18 = 10, 10 + 28 = 38. 3 marks all correct; 2 marks for three; 1 mark for net cash flows only.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the largest overdraft the orchard will need.
parts.answer: Rs 8,000 (in July)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Outline two ways Swat Apple Orchards could use this forecast.
parts.answer: e.g. arrange an overdraft of at least Rs 8,000 with the bank before June; plan to delay buying new equipment until September when cash is available; show it to a bank to support a loan.
parts.working: For each: 1 mark use, 1 mark link to the orchard's seasonal pattern.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Mazhar Builders builds houses in Islamabad. Its customers often pay 90 days after the work is finished, and it has had to use its overdraft every month this year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'trade receivables'.
parts.answer: Money owed to the business by customers who have bought goods or services on credit.
parts.working: 1 mark: money owed to the business; 1 mark: by customers who bought on credit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways Mazhar Builders could improve its cash flow. Which way is likely to be the most important? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: e.g. (1) Ask customers for stage payments / deposits as building progresses, so cash comes in before the 90 days. (2) Negotiate longer credit from suppliers of cement and steel so outflows match inflows. Most important: stage payments, because the main cause is the 90-day wait and builders' costs come early in each project.
parts.working: Other ways: chase late payers; offer discount for early payment; lease equipment instead of buying. Marks: 1 knowledge for each point (2), 1 analysis for each developed point (2), 2 evaluation for a justified choice of the most important that says why it beats the other.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Gulf Tyres is a tyre wholesaler in Sharjah, UAE. Extract (AED): inventory 85,000; trade receivables 40,000; cash 10,000; trade payables 60,000; bank overdraft 45,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Gulf Tyres' working capital. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why holding too much inventory can cause cash-flow problems for Gulf Tyres.
parts.answer: Cash has been spent buying tyres that are not yet sold, so less cash is available to pay suppliers and the overdraft; tyres also cost money to store and insure, and some may become out of date or damaged and have to be sold cheaply.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: cash tied up (1), cannot pay current liabilities (1), storage/insurance costs (1), risk of obsolescence / selling at a loss (1); application to tyres.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Valley View Hotel in Swat is busy from May to September but has few guests from December to February. The owner plans to renovate all 40 rooms next winter, paying the builders in monthly instalments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the owner should prepare a cash-flow forecast before starting the renovation.
