parts.answer: (1) To identify months when cash will be negative – winter has low inflows at the same time as builders' payments, so the owner can arrange an overdraft in advance. (2) To support an application for finance – a bank will want to see when the loan can be repaid from summer income. Also: to decide when to start, to control spending against plan.
parts.working: For each of two points: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to the case, 2 marks developed analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Lyallpur Looms forecasts these closing bank balances (without a new machine): March $35,000; April $40,000; May $46,000; June $52,000. It wants to buy a machine in March.
Option 1: pay $60,000 cash in March.
Option 2: pay four monthly instalments of $16,000 from March to June.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the closing balance in March and in June under each option. Show your working.
parts.answer: Option 1: March −$25,000; June −$8,000. Option 2: March $19,000; June −$12,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think Lyallpur Looms should choose Option 2? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Option 2 keeps the balance positive until May, so a large overdraft is not needed at once, but it costs $4,000 more and leaves the business $4,000 worse off by June. Option 1 needs a $25,000 overdraft in March (with interest) but is cheaper overall. Judgement e.g.: Option 2, because a small overdraft in May–June is easier to arrange than $25,000 in March – unless overdraft interest on Option 1 is below $4,000.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Paktex Uniforms makes school uniforms in Faisalabad. Its forecast shows a cash shortfall of Rs 1.2 million for two months before schools pay in August.
Option A: a bank overdraft of Rs 1.2 million for two months at 24% interest a year.
Option B: sell surplus inventory of cloth that cost Rs 1.5 million to another manufacturer for Rs 1.2 million.
Option C: delay paying suppliers by two months. Paktex would lose the 2% discount it gets for paying on time on Rs 3 million of purchases, and one supplier has warned it may stop supplying.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which option should Paktex Uniforms choose? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Costs: A = 1.2m × 24% × 2/12 = Rs 48,000; B = loss of Rs 300,000 (1.5m − 1.2m) and less cloth for future orders; C = Rs 60,000 lost discount plus risk of losing a supplier. A is cheapest and does not damage supplier relationships or production; the shortfall is short-term and the schools' payments will repay it. B is most expensive; C is cheap but risky.
parts.working: Calculations: 1,200,000 × 0.24 × 2 ÷ 12 = 48,000; 1,500,000 − 1,200,000 = 300,000; 3,000,000 × 2% = 60,000. Levels: L3 (9–12) a justified recommendation that weighs the options against each other, uses the case data (and calculations where asked) and explains why the rejected option is weaker; L2 (5–8) developed analysis of the options applied to the business, decision only partly supported; L1 (1–4) relevant knowledge with limited application, or a bare decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bloom Florist is a new flower shop in Nairobi, Kenya. The owner expects 60% of sales to be paid in cash in the month of sale and 40% to be paid by businesses one month later. Forecast sales: Month 1 $50,000; Month 2 $60,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the forecast cash inflow from sales in Month 2. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think a cash-flow forecast is useful for Bloom Florist when its sales are so uncertain? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Useful: shows when cash may run short (e.g. Month 1 inflow is only $30,000), helps arrange an overdraft, required by banks, lets the owner plan purchases of perishable flowers. Limits: based on guesses for a new business; sales of flowers depend on events and seasons; forecasts may give false confidence. Judgement: still useful if updated monthly and prepared with a best and worst case.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Shifa Clinic is a private medical clinic in Mardan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'non-current assets'.
parts.answer: Items owned by the business that it expects to keep and use for more than 12 months.
parts.working: 1 mark: owned resources; 1 mark: kept/used for more than one year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two non-current assets that Shifa Clinic is likely to own.
parts.answer: Any two: the clinic building; an X-ray machine; an ambulance; examination beds; computers.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Riverbank Rice Mills Ltd has borrowed money to buy a new husking machine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'non-current liabilities'.
parts.answer: Debts of the business that do not have to be repaid within the next 12 months.
parts.working: 1 mark: debts/amounts owed; 1 mark: repayable after more than one year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two examples of non-current liabilities.
parts.answer: Any two: long-term bank loan; mortgage; debentures; long-term lease payments owed.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Lahore Paints Ltd has total assets of Rs 2,600,000 and total liabilities of Rs 950,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the shareholders' equity of Lahore Paints Ltd. Show your working.
parts.working: Equity = total assets − total liabilities (M1) = 2,600,000 − 950,000 = 1,650,000 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'trade payables'.
parts.answer: Money the business owes to suppliers for goods or services bought on credit.
parts.working: 1 mark: owed to suppliers; 1 mark: bought on credit.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Crumbs Bakery in Rawalpindi has an oven, flour in its store room, a five-year bank loan and money in its till.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between an asset and a liability.
parts.answer: An asset is something the business owns (or is owed); a liability is something the business owes to others.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: From the items in the stem, identify one current asset and one non-current liability.
parts.answer: Current asset: flour (inventory) or money in the till (cash). Non-current liability: the five-year bank loan.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Meezan Office Supplies sells stationery to schools on credit. Extract from its statement of financial position (Rs): inventory 120,000; trade receivables 210,000; cash 15,000; trade payables 140,000; bank overdraft 90,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total current assets and the percentage of current assets that are trade receivables. Give the percentage to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the owner might be worried that trade receivables make up most of the current assets.
parts.answer: Only Rs 15,000 is cash, so the business cannot pay its Rs 230,000 current liabilities until schools pay; if schools pay late or some never pay (bad debts), it may need a bigger overdraft with interest and suppliers may not be paid.
parts.working: Up to 4: cash low (1); relies on schools paying (1); risk of late payment/bad debts (1); consequence – overdraft/interest or cannot pay suppliers (1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Cold Chain Logistics in Karachi has these items (Rs 000): land and buildings 900; refrigerated vehicles 250; inventory 80; trade receivables 60; cash 10; trade payables 70; bank overdraft 30; long-term loan 400.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate total assets. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate total liabilities.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the owner's equity.
parts.working: 1,300 − 500 = 800 (Rs 000): M1 A1 (own figure rule).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Dhaka Denim Ltd in Bangladesh takes a five-year bank loan of $200,000 and uses all of it to buy a new cutting machine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the effect of this on (i) non-current assets and (ii) non-current liabilities.
parts.answer: (i) increase by $200,000; (ii) increase by $200,000.
parts.working: 1 mark each (direction and amount).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two limitations of using the statement of financial position to judge how well Dhaka Denim Ltd is doing.
parts.answer: (1) It shows the position on one day only, so it may not be typical (e.g. inventory is high just before a big order is shipped). (2) It does not show revenue or profit, or non-financial strengths such as skilled workers and customer loyalty; asset values may also be out of date.
parts.working: 2 × (1 mark limitation + 1 mark explanation/application).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Hilltop Supermarket in Murree has asked a dairy supplier for 30 days' trade credit.
Appendix: statement of financial position extract (Rs million)
Non-current assets 4.0
Inventory 0.9
Trade receivables 0.25
Cash 0.05
Current liabilities 1.0
Non-current liabilities 2.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the appendix, explain two things the statement of financial position tells the dairy supplier about Hilltop Supermarket.
parts.answer: (1) Liquidity is weak: current ratio 1.2 (1.2 ÷ 1.0) but acid test 0.3 (0.3 ÷ 1.0) – it relies on selling inventory to pay debts, so the supplier might be paid late. (2) It has large long-term debt (Rs 2.5m) compared with equity of Rs 1.7m, so much of its cash goes on loan repayments; but non-current assets of Rs 4m could be sold if needed.
parts.working: Calculations: current assets 0.9 + 0.25 + 0.05 = 1.2; CR 1.2; acid test (1.2 − 0.9) ÷ 1.0 = 0.3; equity 5.2 − 3.5 = 1.7. For each of two points: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to the case, 2 marks developed analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Gilgit Glacier Water Ltd: shareholders' equity Rs 1,400,000; non-current liabilities Rs 600,000; current liabilities Rs 250,000; current assets Rs 450,000. It wants a bank loan to buy a second bottling line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of its non-current assets. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think the statement of financial position is more useful than the income statement to the bank? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: SFP: shows assets that could be security (Rs 1.8m non-current assets), existing debts and liquidity (current ratio 1.8). Income statement: shows whether profit is enough to pay interest and repayments. Judgement: the bank needs both – SFP shows security and existing debts, but the income statement (and cash-flow forecast) shows ability to repay, which matters most for a loan.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Sunrise Stationers makes four transactions:
(i) buys a delivery van for $25,000 cash
(ii) receives a long-term bank loan of $100,000 into its bank account
(iii) buys inventory of $8,000 on credit
(iv) pays a supplier $5,000 it owed

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each transaction, state the effect on total assets and on working capital.
parts.answer: (i) total assets no change; working capital −$25,000. (ii) total assets +$100,000; working capital +$100,000. (iii) total assets +$8,000; working capital no change. (iv) total assets −$5,000; working capital no change.
parts.working: 1 mark per transaction with both effects correct. Working capital = current assets − current liabilities.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why transaction (i) reduces the liquidity of Sunrise Stationers even though total assets do not change.
parts.answer: Cash (a current asset) has been swapped for a van (a non-current asset), so fewer liquid assets are available to pay current liabilities.
parts.working: 1 mark cash → non-current asset; 1 mark less available to pay short-term debts.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Kissan Agri Store sells seeds and fertiliser. The owner wants to borrow a further Rs 1,000,000 to open a second store.
Appendix: statements of financial position (Rs 000)
Item | Year 1 | Year 2
Non-current assets | 2,000 | 2,600
Inventory | 300 | 650
Trade receivables and cash | 200 | 150
Current liabilities | 250 | 600
Non-current liabilities | 800 | 1,400

parts.label: a
parts.text: Do you think the bank should lend Kissan Agri Store another Rs 1,000,000? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Current ratio 2.0 → 1.33; acid test 0.8 → 0.25; equity 1,450 → 1,400; non-current liabilities rose by 600 and current liabilities more than doubled. Liquidity has worsened sharply and borrowing is already high compared with equity, so a further loan is risky – the bank should refuse, or lend only with security over the extra non-current assets and a cash-flow forecast showing repayment. Counter: non-current assets rose by 600, so the business is investing and has security.
parts.working: Calculations: CA Y1 300 + 200 = 500, Y2 650 + 150 = 800; CR 500 ÷ 250 = 2.0, 800 ÷ 600 = 1.33; acid test 200 ÷ 250 = 0.8, 150 ÷ 600 = 0.25; equity = total assets − total liabilities: 2,500 − 1,050 = 1,450; 3,400 − 2,000 = 1,400. Levels: L3 (9–12) a justified recommendation that weighs the options against each other, uses the case data (and calculations where asked) and explains why the rejected option is weaker; L2 (5–8) developed analysis of the options applied to the business, decision only partly supported; L1 (1–4) relevant knowledge with limited application, or a bare decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A hospital in Quetta must choose one supplier of medical gloves for the next five years. It is worried that the supplier could go out of business.
Item ($000) | Supplier A | Supplier B
Non-current assets | 1,000 | 2,000
Current assets | 900 | 400
Current liabilities | 750 | 200
Non-current liabilities | 200 | 900

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the working capital of each supplier. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which supplier appears to be in the stronger financial position? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: B: higher working capital and current ratio 2.0 v 1.2, and higher equity ($1,300,000 v $950,000). But B has large long-term debt ($900,000) that must be repaid with interest, while A's debts are mostly short-term. Judgement e.g.: B is stronger for a five-year contract because it can pay short-term debts easily and has more equity; the hospital should still check profitability.
parts.working: Equity A 1,900 − 950 = 950; B 2,400 − 1,100 = 1,300; CR A 1.2, B 2.0. Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: CareWell Pharmacies has grown from one shop to 12 shops in Peshawar. The owners now want to buy a rival chain of 8 pharmacies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'external growth'.
parts.answer: Growth by joining with another business through a merger or a takeover.
parts.working: 1 mark: joining/combining with another business; 1 mark: merger or takeover.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two reasons why the owners of a business may want it to grow.
parts.answer: Any two: higher profit; larger market share; economies of scale; more status/prestige; spreading risk; less risk of being taken over.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The government of a country runs a youth business scheme. It gives low-interest loans and free business advice to people aged 21–45 who want to start a business.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two risks an entrepreneur takes when starting a business.
parts.answer: Any two: losing the money invested (savings); unlimited liability for debts; giving up a secure job and income; long working hours/stress; business failure.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why a government wants to support people who start new businesses.
parts.answer: (1) New businesses create jobs, so unemployment falls and the government pays less in benefits and collects more income tax. (2) They increase competition and innovation, giving consumers more choice and lower prices; successful ones grow into large firms that may export. Also: more output/economic growth; develop regions outside big cities.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Crispy Naan opened its first restaurant in Islamabad four years ago. Last year it opened 11 more restaurants in three cities. Customers now complain that food quality varies between branches, and the owner spends all her time travelling between restaurants.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two problems Crispy Naan may face because it has grown so quickly.
parts.answer: (1) Management/control: the owner cannot supervise 12 branches, so quality and service vary, damaging the brand's reputation. (2) Cash flow: opening 11 restaurants in a year uses large amounts of cash for rent and equipment before they make profits, so it may struggle to pay suppliers. Others: communication problems, recruiting enough trained cooks, keeping a consistent menu.
parts.working: For each of two points: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to the case, 2 marks developed analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Zarin Cement Ltd has bought a chain of five hotels in northern Pakistan. The managing director says this will "protect the company when building activity slows down".

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of integration shown and give one reason why.
parts.answer: Conglomerate integration – the hotels are in a different industry, unrelated to cement.
parts.working: 1 mark type; 1 mark reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think buying the hotels is a good way for Zarin Cement Ltd to grow? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: diversification spreads risk – hotel profits from tourism may continue when cement demand falls in a construction slowdown. Against: managers have no experience in hospitality; the takeover may cost a lot; cement's own economies of scale (e.g. a horizontal takeover of a rival) are not gained; tourism may also fall in a recession. Judgement e.g.: not a good way on its own, because the managers lack hospitality skills; organic growth in cement or a joint venture would be safer.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bright Future Schools Ltd is a private limited company that runs three schools. Its owners are thinking of becoming a public limited company.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'limited liability'.
parts.answer: Shareholders can lose only the money they invested in the business; their personal possessions are not at risk if the business fails.
parts.working: 1 mark: lose only amount invested; 1 mark: personal assets safe.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two differences between a private limited company and a public limited company.
parts.answer: Any two: a plc can sell shares to the general public / on a stock exchange, a private limited company cannot; a private limited company's shares can be sold only with the agreement of other shareholders; a plc must publish more financial information; a plc usually needs more capital to set up.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A Pakistani food company and a Turkish food company plan to build a pasta factory together in Pakistan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'joint venture'.
parts.answer: Two or more businesses agree to work together on a project, sharing the costs, risks and profits.
parts.working: 1 mark: businesses work together on a project; 1 mark: share costs/profits/risks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why the companies might form a joint venture.
parts.answer: Any two: share the cost of the factory; share risk; combine knowledge/skills (Turkish pasta know-how, Pakistani local market knowledge); enter a new market more easily.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Four businesses are described below.
(i) A barber's shop owned and run by one person who is personally liable for all debts.
(ii) A business whose shares are traded on the stock exchange.
(iii) The national postal service, owned and controlled by the government.
(iv) An accountancy firm owned by five people who share profits under a written agreement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of business organisation for each business.
parts.answer: (i) sole trader; (ii) public limited company; (iii) public corporation; (iv) partnership.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one objective that the business in (iii) is likely to have.
parts.answer: e.g. provide a reliable service to all areas of the country at an affordable price (or: break even / cover its costs; keep people employed).
parts.working: 1 mark objective; 1 mark developed/linked to postal service.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Khan & Baig Architects is a partnership. Partner Khan invested more capital, so the partners share profit in the ratio 3 : 2. Last year the partnership made a profit of Rs 2,500,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate each partner's share of the profit. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two disadvantages to the partners of running the business as a partnership.
parts.answer: (1) Unlimited liability: if a big building project fails and the firm is sued, the partners could lose personal possessions. (2) Disagreements: partners may disagree about which projects to accept, slowing decisions; the partnership may also end if one partner dies or leaves. Also: profit must be shared; limited capital.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Usman wants to open a Pizza Planet franchise in Multan. He must pay an initial fee of Rs 3,000,000 and then a royalty of 4% of revenue each year. He forecasts first-year revenue of Rs 20,000,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total amount Usman would pay to Pizza Planet in the first year. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to Usman (the franchisee) of buying the franchise.
parts.answer: Advantage: well-known brand and tested recipes, so customers come from the first day and the risk of failure is lower; training and national advertising are provided. Disadvantage: high costs (Rs 3.8 million in year 1) reduce his profit, and he must follow the franchisor's rules on menu, prices and suppliers, so he has little freedom.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Nadia is a sole trader who runs a successful interior design studio in Karachi. She is offered a large contract to design 50 hotel rooms but cannot do it alone. A former colleague, Sara, has offered to invest Rs 4 million and become a partner.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two factors Nadia should consider before taking Sara as a partner.
parts.answer: (1) Control: Nadia would share decisions with Sara, so they must agree on design style and which clients to accept – a partnership agreement is needed. (2) Profit sharing and liability: profits from the hotel contract would be shared, and Nadia would also be liable for debts caused by Sara's decisions. Others: Sara's skills/experience; extra capital of Rs 4 million; whether a private limited company would be better.
parts.working: For each of two points: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to the case, 2 marks developed analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Medix Ltd, a Pakistani hospital company, plans a joint venture with a Gulf healthcare group to build a cancer hospital in Lahore costing Rs 2,000 million. Medix would provide 40% of the money and receive 40% of the profit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Medix's contribution, and its share of a forecast annual profit of Rs 150 million. Show your working.
parts.answer: Contribution Rs 800 million; profit share Rs 60 million

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think a joint venture is the best way for Medix Ltd to build the new hospital? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: shares the large cost and risk; gains specialist cancer-care knowledge and equipment contacts from the Gulf group. Against: only 40% of profit; possible disagreements and different cultures; Medix loses full control over decisions and its brand. Alternative: build alone with a loan (all profit but all risk). Judgement linked to cost and expertise.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Three friends, Ali, Bina and Chen, are starting an event-management business in Dubai. They need $60,000 to buy sound and lighting equipment. They will organise large weddings and conferences, where one accident or cancelled event could lead to a claim of over $100,000. Ali has $40,000; Bina and Chen have $10,000 each. Options: (1) Ali becomes a sole trader and employs the other two; (2) a partnership of all three; (3) a private limited company with all three as shareholders.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which type of business organisation should the friends choose? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Private limited company is best: limited liability protects their personal possessions from a large claim; all three can invest (40,000 + 10,000 + 10,000 = $60,000) and share control by shareholding (Ali 2/3). Sole trader: Ali alone cannot raise $60,000 and has unlimited liability. Partnership: raises the money but each partner has unlimited liability for the others' mistakes. Drawbacks of Ltd: set-up cost, accounts must be filed – but outweighed by risk protection.
parts.working: Ali's share 40,000 ÷ 60,000 = 66.7%. Levels: L3 (9–12) a justified recommendation that weighs the options against each other, uses the case data (and calculations where asked) and explains why the rejected option is weaker; L2 (5–8) developed analysis of the options applied to the business, decision only partly supported; L1 (1–4) relevant knowledge with limited application, or a bare decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Northern Power is a public corporation that supplies electricity to homes and businesses in a mountainous region.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two objectives that a public sector organisation such as Northern Power might have.
parts.answer: Any two: provide a reliable service to everyone, including remote villages; keep prices affordable; break even / cover its costs; protect jobs; reduce environmental damage.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two objectives that the employees of Northern Power might have.
parts.answer: Any two: good/fair pay; job security; safe working conditions; promotion/training opportunities.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hira has just opened a tuition centre in Bahawalpur. She has written down her objectives for the first year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why it is important for Hira to set business objectives.
parts.answer: Objectives give the business a clear target to aim for and a way to measure success (and help in planning and decision-making).
parts.working: 1 mark: target/direction; 1 mark: measure progress / guide decisions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two objectives that a new business such as Hira's is likely to have.
parts.answer: Any two: survival; break even; build a customer base / market share; make a small profit.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Pak Steel Pipes plc has these stakeholder groups: shareholders; suppliers; the government; the local community.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one objective of each stakeholder group.
parts.answer: Shareholders: high dividends / rising share price. Suppliers: regular orders and prompt payment. Government: taxes paid, jobs created, laws obeyed. Local community: jobs, low pollution and safe roads.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: RideNow is a ride-hailing app that started in Lahore three years ago. In its first year its only aim was survival. Its revenue rose from Rs 12 million last year to Rs 18 million this year, and it now plans to expand to five more cities.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in RideNow's revenue. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why RideNow's objectives have changed since it started.
parts.answer: (1) It has survived and has a growing customer base, so it can now aim for growth/market share in new cities. (2) Competition from other ride apps means it must expand quickly to gain economies of scale and brand recognition before rivals; investors may also now expect profit. Other reasons: change of owners/managers, economic conditions.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Meadow Bank plans to close its branch in a small town in Sindh because most customers now use mobile banking.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two stakeholder groups that might object to the closure.
parts.answer: Any two: employees at the branch; local customers (especially older customers); the local community / shopkeepers; local government.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline two ways the bank's managers could reduce conflict with these stakeholders.
parts.answer: e.g. consult employees and offer transfers to other branches instead of redundancy; keep a cash machine/agent in the town and train older customers to use mobile banking.
parts.working: 2 × (1 mark method + 1 mark link to stakeholder).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Sparkle Detergents sells washing powder. Last year its sales were Rs 6 million in a market worth Rs 40 million. It cut prices by 15% and this year its sales are Rs 8 million; the market is still worth Rs 40 million. Its profit fell.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Sparkle Detergents' market share in each year. Show your working.
parts.answer: Last year 15%; this year 20%

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the objective of increasing market share may conflict with the objective of increasing profit.
parts.answer: To win market share Sparkle cut prices, so each packet earns a lower profit margin; extra sales did not make up for it, so profit fell. Spending on promotion to gain share also raises costs in the short term.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: lower price → lower margin (1+1); higher costs of promotion (1); application to Sparkle's figures (1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Chagai Minerals Ltd wants to open a copper mine in Balochistan. The mine will create 600 jobs, but it will use large amounts of water in a dry area and lorries will use village roads.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways stakeholders could influence the decisions of Chagai Minerals Ltd.
parts.answer: (1) Government: can refuse planning permission or set conditions such as limits on water use and pollution, so the company may have to build a water recycling plant, raising costs. (2) Local community: could protest or form a pressure group, block roads or attract media attention, damaging reputation and delaying the project; the company may build a new road or school to win support. Also: employees/trade unions, shareholders voting.
parts.working: For each of two points: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to the case, 2 marks developed analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Meridian Foods plc makes cooking oil and margarine. Its chief executive says, "Our shareholders own the company, so their objectives must always come first."

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one objective of the shareholders of Meridian Foods plc.
parts.answer: e.g. a high dividend each year, or a rising share price so they gain when they sell their shares.
parts.working: 1 mark objective; 1 mark developed/linked.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think shareholders are the most important stakeholder group for Meridian Foods plc? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: they own the company, elect the directors and provide capital; if they sell shares, the price falls and takeover risk rises. Against: without customers there is no revenue; employees determine quality; government can fine or close the business; ignoring stakeholders can damage reputation and long-term profit. Judgement e.g.: customers matter most in the long run because they generate the profit shareholders want.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Ravi Textiles employs 400 workers in Faisalabad. To cut costs it is considering two options.
Option A: move half of production to a cheaper area. 200 workers would be made redundant at Rs 150,000 each; the move costs Rs 60 million; wage savings are Rs 30 million a year.
Option B: stay and buy automated machines costing Rs 80 million, saving Rs 20 million a year. No workers lose their jobs; 60 workers would be retrained.
The local community and the trade union strongly oppose Option A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which option should Ravi Textiles choose? Justify your answer using suitable calculations and the objectives of its stakeholders.
parts.answer: Option A: one-off cost 60m + (200 × 150,000 = 30m) = Rs 90 million; payback 90 ÷ 30 = 3 years. Option B: Rs 80 million; payback 80 ÷ 20 = 4 years. A recovers its cost faster and suits shareholders, but conflicts with workers, the union (possible strikes) and the community (reputation, lost local sales). B is slower but keeps workers, avoids conflict and raises productivity long-term. Judgement e.g.: B, because a strike or bad publicity could easily cost more than the one-year difference in payback.
parts.working: Calculations: redundancy 200 × 150,000 = 30,000,000; total A = 90,000,000; payback A = 3 years; payback B = 4 years. Levels: L3 (9–12) a justified recommendation that weighs the options against each other, uses the case data (and calculations where asked) and explains why the rejected option is weaker; L2 (5–8) developed analysis of the options applied to the business, decision only partly supported; L1 (1–4) relevant knowledge with limited application, or a bare decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Clean Flame is a social enterprise in Pakistan that sells clean-burning cookstoves to rural families. Last year it sold 12,000 stoves at Rs 4,500 each. Each stove cost Rs 3,800 to make, and its other costs were Rs 6,000,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Clean Flame's surplus (profit) for the year. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think Clean Flame should aim to increase its profit? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: profit can be reinvested to make more stoves, reach more villages and survive without donations. Against: raising prices to increase profit may make stoves unaffordable for poor families, conflicting with its social objective of reducing indoor smoke. Judgement: aim for enough surplus to grow, e.g. by cutting costs rather than raising prices.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Rashid grows wheat on a farm near Okara. He uses land, tractors, workers and his own skill in running the farm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the four factors of production.
parts.answer: Land, labour, capital, enterprise.
parts.working: 2 marks all four; 1 mark two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'scarcity'.
parts.answer: The lack of enough resources to satisfy all of people's wants, because wants are unlimited but resources are limited.
parts.working: 1 mark: limited resources; 1 mark: unlimited wants.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A family in Quetta has a monthly budget. They want to buy food, rent, a new television and a holiday.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a need and a want.
parts.answer: A need is a good or service essential for survival (e.g. food, shelter); a want is something people would like to have but can live without.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: From the list in the stem, identify two needs and two wants.
parts.answer: Needs: food, rent (shelter). Wants: a new television, a holiday.
parts.working: 1 mark needs; 1 mark wants.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Chiniot Crafts makes wooden chairs. Each chair sells for Rs 9,500. The wood, polish and screws for one chair cost Rs 3,800. Last month it sold 40 chairs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total added value from the chairs sold last month. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why added value is not the same as profit.
parts.answer: Added value only subtracts bought-in materials; the business must still pay other costs from it, such as wages, rent and electricity, so profit is lower.
parts.working: 1 mark: other costs not deducted; 1 mark: example/explanation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Zainab is 17. She can work in a café on Saturdays or use the time to attend a weekend coding course.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two purposes of business activity.
parts.answer: Any two: combine factors of production to make goods and services; satisfy people's needs and wants; employ people and pay incomes; add value.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Zainab chooses the café job. Identify the opportunity cost of her choice and explain why it is an opportunity cost.
parts.answer: The coding course – it is the next best alternative she gives up by choosing the job.
parts.working: 1 mark identification; 1 mark 'next best alternative given up'.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hundreds of businesses in Sialkot specialise in making surgical instruments. Many small firms each specialise in one stage, such as forging, polishing or packing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one disadvantage of specialisation for a worker.
parts.answer: e.g. the work becomes repetitive and boring, lowering motivation (or: if demand for that one skill falls, the worker may become unemployed).
parts.working: 1 mark disadvantage; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits of specialisation to the businesses in Sialkot.
parts.answer: (1) Workers become highly skilled at one stage (e.g. polishing), so output per worker rises and costs fall. (2) Quality improves because each firm concentrates on what it does best, building Sialkot's reputation so buyers from abroad come to the town. Also: less time lost switching tasks; specialist machinery can be used.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A city government has Rs 500 million. It can build a new hospital or repair the city's main roads, but not both. It chooses the hospital.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the opportunity cost of building the hospital.
parts.answer: The repaired roads – the next best alternative that was given up.
parts.working: 1 mark roads; 1 mark 'next best alternative given up'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why scarcity means that the government and businesses must make choices.
parts.answer: Resources such as money, land and labour are limited, while wants are unlimited, so not every want can be satisfied; choosing one use (the hospital) means giving up another (roads). Businesses face the same problem, e.g. choosing between a new machine and more advertising.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: limited resources (1); unlimited wants (1); choice means sacrifice/opportunity cost (1); application/example (1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Swat Valley Honey sells honey. Bought-in costs for one jar are Rs 600 for raw honey and Rs 80 for the jar and a plain label. Unbranded jars sell for Rs 900. If it uses a premium gift box costing an extra Rs 100 per jar and a strong brand, it can sell each jar for Rs 1,400.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the added value per jar for the unbranded and the branded honey. Show your working.
parts.answer: Unbranded Rs 220; branded Rs 620

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline two ways, other than branding, that Swat Valley Honey could increase its added value.
parts.answer: e.g. offer a better service such as home delivery/online ordering; add new features such as flavoured honey or organic certification; sell direct to customers instead of through shops; reduce the cost of bought-in materials by buying jars in bulk.
parts.working: 2 × (1 mark way + 1 mark link to honey).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Desert Dates in Khairpur grows dates and sells them loose to wholesalers by the kilogram. The owner's daughter has returned from university and wants the business to increase its added value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways Desert Dates could increase its added value.
parts.answer: (1) Process the dates – e.g. date paste, stuffed dates or date syrup – which sell at much higher prices than loose dates, so the gap between price and bought-in costs widens. (2) Package and brand them as premium gift boxes for Ramadan and Eid, or for export, so customers will pay more; selling online directly to customers also removes the wholesaler. Must consider extra costs.
parts.working: For each of two points: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to the case, 2 marks developed analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Mehwish earns Rs 120,000 a month as a bank officer. She plans to leave her job to open a bakery. She forecasts a profit of Rs 1,200,000 in the bakery's first year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the opportunity cost of one year of running the bakery, and how much more or less this is than the forecast profit. Show your working.
parts.answer: Rs 1,440,000; the forecast profit is Rs 240,000 less than her salary.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think Mehwish should leave her job to open the bakery? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Against: in year 1 she would earn Rs 240,000 less and lose a secure job; the forecast may be too optimistic and the business might fail. For: profit may grow in later years as the bakery becomes known, she controls her own work and may enjoy it more. Judgement e.g.: open only if she has a business plan showing profit rising above Rs 1.44 million within two years, or start part-time first.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ten Stitch Garments employs 5 tailors. Before, each tailor made whole shirts and together they made 100 shirts a day. Now each tailor does one task (cutting, collars, sleeves, buttons or ironing) and together they make 160 shirts a day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in output. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think specialisation benefits the workers at Ten Stitch Garments? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Benefits: higher output may mean higher piece-rate pay or bonuses and more job security; workers become skilled in their task. Drawbacks: work is repetitive and boring, lowering motivation; workers have fewer skills, so harder to find another job; if one tailor is absent the line stops. Judgement e.g.: benefits the business more than the workers unless job rotation or higher pay is introduced.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Sindh Mango Exports sells 100 tonnes of fresh mangoes a year at $500 per tonne to a trader. It wants to add value.
Option 1: turn mangoes into pulp. Each tonne of mangoes makes 0.6 tonnes of pulp, which sells for $1,400 per tonne of pulp. Processing costs $250 per tonne of mangoes. A pulping machine costs $40,000.
Option 2: sell premium boxed fresh mangoes to supermarkets in Dubai for $750 per tonne. Boxes and air freight cost $180 per tonne. No new machine is needed, but mangoes must be picked to strict quality standards.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which option should Sindh Mango Exports choose? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Net income per tonne: now $500; Option 1 0.6 × 1,400 − 250 = $590 (+$90/tonne = +$9,000 a year, so the $40,000 machine takes about 4.4 years to pay back); Option 2 750 − 180 = $570 (+$70/tonne = +$7,000 a year with no investment). Option 2 gives a return at once and less risk; Option 1 gives more per tonne, pulp keeps longer (less waste) and has a larger market. Either answer with justification.
parts.working: Calculations: 0.6 × 1,400 = 840; 840 − 250 = 590; 750 − 180 = 570; (590 − 500) × 100 = 9,000; (570 − 500) × 100 = 7,000; 40,000 ÷ 9,000 = 4.4 years. Levels: L3 (9–12) a justified recommendation that weighs the options against each other, uses the case data (and calculations where asked) and explains why the rejected option is weaker; L2 (5–8) developed analysis of the options applied to the business, decision only partly supported; L1 (1–4) relevant knowledge with limited application, or a bare decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Businesses in Pakistan work in all three sectors of the economy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'secondary sector'.
parts.answer: Businesses that manufacture or process raw materials into finished or semi-finished goods (including construction).
parts.working: 1 mark: manufacturing/processing; 1 mark: raw materials into goods.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'tertiary sector'.
parts.answer: Businesses that provide services to consumers and to other businesses.
parts.working: 1 mark: services; 1 mark: to consumers/other businesses, or example.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A T-shirt passes through three businesses: Cotton Fields grows cotton in Rahim Yar Khan; Sunrise Mills spins the cotton and makes T-shirts; Trendz sells the T-shirts in a shopping mall.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the sector of economic activity for each of the three businesses.
parts.answer: Cotton Fields – primary; Sunrise Mills – secondary; Trendz – tertiary.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two tertiary-sector businesses that Trendz depends on.
parts.answer: Any two: a bank; a transport/delivery company; an insurance company; an advertising agency; a mobile phone/internet provider.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In Country K, 22% of output comes from the primary sector and 19% from the secondary sector.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of output that comes from the tertiary sector.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why the share of the primary sector usually falls as a country develops.
parts.answer: Any two: farming becomes mechanised so fewer workers are needed; natural resources run out; people move to cities for better-paid jobs; rising incomes are spent more on manufactured goods and services; cheaper imports of raw materials.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Pakistan has a mixed economy: some businesses are owned by private individuals and some by the government.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'mixed economy'.
parts.answer: An economy that has both a private sector and a public sector.
parts.working: 1 mark private sector; 1 mark public sector (both needed for 2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two reasons why a government may provide some goods and services in the public sector.
parts.answer: Any two: to provide essential services to everyone (e.g. water, health); private firms may not provide them because they are unprofitable; to control strategic industries such as defence or electricity; to protect jobs; to stop private monopolies charging high prices.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In the last 40 years many factories in the UK have closed, while service businesses such as banking, tourism and software have grown.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'deindustrialisation'.
parts.answer: The decline in the importance of the secondary (manufacturing) sector in an economy.
parts.working: 1 mark: decline of manufacturing; 1 mark: share of output or employment falls.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two effects of deindustrialisation on businesses in the UK.
parts.answer: (1) Manufacturing firms face cheaper imports and some close or move production abroad, so suppliers of parts lose orders. (2) Service businesses grow and need skilled workers, so they may struggle to recruit and must pay higher wages/train staff; former factory workers may be unemployed in some regions, reducing local spending in shops.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: In Country M the number of workers in manufacturing rose from 4.2 million in 2005 to 6.3 million in 2025 as many new factories opened.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in manufacturing workers. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the secondary sector might grow in a developing country such as Country M.
parts.answer: (1) Low wages attract multinational companies to build factories, creating jobs. (2) Better roads, electricity and ports make it cheaper to manufacture and export; rising incomes increase demand for manufactured goods; government incentives (tax breaks, export zones).
parts.working: 2 × (1 mark reason + 1 mark explanation).

author: HomiLabs

stem: In many countries water supply and sewage services are run by the public sector.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two features of a public sector organisation.
parts.answer: Any two: owned by the government; controlled by government ministers/appointees; financed by taxes or government grants; aims to provide a service rather than maximise profit.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why water supply might be kept in the public sector.
parts.answer: (1) It is essential for health, so everyone must have access even if they are poor; a private firm might raise prices or not supply remote areas. (2) It is a natural monopoly with huge costs for pipes and dams; a single private owner could exploit customers, while public control keeps prices fair. Also: safety/quality standards, long-term investment that private firms may avoid.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: SoftEdge is a software house in Islamabad with 60 programmers. The tertiary sector in Pakistan is growing fast, especially banking, online shopping and telecom services.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways the growth of the tertiary sector creates opportunities for SoftEdge.
parts.answer: (1) Banks and online shops need apps, websites and payment systems, so demand for SoftEdge's services rises and it can win larger contracts. (2) A growing service sector creates more trained IT graduates and better internet infrastructure, making it easier to recruit staff and to sell services abroad. Must link to SoftEdge.
parts.working: For each of two points: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to the case, 2 marks developed analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In Country R, factories employed 30% of workers in 2000 but only 18% in 2025. Imports of manufactured goods have grown. A politician says, "We must protect our factories at any cost."

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fall in the share of workers in factories, in percentage points and as a percentage. Show your working.
parts.answer: 12 percentage points; a 40% fall

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think Country R should try to keep a large manufacturing sector? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: factories give many jobs for less-skilled workers, exports earn foreign currency, and depending on imports is risky. Against: protecting inefficient factories (e.g. with tariffs) raises prices for consumers; services may give higher-paid jobs and faster growth. Judgement: support competitive manufacturing (training, infrastructure) rather than protect it 'at any cost'.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: SkyHigh Airways is a private sector airline that is close to bankruptcy. The government is considering buying it so that flights to remote cities continue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two objectives the airline might have if it were in the public sector.
parts.answer: Any two: provide flights to remote areas even if unprofitable; keep fares affordable; protect jobs; break even.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think the government should buy SkyHigh Airways? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: keeps essential links to remote cities and protects thousands of jobs. Against: taxpayers' money may be wasted if the airline keeps making losses; government managers may lack the profit motive to cut costs; money could be spent on schools or hospitals instead (opportunity cost); subsidising private airlines for remote routes may be cheaper. Judgement e.g.: buy only if the routes are essential and a cheaper subsidy to private airlines would not do the same job.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Bahawal Agro grows cotton on 2,000 acres (primary sector). Its current profit is Rs 40 million a year. It wants to expand into another sector.
Option 1 (secondary): build a cotton-ginning mill costing Rs 120 million; forecast extra profit Rs 18 million a year.
Option 2 (tertiary): start a lorry transport service for farmers costing Rs 60 million; forecast extra profit Rs 8 million a year.
Ginning profits depend on the cotton harvest. Many farmers in the area already complain that there are too few lorries.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which option should Bahawal Agro choose? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Annual return: Option 1 18 ÷ 120 = 15%, payback 6.7 years; Option 2 8 ÷ 60 = 13.3%, payback 7.5 years. Option 1 earns more profit and a higher return and uses Bahawal's own cotton (vertical link), but it doubles dependence on the cotton harvest – a bad harvest hits both businesses. Option 2 is cheaper, spreads risk and meets clear unmet demand. Either answer with justification.
parts.working: Calculations: 18 ÷ 120 × 100 = 15%; 8 ÷ 60 × 100 = 13.3%; 120 ÷ 18 = 6.7 years; 60 ÷ 8 = 7.5 years. Levels: L3 (9–12) a justified recommendation that weighs the options against each other, uses the case data (and calculations where asked) and explains why the rejected option is weaker; L2 (5–8) developed analysis of the options applied to the business, decision only partly supported; L1 (1–4) relevant knowledge with limited application, or a bare decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A foreign bank wants to open branches in one country. Country A has a labour force of 30 million, of whom 75% work in the tertiary sector. Country B has a labour force of 60 million, of whom 35% work in the tertiary sector.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of tertiary-sector workers in each country. Show your working.
parts.answer: Country A 22.5 million; Country B 21 million

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think the bank should choose Country A because a larger share of its workers are in the tertiary sector? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For A: a developed service economy, likely higher incomes and more people who use banking services. For B: almost the same number of service workers (21m v 22.5m) and a much larger population; a developing economy may have many people without bank accounts, so faster growth and less competition. Other factors: competition, regulation, incomes. Judgement e.g.: Country B, because its large population and low use of banks give more customers to win, unless its regulation or competition is too strong; the share alone is misleading.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: SmileBright plans to launch a new toothpaste for children. It cannot ask every parent in the country, so it will question a sample.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'sample'.
parts.answer: A small group of people chosen from the target market to take part in market research, who represent the whole population.
parts.working: 1 mark: small group selected; 1 mark: represents the target population.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why businesses use a sample rather than asking everyone in the target market.
parts.answer: Any two: cheaper; quicker; impossible/impractical to contact everyone; results are good enough if the sample is representative.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: StepUp Shoes asks customers what styles and sizes they want before it designs each new range of school shoes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'market-orientated business'.
parts.answer: A business that carries out market research to find out what customers want before developing and producing products to meet those wants.
parts.working: 1 mark: research customer wants first; 1 mark: then produces products to meet them.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two benefits to StepUp Shoes of being market-orientated.
parts.answer: Any two: products are more likely to sell; less risk of failure / wasted production; can respond quickly to changing tastes; higher customer satisfaction and loyalty.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: QuickCart, an online grocery business in Karachi, asked 250 customers when they prefer deliveries: 45 said morning, 70 said afternoon and 135 said evening.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of customers who prefer evening deliveries. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways QuickCart could present these results.
parts.answer: Any two: pie chart; bar chart; table; pictogram.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Helix Pharma's scientists develop new medicines they find interesting and then look for people to buy them. It does little market research.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'product-orientated business'.
parts.answer: A business that concentrates on the product itself – making it well or using new technology – and then tries to sell it, rather than first researching what customers want.
parts.working: 1 mark: focus on product/production; 1 mark: without first researching customer wants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to Helix Pharma of being product-orientated.
parts.answer: Advantage: scientists can develop genuinely new, high-quality medicines that customers did not know they needed, giving a lead over rivals and possibly patents. Disadvantage: some medicines may have too few patients/buyers, so huge research costs are wasted and profit falls.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Lakeside Resort in Naran wants feedback from guests. An online questionnaire would cost $1,200 and is expected to receive 600 replies. Face-to-face interviews would cost $3,000 for 150 interviews.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost per response for each method. Show your working.
parts.answer: Online $2; interviews $20

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline two reasons why Lakeside Resort might still choose the face-to-face interviews.
parts.answer: e.g. interviewers can ask follow-up questions and get detailed reasons for complaints; they can choose guests to make a representative sample (online replies may come mostly from very happy or very angry guests); response is guaranteed.
parts.working: 2 × (1 mark reason + 1 mark development/link).

author: HomiLabs

stem: FreshWay is planning to open a supermarket in a growing suburb of Lagos, Nigeria. It has a small research budget and wants to use secondary research first.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two sources of secondary research FreshWay could use and how each would help it.
parts.answer: (1) Government population/census statistics – show how many households and what age groups live in the suburb, so FreshWay can estimate demand and choose the product range. (2) Competitors' websites and price lists, or market reports – show what rivals charge and which products are popular, helping FreshWay set competitive prices. Also: newspaper articles on new housing, trade association reports, internet data.
parts.working: For each of two points: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to the case, 2 marks developed analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Rafia is opening a small handmade-soap business in Islamabad with a total budget of Rs 2,000,000. A market research agency offers to carry out a survey and taste-and-smell tests for Rs 250,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the research cost as a percentage of Rafia's total budget. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think Rafia should pay the agency to carry out the market research? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: reduces the risk of making soaps people do not want; identifies prices and scents customers prefer; a professional sample may be more reliable. Against: 12.5% of the budget is a lot for a small business; she could do cheap research herself (social media polls, testing at a local market, competitors' prices). Judgement e.g.: do her own low-cost primary research, because the money is needed for stock and equipment.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Chill Fizz makes soft drinks and will launch one new flavour. Appendix:
Survey 1: online poll of the company's own social-media followers – 2,000 replies; 70% chose Flavour A (lemon-mint).
Survey 2: blind taste test of 300 shoppers chosen at random in Lahore, Karachi and Multan – 58% preferred Flavour B (mango-chilli).
Flavour A costs Rs 5 more per bottle to make.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the appendix, which flavour should Chill Fizz launch? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Survey 1: 1,400 people chose A, but the sample is only existing fans, self-selected and online, so it is biased; no tasting. Survey 2: 174 people chose B; smaller sample but random, in three cities, and based on actual taste – more representative of the whole market. B is also cheaper to make. Recommendation: Flavour B (perhaps after a wider test), because Survey 2 is more reliable; A would suit if the target market is existing loyal customers.
parts.working: Calculations: 70% × 2,000 = 1,400; 58% × 300 = 174. Levels: L3 (9–12) a justified recommendation that weighs the options against each other, uses the case data (and calculations where asked) and explains why the rejected option is weaker; L2 (5–8) developed analysis of the options applied to the business, decision only partly supported; L1 (1–4) relevant knowledge with limited application, or a bare decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Daily Fresh sells bread to supermarkets all over Pakistan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'mass market'.
parts.answer: A large market in which the same (or very similar) products are sold to a very large number of customers.
parts.working: 1 mark: large number of customers; 1 mark: same/standard product, not targeted at a small segment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two advantages to Daily Fresh of selling to a mass market.
parts.answer: Any two: large sales volume; economies of scale lower unit costs; less risk than relying on a small niche; can build a well-known brand.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Chai Wala Café in Islamabad wants customers to keep coming back instead of trying the new cafés nearby.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'customer loyalty'.
parts.answer: When customers repeatedly buy from the same business or brand rather than switching to competitors.
parts.working: 1 mark: repeat purchases; 1 mark: rather than rivals.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two ways Chai Wala Café could build customer loyalty.
parts.answer: Any two: loyalty card / free drink after a number of purchases; excellent customer service; keeping quality high; personal relationships (remembering regular customers); special offers for members.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In one country 125,000 electric fans were sold last year. Brand A sold 45,000, Brand B sold 30,000 and Brand C sold 25,000; small brands sold the rest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the market share of Brand B. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the combined market share of Brands A, B and C. Show your working.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Spice Garden sells packaged spice mixes in Pakistan and to Pakistani communities in the UK.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two roles of marketing.
parts.answer: Any two: identify customer needs; satisfy customer needs; maintain customer loyalty; build relationships with customers; anticipate changes in customer wants; gain information about customers.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'market share'.
parts.answer: The percentage of total market sales that are made by one business or brand.
parts.working: 1 mark: percentage/proportion; 1 mark: of total market sales.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Online clothing sales in Pakistan rose from Rs 40 billion to Rs 58 billion in two years. Style Street sells clothes only from its five shops.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in online clothing sales. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why customers' spending patterns may be changing, and how this affects Style Street.
parts.answer: (1) More people have smartphones and internet access and want convenience, so they buy online instead of visiting shops – Style Street's shop sales may fall unless it sells online. (2) Rising prices (inflation) make customers compare prices online and choose cheaper brands, so Style Street must compete on price or offer better service. Also: changes in fashion/tastes, changes in income.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Pak Motors sells cars. It has divided its market into first-time buyers, families and wealthy professionals, and has a different model and advertising campaign for each group.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ways a market can be segmented, other than by income.
parts.answer: Any two: age; gender; location; lifestyle/interests; use of the product (e.g. business or personal).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits to Pak Motors of segmenting its market.
parts.answer: (1) Each model meets the needs of a group better (e.g. low fuel use for first-time buyers), increasing sales and customer satisfaction. (2) Advertising can be targeted to the media each group uses, so promotion spending is not wasted, lowering cost per sale; it can also charge higher prices to wealthy professionals. Also: identify gaps in the market, spread risk.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Noor Naturals makes halal, plant-based cosmetics sold only online to a small group of customers in Pakistan, Malaysia and the UK.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline why competition is important to customers.
parts.answer: Competition gives customers more choice and pushes businesses to keep prices lower and quality higher.
parts.working: 1 mark choice; 1 mark lower prices / better quality.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to Noor Naturals of selling in a niche market.
parts.answer: Advantage: few competitors and customers who care about halal/plant-based products, so it can charge higher prices and build strong loyalty. Disadvantage: sales volume is small, so it cannot gain economies of scale; if large cosmetics companies enter the niche, they could take its customers.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Coral Bay Hotel in Gwadar gets most of its bookings through travel websites, where guests post reviews and star ratings. A rival hotel with a swimming pool opened last month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why it is important for Coral Bay Hotel to build good relationships with its customers.
parts.answer: (1) Repeat guests and recommendations: satisfied guests return and tell friends, giving cheap promotion and steady revenue despite the new rival. (2) Online reviews: poor service leads to bad reviews and lower ratings, so future guests choose the rival; good relationships produce positive reviews and allow higher room prices. Also: feedback helps the hotel improve.
parts.working: For each of two points: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to the case, 2 marks developed analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Kool Kulfi sells ice cream. Last year its sales were Rs 10 million in a market worth Rs 80 million. This year a hot summer was followed by early rains; its sales were Rs 9 million in a market worth Rs 60 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Kool Kulfi's market share in each year. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Last year 12.5%; this year 15.0%

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think the managers of Kool Kulfi should be pleased with this year's results? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Pleased: market share rose 2.5 points, so it did better than rivals and may be gaining loyal customers. Not pleased: its sales fell by Rs 1 million (10%), so revenue and probably profit fell; the whole market shrank by 25%. Judgement: pleased with its competitive position, but concerned about revenue – weather is outside its control, so it could add products for the rainy season.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: TrailBlaze makes high-priced mountain bikes for a small group of serious cyclists. The owner wants to start selling a cheaper bike to the mass market of everyday riders.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between a niche market and a mass market.
parts.answer: Any two: niche is small, mass is large; niche has specialised products, mass has standard products; niche often has higher prices/margins, mass relies on high volume; niche has fewer competitors.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two factors TrailBlaze should consider before entering the mass market. Which factor is the most important? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: (1) Competition: large brands already sell cheap bikes with economies of scale, so TrailBlaze may not match their prices. (2) Brand image: selling cheap bikes may damage its premium reputation with serious cyclists, so it could lose its niche customers. Also: production capacity, finance for higher output. Most important e.g. brand image, because the niche gives its current profit.
parts.working: Marks: 1 knowledge for each point (2), 1 analysis for each developed point (2), 2 evaluation for a justified choice of the most important that says why it beats the other.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
City Mart is a supermarket in Rawalpindi. A large discount supermarket has opened nearby. City Mart's monthly revenue is Rs 30 million and its cost of goods is 80% of revenue (gross profit Rs 6 million a month).
Option 1: cut all prices by 5%.
Option 2: a loyalty card giving members 2% back on purchases. 60% of revenue is expected to come from members; the card system costs Rs 0.2 million a month.
Option 3: a free home-delivery service costing Rs 0.8 million a month, expected to keep Rs 3 million of monthly revenue that would otherwise be lost to the rival.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which option should City Mart choose to respond to the new competitor? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Option 1: if volume does not change, revenue falls to Rs 28.5m and gross profit to Rs 4.5m (−Rs 1.5m); volume must rise by about 33% just to keep Rs 6m gross profit, and the discounter can always cut further. Option 2: cost 2% × 18m = Rs 0.36m + 0.2m = Rs 0.56m a month; builds loyalty and gives customer data. Option 3: keeps Rs 3m revenue = Rs 0.6m gross profit for Rs 0.8m cost (−Rs 0.2m) unless it also attracts new customers; differentiates City Mart from the discounter. Judgement e.g.: Option 3: on the figures given it costs least (net Rs 0.2m a month). Option 2 would need to keep about Rs 1.8m of extra monthly revenue (20% gross margin) to match it, and Option 1 costs about Rs 1.5m a month of gross profit.
parts.working: Calculations: 30m × 0.95 = 28.5m; 28.5m − 24m = 4.5m; required sales at old prices 6m ÷ 0.15 = 40m (+33.3%); 0.02 × 0.6 × 30m = 0.36m; 0.36m + 0.2m = 0.56m; 20% × 3m = 0.6m. Option 2 match: 20% × R − 0.56m = −0.2m gives R = Rs 1.8m. Levels: L3 (9–12) a justified recommendation that weighs the options against each other, uses the case data (and calculations where asked) and explains why the rejected option is weaker; L2 (5–8) developed analysis of the options applied to the business, decision only partly supported; L1 (1–4) relevant knowledge with limited application, or a bare decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Laws in many countries control how businesses market their products.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ways the law protects consumers from unfair marketing.
parts.answer: Any two: bans misleading/false advertising and labelling; requires goods to be of acceptable quality and fit for purpose; gives refunds/repairs for faulty goods; prevents exploitation, e.g. unfair pricing or pressure selling; controls weights and measures.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one reason why governments control marketing activities.
parts.answer: Consumers usually know less than businesses about a product, so without laws they could be misled into buying unsafe or poor-value goods.
parts.working: 1 mark reason; 1 mark development.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Basmati Gold sells rice in Pakistan, where it has 30% of the market. It plans to start selling in East Africa.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two opportunities for Basmati Gold of selling in foreign markets.
parts.answer: Any two: more customers and higher sales; growth when the home market is saturated; spreads risk across countries; economies of scale; higher prices abroad.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways Basmati Gold could reduce the problems of entering a foreign market.
parts.answer: Any two: form a joint venture with a local business; use a local agent/distributor; licensing; carry out market research in the new country; adapt packaging/product to local tastes.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Zest Juices wants to increase its sales to teenagers by 20% next year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'marketing strategy'.
parts.answer: A plan that combines the elements of the marketing mix (product, price, place, promotion) to achieve a marketing objective.
parts.working: 1 mark: plan; 1 mark: using the marketing mix to achieve marketing objectives.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two marketing objectives, other than increasing sales, that a business might have.
parts.answer: Any two: increase market share; enter a new market; improve brand image/awareness; develop new products; increase customer loyalty.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Two products: (i) a luxury Swiss-style wristwatch costing $3,000; (ii) a bar of washing soap costing $0.50.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline which element of the marketing mix is likely to be most important to customers when buying each product.
parts.answer: (i) Product/brand (or promotion of image): buyers want quality, prestige and design, and price is less important. (ii) Price (or place): soap is an everyday product with many similar brands, so customers choose the cheapest one that is easily available.
parts.working: For each product: 1 mark element, 1 mark reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hill Top Tea is launching a cold, ready-to-drink green tea aimed at university students in Pakistan's big cities.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two features of the target market for this product.
parts.answer: Any two: aged about 18–24; live in cities; limited incomes; use social media; health-conscious; want convenience.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two elements of a suitable marketing strategy for the new drink.
parts.answer: (1) Promotion: social-media campaigns with student influencers and free samples on campuses, because students spend a lot of time online. (2) Price/place: a low price per bottle and sales through campus cafés, convenience stores and vending machines, because students have limited money and want drinks on the go. Product/packaging points also acceptable.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hot Pot sells electric kettles. A fault means some kettles can overheat. Consumer law requires it to offer customers a full refund. 3,000 kettles have been sold at Rs 2,200 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum cost of refunds if every customer returns a kettle. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways consumer protection laws could affect Hot Pot.
parts.answer: (1) Costs rise: refunds, recall and testing costs (up to Rs 6.6 million) reduce profit. (2) Reputation: the recall may be reported in the media, so customers may avoid Hot Pot products; it must also change labelling/advertising so claims are accurate. Also: may be fined if it ignores the law; must improve quality control.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Toon Town, a Pakistani company that owns a popular cartoon character, licenses a company in Saudi Arabia to use the character on toys and clothing. It receives 7% of the Saudi company's sales.

parts.label: a
