parts.text: Calculate Toon Town's licence income if the Saudi company's sales are $1.8 million. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to Toon Town of entering the Saudi market by licensing.
parts.answer: Advantage: income with almost no investment or risk, and the Saudi company knows local tastes, laws and shops. Disadvantage: only 7% of sales – much less than selling directly – and little control over product quality, which could damage the character's image.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Punjab Grains exports rice to the Middle East. It now wants to sell packaged rice in supermarkets in Kenya, where it has no contacts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two problems Punjab Grains might face when entering the Kenyan market.
parts.answer: (1) Lack of local knowledge: it does not know Kenyan tastes, prices or which supermarkets to approach, so its products may not sell. (2) Different laws and import rules: labelling and food-safety rules may differ, so packaging must change, increasing costs; import tariffs could also raise prices. Also: strong local competitors, exchange-rate risk, transport costs/distance, cultural/language differences.
parts.working: For each of two points: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to the case, 2 marks developed analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Thread Art sells embroidered cushions in Pakistan for Rs 2,800. It wants to sell in Saudi Arabia, where the exchange rate is 1 Saudi riyal (SAR) = Rs 75.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price of one cushion in SAR if the Pakistani price is simply converted. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think Thread Art should change its marketing mix for the Saudi market? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Change: Saudi customers may prefer different colours and designs, so the product may need adapting; prices must cover transport and tariffs and match local incomes and competitors; promotion must suit local culture and language; selling through local retailers or online platforms. Keep the same: lower costs, consistent brand, economies of scale. Judgement: adapt price and promotion at least, possibly product, based on market research.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Burger Bay, a fast-food chain with 25 restaurants in Pakistan, wants to open in Malaysia.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two legal controls that could affect Burger Bay's marketing in Malaysia.
parts.answer: Any two: rules on misleading advertising; food labelling and halal certification rules; product safety/hygiene standards; consumer rights to refunds; controls on advertising to children.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two methods Burger Bay could use to enter the Malaysian market. Which method is likely to be the best? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: (1) Franchising: Malaysian franchisees pay fees and run restaurants with local knowledge, so growth is fast and low-cost, but Burger Bay has less control over quality. (2) Joint venture with a Malaysian food company: shares costs and local knowledge, but profits and decisions are shared. Also: own restaurants (full control, high risk). Best e.g. franchising, because it suits a restaurant format and reduces risk.
parts.working: Marks: 1 knowledge for each point (2), 1 analysis for each developed point (2), 2 evaluation for a justified choice of the most important that says why it beats the other.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
VoltRide plans to launch an electric scooter in Lahore. It must choose a marketing strategy.
Option 1: premium strategy – price Rs 180,000; sold only in its own showroom; promoted by social-media influencers costing Rs 20 million; forecast sales 1,500 scooters; cost of making each scooter Rs 120,000.
Option 2: mass-market strategy – price Rs 150,000; sold through electronics retailers, who keep 10% of the price; newspaper and radio advertising costing Rs 8 million; forecast sales 3,000 scooters; making cost falls to Rs 115,000 per scooter because of bulk buying.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which marketing strategy should VoltRide choose? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Option 1 profit: 1,500 × (180,000 − 120,000) − 20m = Rs 70 million. Option 2: retailer keeps 15,000, so VoltRide receives 135,000; 3,000 × (135,000 − 115,000) − 8m = Rs 52 million. Option 1 gives Rs 18 million more forecast profit and a premium image, but relies on only one showroom and influencer success. Option 2 sells twice as many scooters, builds market share and wide availability. Judgement e.g.: Option 1 for the launch (higher profit, lower volume risk), moving to wider distribution later.
parts.working: Calculations: 1,500 × 60,000 = 90m; 90m − 20m = 70m; 10% × 150,000 = 15,000; 3,000 × 20,000 = 60m; 60m − 8m = 52m. Levels: L3 (9–12) a justified recommendation that weighs the options against each other, uses the case data (and calculations where asked) and explains why the rejected option is weaker; L2 (5–8) developed analysis of the options applied to the business, decision only partly supported; L1 (1–4) relevant knowledge with limited application, or a bare decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
LearnHub is a Pakistani online-learning app. It wants to enter the Saudi Arabian market. Forecast annual sales in Saudi Arabia are $2 million.
Option A: license its content to a Saudi education company, receiving a 12% royalty on sales. No set-up cost.
Option B: open its own office in Riyadh. Set-up cost $500,000. LearnHub would keep all sales but have annual running costs of $1.6 million. With full control of marketing it expects sales of $2.4 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which option should LearnHub choose? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Option A: 12% × 2m = $240,000 a year, almost no risk. Option B: profit 2.4m − 1.6m = $800,000 a year; first year after set-up $300,000; set-up repaid in 0.625 years of profit. B earns far more if forecasts are right and gives full control of brand and content, but it risks $500,000 in a market LearnHub does not know, with local laws and culture to learn. A is safe but low return and less control. Judgement e.g.: B if research supports the $2.4m forecast; otherwise start with A to test demand.
parts.working: Calculations: 0.12 × 2,000,000 = 240,000; 2,400,000 − 1,600,000 = 800,000; 800,000 − 500,000 = 300,000; 500,000 ÷ 800,000 = 0.625 years. Levels: L3 (9–12) a justified recommendation that weighs the options against each other, uses the case data (and calculations where asked) and explains why the rejected option is weaker; L2 (5–8) developed analysis of the options applied to the business, decision only partly supported; L1 (1–4) relevant knowledge with limited application, or a bare decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: AutoCare Service Centre in Hyderabad has taken on four trainee mechanics. They will learn by working alongside experienced mechanics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'on-the-job training'.
parts.answer: Training given at the workplace while the employee does the job, usually by watching and helping an experienced worker.
parts.working: 1 mark: at the workplace / while working; 1 mark: learning from experienced worker.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two disadvantages to AutoCare of on-the-job training.
parts.answer: Any two: the experienced mechanic's work slows down; trainees may learn bad habits; mistakes on customers' cars; training is limited to the centre's own methods.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Shifa General Hospital is recruiting 20 new nurses. At present it selects nurses only by interview.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two selection methods, other than interviews, that the hospital could use.
parts.answer: Any two: skills/practical tests; written tests; checking references; checking qualifications/certificates; trial shift/assessment centre.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the hospital should use tests as well as interviews to select nurses.
parts.answer: (1) Tests show whether applicants really have practical skills such as giving injections safely – an interview only shows how well they talk, and mistakes can harm patients. (2) Tests are the same for everyone, so selection is fairer and easier to compare, reducing the risk of choosing the wrong person and the cost of recruiting again.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Royal Palm Hotel in Lahore employs 180 staff in kitchens, housekeeping and reception. It has recently been fined for unsafe kitchen equipment, and a receptionist has complained that she was paid less than a male colleague doing the same job.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways legal controls over employment affect Royal Palm Hotel.
parts.answer: (1) Health and safety laws: the hotel must provide safe equipment, training and protective clothing – this raises costs and fines show non-compliance damages profit and reputation. (2) Discrimination/equal pay laws: it must pay men and women equally for the same work, so it may have to raise the receptionist's pay and could face legal claims; recruitment must also be fair. Also: minimum wage, contracts of employment, unfair dismissal rules.
parts.working: For each of two points: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to the case, 2 marks developed analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: SkyLink Airways must train 25 new cabin crew. An off-the-job course at an aviation academy costs $1,400 per person and takes four weeks. On-the-job training on real flights would cost about $600 per person, mainly for the time of senior crew.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how much more the off-the-job course would cost in total than on-the-job training. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think SkyLink Airways should choose off-the-job training for its new cabin crew? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Off-the-job: expert trainers, safety and emergency procedures practised in simulators without risk to passengers, recognised certificates – but costs $20,000 more and crew cannot work for four weeks. On-the-job: cheaper, learn the airline's own routines, but safety mistakes on real flights could be serious. Judgement e.g.: off-the-job, because safety training is essential and legally required in aviation.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Tech Bazaar has grown from 6 to 70 employees. The owner has drawn its first organisational chart.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'organisational structure'.
parts.answer: The way a business is arranged into levels and departments, showing who is responsible to whom and how communication flows.
parts.working: 1 mark: arrangement/levels/departments; 1 mark: roles, responsibility or lines of authority.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two advantages to Tech Bazaar of having a clear organisational structure.
parts.answer: Any two: everyone knows who their manager is; clear responsibilities; easier communication; shows routes for promotion; helps new staff understand the business.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Golden Harvest Ltd processes rice. It has directors, managers, supervisors and production workers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two responsibilities of a supervisor.
parts.answer: Any two: watch over/check the work of a team of workers; make sure targets are met; deal with day-to-day problems; help train workers; report to managers.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two responsibilities of directors.
parts.answer: Any two: set the objectives and long-term strategy; make major decisions such as new factories; represent shareholders' interests; appoint senior managers; are accountable for the company's performance.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: BlueSky Couriers has 4 levels of hierarchy. The managing director manages 4 regional managers; each regional manager manages 4 depot managers; each depot manager manages 4 drivers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total number of people in the organisation. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of a wider span of control for BlueSky's depot managers.
parts.answer: Advantage: fewer managers needed and a flatter structure, so lower costs and faster communication with drivers. Disadvantage: each manager has less time per driver, so supervision and support may be weaker and mistakes in deliveries may increase.
parts.working: Advantage 1 + 1 development; disadvantage 1 + 1 development.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Workers at Karakoram Bottling Ltd belong to a trade union. Instead of each worker discussing pay with managers, the union negotiates pay and conditions for all of them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'collective bargaining'.
parts.answer: Negotiation between a trade union, on behalf of all its members, and employers about pay and working conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark: negotiation between union and employer; 1 mark: on behalf of all members / about pay and conditions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits to Karakoram Bottling Ltd's managers of negotiating with the trade union.
parts.answer: (1) Saves time: managers negotiate once with union representatives instead of with hundreds of workers, so agreements are reached faster. (2) Better communication and fewer disputes: the union passes on workers' views and explains decisions to members, so strikes and lost production are less likely. Also: agreements are clearer and fairer, reducing complaints.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: PixelForge is a new video-game studio in Karachi with 12 highly skilled programmers and artists. The founder lets the team decide how to do their work and only checks progress once a month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why delegation may fail.
parts.answer: Any two: staff lack the skills or training; manager does not give enough authority; poor communication of what is expected; manager unwilling to let go / interferes; staff overloaded.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think a laissez-faire leadership style is suitable for PixelForge? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Suitable: skilled, creative staff are motivated by freedom and may produce original game ideas; the founder can focus on finance and marketing. Unsuitable: without deadlines and checks a new studio may miss launch dates and run out of money; staff may lack direction. Judgement e.g.: suitable for creative work, but combined with agreed deadlines and regular progress reviews, because a new business cannot afford delays.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Value Plus runs 10 discount stores, each with 40 staff. For six months it trialled two leadership styles. Each store's output (sales) is worth Rs 50 million a year and its gross profit is 30% of sales. Replacing each worker who leaves costs Rs 80,000.
Appendix:
Item | Store X (autocratic manager) | Store Y (democratic manager)
Increase in sales | 12% | 6%
Absence rate | 9% | 3%
Staff leaving each year | 25% | 10%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which leadership style should Value Plus use in its stores? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Store X: extra sales Rs 6 million, so extra gross profit 30% × 6m = Rs 1.8 million; 10 leavers × 80,000 = Rs 800,000 replacement cost; net gain Rs 1.0 million. Store Y: extra sales Rs 3 million, so extra gross profit Rs 0.9 million; 4 leavers × 80,000 = Rs 320,000; net gain Rs 0.58 million. On these figures X gives about Rs 0.42 million more a year, but high absence and turnover suggest low morale that may cut service quality and sales later; Y's style gives a more stable, motivated workforce. A sound answer may choose either, or a mix (autocratic for urgent tasks, democratic otherwise), and should note the trial is only one store each for six months.
parts.working: Calculations: 12% × 50m = 6m; 30% × 6m = 1.8m; 25% × 40 = 10; 10 × 80,000 = 800,000; net 1.8m − 0.8m = 1.0m; 6% × 50m = 3m; 30% × 3m = 0.9m; 10% × 40 = 4; 4 × 80,000 = 320,000; net 0.9m − 0.32m = 0.58m. Levels: L3 (9–12) a justified recommendation that weighs the options against each other, uses the case data (and calculations where asked) and explains why the rejected option is weaker; L2 (5–8) developed analysis of the options applied to the business, decision only partly supported; L1 (1–4) relevant knowledge with limited application, or a bare decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Sapphire Call Centre in Islamabad wants to motivate its staff without increasing pay.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two non-financial methods of motivation.
parts.answer: Any two: job rotation; job enlargement; job enrichment; teamworking; training; opportunities for promotion; praise/recognition.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'job enrichment'.
parts.answer: Giving workers more responsibility and more challenging, interesting tasks, often including some decision-making.
parts.working: 1 mark: more responsibility/challenging tasks; 1 mark: e.g. decision-making, using more skills.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bilal sells solar panels for SunPower. He receives a basic salary of Rs 40,000 a month plus a commission of 2% of the value of his sales. Last month he sold panels worth Rs 1,500,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'commission'.
parts.answer: Payment to a salesperson based on a percentage of the value of the sales they make.
parts.working: 1 mark: payment related to sales; 1 mark: percentage of value of sales.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Bilal's total pay last month. Show your working.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The manager of Prime Garments has noticed that many workers are often absent and output has fallen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two signs that a workforce is poorly motivated.
parts.answer: Any two: high absenteeism; high labour turnover (many leaving); low output/productivity; poor quality work; many complaints/disputes; lateness.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'fringe benefits' and give one example.
parts.answer: Benefits given to employees in addition to their wage or salary, e.g. a company car, free meals, health insurance or discounts.
parts.working: 1 mark definition (non-wage benefits); 1 mark example.

author: HomiLabs

stem: City Hospital is considering paying its nurses according to how many patients each one treats per shift, as a way of increasing output.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline Taylor's view of what motivates workers.
parts.answer: Taylor believed workers are motivated mainly by money, so they should be paid by output (piece rate) and work should be broken into simple, measured tasks.
parts.working: 1 mark: money is the main motivator; 1 mark: pay by output / scientific management of tasks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Taylor's approach may not work for City Hospital's nurses.
parts.answer: (1) Nursing quality matters more than quantity – paying per patient may encourage rushing, putting patients at risk. (2) Nurses are often motivated by caring for patients, teamwork and recognition rather than only money, and some patients need much more time than others, so output is hard to measure fairly.
parts.working: 2 × (1 mark reason + 1 mark development/application).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Herzberg divided factors at work into hygiene factors and motivators. Consider these factors at Lucky Tiles Ltd: salary; recognition for good work; working conditions; responsibility; company rules; promotion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each of the six factors as a hygiene factor or a motivator.
parts.answer: Hygiene factors: salary, working conditions, company rules. Motivators: recognition, responsibility, promotion.
parts.working: 3 marks all six correct; 2 marks four or five; 1 mark two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why improving hygiene factors alone may not motivate workers at Lucky Tiles Ltd.
parts.answer: According to Herzberg, hygiene factors only prevent dissatisfaction; once they are adequate, better pay or conditions will not make workers work harder. To motivate, the business needs motivators such as recognition or more responsibility.
parts.working: 1 mark: hygiene factors remove dissatisfaction; 1 mark: they do not motivate on their own; 1 mark: need motivators / example.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Evergreen Furniture plans to share 5% of its annual profit equally among its 80 employees. Last year profit was Rs 24 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how much each employee would receive. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to Evergreen Furniture of introducing profit sharing.
parts.answer: Advantage: workers share in success, so they may work harder, waste less and suggest cost savings, which raises profit. Disadvantage: it reduces profit available for owners/reinvestment (Rs 1.2 million), and if profit falls the payment shrinks, which could demotivate workers whose individual effort cannot change total profit much.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Star Apparel employs 300 sewing machinists in Lahore. Each machinist sews the same part of a shirt all day. Absence is high and many workers leave within a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two non-financial methods Star Apparel could use to motivate its machinists.
parts.answer: (1) Job rotation: machinists move between sewing collars, sleeves and buttons, which reduces boredom and makes the workforce more flexible when someone is absent. (2) Teamworking: small teams responsible for completing whole shirts and checking their own quality, giving a sense of belonging and responsibility, which may reduce absence and labour turnover. Also: training and promotion to supervisor, recognition (worker of the month).
parts.working: For each of two points: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to the case, 2 marks developed analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: QuickConnect, a call centre in Rawalpindi, offers its staff: (i) a free hot lunch; (ii) a permanent contract after six months; (iii) a monthly team award presented by the director; (iv) training to become a team leader.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the level of Maslow's hierarchy satisfied by (i) and by (iv).
parts.answer: (i) physiological needs; (iv) self-actualisation (or esteem – accept either with reason).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think financial rewards are more important than non-financial rewards in motivating QuickConnect's staff? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Financial: pay meets basic and security needs; if pay is low, staff leave for slightly higher pay elsewhere (Taylor; Herzberg's hygiene factor). Non-financial: recognition, security and training meet higher needs and keep staff once pay is fair (Maslow, Herzberg's motivators). Judgement e.g.: pay must first be fair, but non-financial rewards matter more for long-term motivation in repetitive call-centre work.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hotel Sunrise pays its kitchen staff Rs 250 an hour for the first 40 hours a week. Overtime hours above 40 are paid at 1.5 times the normal rate. Last week Asif worked 48 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Asif's pay for last week. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think offering overtime is a good way for Hotel Sunrise to motivate its kitchen staff? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: staff earn more, which helps meet basic needs; hotel can cover busy periods without recruiting. Against: long hours cause tiredness, mistakes and accidents in a kitchen; overtime costs 50% more per hour; staff may work slowly to gain overtime; it does not meet higher needs. Judgement e.g.: useful for short busy periods but not a long-term motivator.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Fresh Basket, a supermarket chain, employs 200 workers. 30% leave each year, and replacing each one costs Rs 90,000 for recruitment and training. The HR manager is considering two options.
Option 1: a 6% pay rise. The wage bill is Rs 5 million a month. Leavers are expected to fall to 40 a year.
Option 2: a training and promotion programme costing Rs 2.5 million to set up and Rs 0.5 million a year to run. Leavers are expected to fall to 30 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which option should Fresh Basket choose to motivate its workers? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Now: 60 leavers × 90,000 = Rs 5.4 million a year. Option 1: cost 6% × 5m × 12 = Rs 3.6 million a year (every year); saving 20 × 90,000 = Rs 1.8 million; net cost Rs 1.8 million a year. Option 2: first-year cost Rs 3.0 million, then Rs 0.5 million a year; saving 30 × 90,000 = Rs 2.7 million; net cost Rs 0.3 million in year 1 and a net gain of Rs 2.2 million a year after. Option 2 is better financially and meets higher-level needs (Maslow/Herzberg), but depends on forecasts; pay may matter more if wages are below competitors'.
parts.working: Calculations: 0.3 × 200 = 60; 60 × 90,000 = 5.4m; 0.06 × 5m × 12 = 3.6m; 20 × 90,000 = 1.8m; 2.5m + 0.5m = 3.0m; 30 × 90,000 = 2.7m. Levels: L3 (9–12) a justified recommendation that weighs the options against each other, uses the case data (and calculations where asked) and explains why the rejected option is weaker; L2 (5–8) developed analysis of the options applied to the business, decision only partly supported; L1 (1–4) relevant knowledge with limited application, or a bare decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Pak Agro Machinery sells tractors to farmers across Punjab.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'external communication'.
parts.answer: The exchange of information between the business and people or organisations outside it, such as customers, suppliers and the government.
parts.working: 1 mark: exchange of messages; 1 mark: with people/organisations outside the business.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two methods Pak Agro Machinery could use to communicate with farmers.
parts.answer: Any two: SMS text messages; radio advertisements; social media; visits by sales staff; leaflets at markets; telephone calls; website.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The manager of Fine Print, a printing company, gives instructions to staff both in writing and verbally.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages of written communication.
parts.answer: Any two: provides a permanent record; can be checked/referred to later; can be sent to many people at once; detailed/technical information can be given accurately.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two disadvantages of verbal communication.
parts.answer: Any two: no permanent record; messages may be forgotten or misunderstood; difficult with large numbers of people; details can be changed as messages are passed on.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Hamdard Logistics' warehouse staff often load the wrong goods because they misunderstand the order sheets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two benefits to a business of effective communication.
parts.answer: Any two: fewer mistakes; more efficient work; better motivation; faster decisions; better relationships with customers.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'feedback' in communication.
parts.answer: The reply or response from the receiver to the sender, showing whether the message has been received and understood.
parts.working: 1 mark: response from receiver; 1 mark: confirms message understood.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Kestrel Bank has 3,000 employees in 150 branches. Head office now sends almost all instructions to staff by email.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to Kestrel Bank of using email for internal communication.
parts.answer: Advantage: the same message reaches all 3,000 staff instantly at very low cost, and gives a written record of instructions (important for banking rules). Disadvantage: staff receive too many emails and may miss important ones, and there is no immediate feedback, so misunderstandings of new procedures may cause errors with customers' accounts.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify one situation where face-to-face communication would be better than email for Kestrel Bank.
parts.answer: e.g. telling staff about branch closures/redundancies, a disciplinary meeting, or training on a new system – because it allows questions, feedback and shows care.
parts.working: 1 mark situation; 1 mark reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Green Leaf Pharmacy wants to tell its 1,200 regular customers about a new home-delivery service. Text messages cost Rs 2.50 each; printed leaflets delivered to homes cost Rs 15 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total cost of each method. Show your working.
parts.answer: Texts Rs 3,000; leaflets Rs 18,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline two factors Green Leaf Pharmacy should consider when choosing the communication method.
parts.answer: e.g. whether customers (some elderly) use mobile phones or read texts; the amount of detail needed (prices, delivery areas) – a leaflet can hold more and can be kept; speed; cost compared with the expected extra sales.
parts.working: 2 × (1 mark factor + 1 mark link to the pharmacy).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A Chinese construction company is building a motorway in Pakistan with 40 Chinese engineers and 900 Pakistani workers. Safety instructions are given in Chinese and English, and many workers speak only Urdu or Pashto.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two barriers to communication on this project.
parts.answer: Any two: language differences; technical jargon; noise on the site; distance between work sites; cultural differences; long chain of command.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways the company could improve communication with its Pakistani workers.
parts.answer: (1) Employ interpreters/bilingual supervisors and translate safety instructions into Urdu and Pashto, so workers understand rules and accidents fall. (2) Use pictures, signs and demonstrations for safety rules, which avoid language problems; hold short daily briefings with feedback to check understanding.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: ShopFast is an online store in Karachi that has grown from 20 to 250 employees in two years. Warehouse staff often hear about special offers only after customers start ordering, and the delivery team complains that they are never told about changes to routes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two problems that poor internal communication may cause for ShopFast.
parts.answer: (1) Mistakes and delays: the warehouse is not ready for orders from special offers, so goods run out or are packed late, customers complain and may switch to rival online stores. (2) Low motivation: delivery staff feel ignored, so morale falls and labour turnover rises, increasing recruitment costs. Also: wasted time, duplication, conflict between departments.
parts.working: For each of two points: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to the case, 2 marks developed analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Glow Skincare sells beauty products mainly to young customers. It now spends most of its communication budget on social media instead of newspapers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ways Glow Skincare could use social media to communicate with customers.
parts.answer: Any two: posting adverts/videos of products; answering questions and complaints; announcing offers; using influencers; customer polls/feedback.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think social media has improved Glow Skincare's communication with its customers? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Improved: two-way, instant and cheap; reaches young customers where they spend time; gives feedback and builds loyalty. Problems: negative comments spread quickly and publicly; requires staff to reply constantly; messages may be lost among many posts; older customers may be missed. Judgement e.g.: yes for its young target market, provided complaints are handled quickly.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Indus Fertilisers Ltd has 8 levels of hierarchy. Instructions from the chief executive pass down through several managers before they reach factory workers, and workers' suggestions rarely reach the top.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a long chain of command can make communication less effective.
parts.answer: Messages pass through many people, so they are slow and may be changed or distorted on the way; feedback from workers rarely reaches senior managers.
parts.working: 1 mark: slow/many levels; 1 mark: distortion or lack of feedback.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways the chief executive could improve communication with factory workers. Which way is likely to be the most important? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: (1) Delayering – remove some management levels so messages pass through fewer people. (2) Regular meetings/visits or an intranet/suggestion scheme so workers hear directly from the chief executive and can reply. Most important e.g. direct two-way meetings, because they are quicker and cheaper than restructuring and give feedback.
parts.working: Marks: 1 knowledge for each point (2), 1 analysis for each developed point (2), 2 evaluation for a justified choice of the most important that says why it beats the other.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
HomeChef has found a fault in 50,000 pressure cookers it has sold. It must tell buyers to return them. It is considering three methods.
Method 1: national newspaper and TV adverts – cost Rs 4.5 million; expected to reach 60% of buyers.
Method 2: SMS and email to buyers who registered their product – cost Rs 0.3 million; 45% of buyers registered.
Method 3: notices in shops that sold the cookers and on HomeChef's website – cost Rs 0.8 million; expected to reach 30% of buyers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which communication method should HomeChef use? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Buyers reached: M1 30,000 (Rs 150 each); M2 22,500 (about Rs 13.33 each); M3 15,000 (about Rs 53.33 each). M2 is by far the cheapest per buyer and personal, but misses 55% of buyers; M1 reaches most but is expensive and public (may damage reputation, though it shows responsibility). Because a dangerous fault could injure people and lead to legal action, the best answer may combine M2 with M1 (or M3) to reach as many buyers as possible; justify the trade-off between safety, cost and reputation.
parts.working: Calculations: 0.6 × 50,000 = 30,000; 0.45 × 50,000 = 22,500; 0.3 × 50,000 = 15,000; 4,500,000 ÷ 30,000 = 150; 300,000 ÷ 22,500 = 13.33; 800,000 ÷ 15,000 = 53.33. Levels: L3 (9–12) a justified recommendation that weighs the options against each other, uses the case data (and calculations where asked) and explains why the rejected option is weaker; L2 (5–8) developed analysis of the options applied to the business, decision only partly supported; L1 (1–4) relevant knowledge with limited application, or a bare decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Several leather tanneries near a river in Punjab release chemical waste into the water. The provincial government wants them to change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ways a government could reduce pollution caused by businesses such as the tanneries.
parts.answer: Any two: laws/regulations with fines; pollution taxes; permits/licences that limit waste; subsidies or grants for cleaner equipment; inspections.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why a tannery might choose to act in an environmentally friendly way.
parts.answer: Any two: avoid fines or closure; improve reputation; attract customers/foreign buyers who demand clean production; reduce waste and costs; avoid pressure group action.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Consumers are paying more attention to how businesses behave.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two examples of unethical business behaviour.
parts.answer: Any two: using child labour; paying workers very low wages / unsafe conditions; misleading advertising; bribery; testing products cruelly on animals; dumping waste illegally.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one way consumers can influence a business to behave more ethically.
parts.answer: Consumers can boycott (stop buying) its products, so sales fall and the business is pressured to change; or they can complain publicly on social media.
parts.working: 1 mark method; 1 mark how it pressures the business.

author: HomiLabs

stem: FoodGo is a food-delivery business in Karachi with 2,500 riders on petrol motorbikes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two external costs created by FoodGo's delivery motorbikes.
parts.answer: Any two: air pollution; noise; traffic congestion; road accidents affecting others; carbon emissions/climate change.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways FoodGo could reduce these external costs.
parts.answer: Any two: switch to electric motorbikes or bicycles; plan routes to reduce distance; group orders into one trip; train riders in safe driving; regular servicing.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A consumer group has started a social-media campaign against Trendy Threads, a clothing brand, claiming that its factories pay workers below the minimum wage. Many young customers have shared the posts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two reasons why pressure groups can be successful.
parts.answer: Any two: strong public support; media/social-media coverage; can organise boycotts that reduce sales; well-funded or expert; the issue affects many people; government may act on their concerns.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways Trendy Threads could respond to the pressure group's campaign.
parts.answer: (1) Investigate and raise wages to at least the minimum, then publish the results – this costs more but can restore its reputation and sales. (2) Use independent inspections/ethical certification and promote this in advertising, so customers trust the brand again. Also: meet the pressure group; public statement/apology; change suppliers.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Gwadar Fisheries Ltd catches fish off the coast of Balochistan. Its annual catch has fallen from 12,000 tonnes to 8,400 tonnes in five years because of overfishing in the area.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in the annual catch. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why sustainable development is important to Gwadar Fisheries Ltd.
parts.answer: (1) Its whole business depends on fish stocks – if overfishing continues, catches and revenue will keep falling until the business cannot survive. (2) Customers and export buyers increasingly want sustainably caught fish, and the government may impose quotas or bans, so acting now protects sales and avoids penalties.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Oasis Hotels owns six hotels in Pakistan. The directors think that becoming more environmentally friendly will only increase costs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways becoming more environmentally friendly could increase Oasis Hotels' profits.
parts.answer: (1) Lower costs: solar panels, LED lighting and water-saving showers reduce electricity and water bills, increasing profit after the initial investment. (2) Higher revenue: many tourists and companies prefer 'green' hotels, so Oasis can attract more guests or charge higher prices; it may also gain good publicity and government support. Also: avoid fines.
parts.working: For each of two points: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to the case, 2 marks developed analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A government plans to introduce a carbon tax of $5 per tonne of carbon dioxide (CO₂). Rock Cement's plant emits 200,000 tonnes of CO₂ a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the carbon tax Rock Cement would pay each year. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think taxes are better than laws (regulations) for reducing pollution from businesses such as Rock Cement? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Taxes: give businesses a reason to cut emissions in the cheapest way and raise government revenue; but firms may just pay and pass the cost to customers, so pollution may not fall much. Laws: set strict limits and can stop dangerous pollution quickly; but need inspection and may be costly for firms to meet all at once. Judgement e.g.: laws for very harmful pollution, taxes for gradual reduction of CO₂.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Ravi Dyeing Ltd releases untreated waste water into a canal used by farmers. The government has started fining it. The directors are considering three options.
Option 1: build its own water-treatment plant – cost Rs 45 million, then running costs Rs 3 million a year.
Option 2: carry on and pay fines of about Rs 8 million a year. Officials warn that the factory could be closed if pollution continues.
Option 3: move to an industrial estate with a shared treatment plant – moving cost Rs 20 million, then a fee of Rs 5 million a year. The estate is 40 km away and some workers may not move.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which option should Ravi Dyeing Ltd choose? Justify your answer using suitable calculations and ethical considerations.
parts.answer: Five-year cost: Option 1 = 45 + 5 × 3 = Rs 60 million; Option 2 = 5 × 8 = Rs 40 million plus risk of closure, damaged reputation and harm to farmers – unethical and probably not allowed to continue; Option 3 = 20 + 5 × 5 = Rs 45 million, cheapest legal option but loses some skilled workers and adds transport costs. Over 10 years: Option 1 = Rs 75 million, Option 3 = Rs 70 million. Judgement e.g.: Option 3 on cost, or Option 1 if keeping the workforce and site matters more; Option 2 should be rejected.
parts.working: Calculations: 45 + 15 = 60; 8 × 5 = 40; 20 + 25 = 45; 10-year: 45 + 30 = 75, 20 + 50 = 70. Levels: L3 (9–12) a justified recommendation that weighs the options against each other, uses the case data (and calculations where asked) and explains why the rejected option is weaker; L2 (5–8) developed analysis of the options applied to the business, decision only partly supported; L1 (1–4) relevant knowledge with limited application, or a bare decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The value of the Pakistani rupee against the US dollar changes every day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'exchange rate'.
parts.answer: The price of one currency in terms of another currency, e.g. $1 = Rs 280.
parts.working: 1 mark: price/value of one currency; 1 mark: in terms of another (or example).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'appreciation' of a currency.
parts.answer: A rise in the value of a currency compared with another currency, so it buys more of the other currency.
parts.working: 1 mark: rise in value; 1 mark: against another currency / buys more foreign currency.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Many countries now trade freely with each other, but some governments still use import controls.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two benefits to businesses of globalisation.
parts.answer: Any two: access to larger markets abroad; cheaper raw materials/components from abroad; can produce where costs are lower; economies of scale; access to new technology and ideas.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why governments introduce import controls.
parts.answer: Any two: protect local businesses and jobs; protect new (infant) industries; reduce imports to improve the balance of trade; raise revenue (tariffs); stop unsafe or harmful goods.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Textile Tech in Faisalabad is buying a knitting machine from Germany for €20,000. When it ordered, the exchange rate was €1 = Rs 300. When it pays, the rate is €1 = Rs 320.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of the machine in rupees at each exchange rate and the increase in cost. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the rupee has appreciated or depreciated against the euro, and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Depreciated – more rupees are now needed to buy €1.
parts.working: 1 mark depreciated; 1 mark reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem: GlobalFoods plc makes packaged food in 30 countries, including a large factory in Pakistan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ways a multinational such as GlobalFoods could benefit local businesses in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any two: buys raw materials (e.g. milk, wheat) from local suppliers; local transport/packaging firms win contracts; workers' spending helps local shops; training spreads skills to local firms.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits to GlobalFoods of producing in many countries.
parts.answer: (1) Lower costs: it can produce where wages, land or raw materials are cheaper, increasing profit margins. (2) Closer to customers: producing inside each country avoids import tariffs and transport costs and allows products to be adapted to local tastes; spreads risk if one market falls. Also: access to local raw materials, government incentives.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A government has cut the number of cars that can be imported each year from 12,000 to 5,000 (an import quota). Indus Auto Assembly assembles cars in Karachi.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in the number of cars that can be imported. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways the import quota could affect Indus Auto Assembly.
parts.answer: (1) Less competition from imported cars, so demand for its locally assembled cars rises and it may sell more or raise prices. (2) If it imports parts or the government's trading partners retaliate, its costs or export opportunities could be hit; with less competition it may also become less efficient. Also: may need to increase capacity/recruit.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Lahore Linen Ltd imports dyes and machinery parts from Europe and exports bed sheets to the UK. Over the last year the rupee has depreciated by 15% against the pound and the euro.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways the depreciation of the rupee could affect Lahore Linen Ltd.
parts.answer: (1) Exports become cheaper in pounds (or more profitable in rupees if the pound price is kept), so UK orders may rise and revenue increases. (2) Imported dyes and parts cost more in rupees, raising costs of production and reducing the profit margin on each sheet unless prices rise. Overall effect depends on how much of its costs are imported compared with export revenue.
parts.working: For each of two points: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to the case, 2 marks developed analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Sialkot Gloves exports 10,000 pairs of sports gloves a year to the USA at $8 a pair. Its costs are Rs 1,800 a pair. The exchange rate has changed from $1 = Rs 280 to $1 = Rs 250.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual profit in rupees at each exchange rate. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think Sialkot Gloves should raise its dollar price to protect its profit? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: profit has fallen by more than half; a price of $8.96 would restore the rupee profit per pair (8.96 × 250 = 2,240). Against: US buyers can switch to suppliers in other countries, so sales may fall; long-term customers may accept a small rise only. Judgement e.g.: raise slightly and cut costs, depending on how unique its gloves are and on competitors' prices.
parts.working: Price needed: 2,240 ÷ 250 = $8.96. Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Mehran Ceramics makes tableware in Pakistan. It wants to sell 100,000 sets a year in Country X at $12 a set.
Option 1: export from Pakistan. Production cost $6 a set; shipping $1.50 a set; Country X charges an import tariff of 20% on the value of the goods including shipping.
Option 2: build a factory in Country X costing $1.2 million. Production cost there would be $7 a set (higher wages) with no shipping or tariff.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which option should Mehran Ceramics choose? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Option 1: tariff 20% × 7.50 = $1.50; profit per set 12 − 6 − 1.50 − 1.50 = $3; annual profit $300,000; no investment. Option 2: profit per set 12 − 7 = $5; annual profit $500,000; it earns $200,000 a year more than exporting, so the $1.2 million factory takes 6 years to pay back from that extra profit. Option 2 earns more each year and avoids future tariff rises, but needs large investment, knowledge of foreign laws and labour, and risk if demand falls. Judgement e.g.: Option 2 only if research confirms demand in Country X and the company can fund Rs 1.2 million; otherwise Option 1, which needs no investment.
parts.working: Calculations: 0.2 × (6 + 1.5) = 1.5; 12 − 6 − 1.5 − 1.5 = 3; 3 × 100,000 = 300,000; 5 × 100,000 = 500,000; 1,200,000 ÷ 200,000 = 6. Levels: L3 (9–12) a justified recommendation that weighs the options against each other, uses the case data (and calculations where asked) and explains why the rejected option is weaker; L2 (5–8) developed analysis of the options applied to the business, decision only partly supported; L1 (1–4) relevant knowledge with limited application, or a bare decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Imported running shoes sell for $40 a pair before tax. A government plans to add an import tariff of 25%. The exchange rate is $1 = Rs 280. Local shoe makers support the tariff; shoe shops that sell imported brands oppose it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price of a pair of imported shoes in rupees after the tariff, assuming the full tariff is added to the price. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think the government should protect local shoe makers with the import tariff? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: local makers face less price competition, so they sell more and keep jobs; government gains tariff revenue. Against: consumers pay more (Rs 11,200 → Rs 14,000); shops selling imports lose sales; local makers may become inefficient; other countries may retaliate against Pakistani exports. Judgement needed – e.g. only short-term protection while local firms improve quality.
parts.working: Price without tariff 40 × 280 = Rs 11,200. Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A government is worried about rising prices and the number of people without jobs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'inflation'.
parts.answer: A continuing rise in the general level of prices in an economy over time.
parts.working: 1 mark: rise in prices; 1 mark: general level / sustained over time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'unemployment'.
parts.answer: When people who are able and willing to work cannot find a job.
parts.working: 1 mark: without a job; 1 mark: able/willing/looking for work.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Country Z's total output (GDP) rose by 4% last year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'economic growth'.
parts.answer: An increase in the total output of goods and services (GDP) of an economy over time.
parts.working: 1 mark: increase in output/GDP; 1 mark: of the whole economy over time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two effects of rising unemployment on businesses.
parts.answer: Any two: lower sales as people have less income; easier to recruit workers; wages may rise more slowly; more demand for cheaper/inferior goods.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: The central bank has lowered interest rates from 15% to 12%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'interest rate'.
parts.answer: The cost of borrowing money (or the reward for saving), shown as a percentage of the amount borrowed per year.
parts.working: 1 mark: cost of borrowing/reward for saving; 1 mark: percentage of the amount per year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why a government or central bank may lower interest rates.
parts.answer: Any two: to encourage spending and borrowing; to increase economic growth; to reduce unemployment; to help the economy out of a recession.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Electro World sells microwave ovens. The price before sales tax is Rs 2,500 per small oven and the government charges sales tax of 18%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the price of the oven including sales tax. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways an increase in sales tax could affect Electro World.
parts.answer: Any two: higher prices reduce sales; lower profit if it absorbs part of the tax; customers may buy cheaper models; more administration.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Growth in Country P's GDP over four years: Year 1 +5%; Year 2 +2%; Year 3 −1%; Year 4 −2%. Speedy Motors sells new cars in Country P.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the stage of the business cycle in Year 4 and give one reason.
parts.answer: Recession (or slump) – GDP is falling for the second year in a row.
parts.working: 1 mark stage; 1 mark reason from data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways Speedy Motors could respond to this stage of the business cycle.
parts.answer: (1) Offer cheaper models or finance deals, because falling incomes mean customers delay buying new cars; this keeps some sales. (2) Cut costs – reduce inventory of new cars and staff overtime – so cash is not tied up and losses are limited; it could also expand repairs and second-hand sales which hold up better in a recession.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: School Smart signed a contract last year to supply uniforms to a group of schools at a fixed price of Rs 1,000 per uniform for three years. When it signed, each uniform cost Rs 800 to make. Inflation has raised its costs by 12%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the new cost of making one uniform and the profit per uniform now. Show your working.
parts.answer: Cost Rs 896; profit Rs 104

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why high inflation makes it difficult for School Smart to plan.
parts.answer: (1) It cannot predict future costs of cloth, wages and transport, so fixed-price contracts may become unprofitable (profit per uniform has already fallen from Rs 200 to Rs 104). (2) Customers' spending power changes, so sales forecasts and cash-flow forecasts are less reliable; wage demands from workers are also harder to predict.
parts.working: 2 × (1 mark reason + 1 mark development/application).

author: HomiLabs

stem: The government has announced a large increase in spending on new roads and bridges. Pioneer Cement makes cement in northern Pakistan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two areas of government spending, other than roads.
parts.answer: Any two: education; health/hospitals; defence; welfare/pensions; water supply; electricity.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways the increase in government spending on roads could affect Pioneer Cement.
parts.answer: (1) Higher demand for cement from construction firms building roads, so sales and profit rise and it may use spare capacity or hire workers. (2) Better roads reduce transport times and costs for delivering cement; but higher demand may also raise prices of fuel/raw materials or attract new competitors, and the government may raise taxes to pay for the spending.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Shan Biscuits Ltd made a profit before tax of Rs 30 million. The government has raised the tax on company profits from 29% to 32%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the increase in tax Shan Biscuits Ltd will pay. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline two ways the higher tax on profits could affect the decisions of Shan Biscuits Ltd.
parts.answer: e.g. less retained profit to finance a new production line, so expansion may be delayed; lower dividends for shareholders; may look for cost savings or raise prices to protect profit after tax.
parts.working: 2 × (1 mark effect + 1 mark development).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Dream Homes builds houses in new housing estates around Islamabad. Most buyers borrow from banks to buy a house. The central bank has just cut interest rates.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways a fall in interest rates could benefit Dream Homes.
parts.answer: (1) Mortgage repayments fall, so more families can afford to borrow and buy houses – demand and sales of Dream Homes' houses rise, and it may be able to raise prices. (2) Dream Homes' own loans for land and building materials cost less in interest, reducing costs and increasing profit, making it cheaper to start new estates.
parts.working: For each of two points: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to the case, 2 marks developed analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In Country Q the labour force is 72 million people, and 5.4 million of them are unemployed. Fresh Pack Foods needs to hire 200 new factory workers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the unemployment rate. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think high unemployment is good for Fresh Pack Foods? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Good: many applicants, so it is easy to recruit 200 workers; wage demands are lower; workers value their jobs and may work harder. Bad: unemployed people have less income, so demand for packaged food may fall (or switch to cheaper brands); government may raise taxes to pay benefits. Judgement depends on whether Fresh Pack sells basic foods (demand stable) or luxury snacks (demand falls).
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Prices in a country rose by 12% last year. Workers at Kohat Garments earn Rs 50,000 a month. The trade union wants a 12% pay rise; the managers offer 8%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate a worker's monthly pay after an 8% rise and after a 12% rise. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think Kohat Garments should give its workers a 12% pay rise? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: with only 8%, workers' real income falls (prices +12%), lowering motivation and possibly causing strikes or labour turnover. Against: higher wage costs reduce profit and competitiveness, especially for exports; the firm's own costs are already rising with inflation; it may lead to further price rises. Judgement e.g.: a rise close to inflation if it can raise prices or productivity; otherwise 8% plus non-financial benefits.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Coastal Cold Storage wants to build a new warehouse costing Rs 50 million, financed by a bank loan. The interest rate is now 20% a year, but economists expect it to fall to 15% next year. Inflation is high, so building costs are expected to rise by 10% if it waits a year. The new warehouse is forecast to add Rs 14 million a year to profit before interest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Should Coastal Cold Storage build the warehouse now or wait one year? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Build now: annual interest 20% × 50m = Rs 10 million; profit after interest Rs 4 million a year, starting a year earlier. Wait: cost 50m × 1.1 = Rs 55 million; interest 15% × 55m = Rs 8.25 million; profit after interest Rs 5.75 million a year – but one year's profit (Rs 4 million) is lost, and the interest-rate fall is only a forecast. Waiting gives Rs 1.75 million more a year from year 2, so it takes over two years to make up the lost first year. Judgement e.g.: build now (and refinance if rates fall) unless the business is uncertain about demand.
parts.working: Calculations: 0.2 × 50 = 10; 14 − 10 = 4; 50 × 1.1 = 55; 0.15 × 55 = 8.25; 14 − 8.25 = 5.75; 5.75 − 4 = 1.75; 4 ÷ 1.75 ≈ 2.3 years. Levels: L3 (9–12) a justified recommendation that weighs the options against each other, uses the case data (and calculations where asked) and explains why the rejected option is weaker; L2 (5–8) developed analysis of the options applied to the business, decision only partly supported; L1 (1–4) relevant knowledge with limited application, or a bare decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
AutoParts Pakistan makes car parts and employs 200 workers, each paid Rs 45,000 a month. A recession has cut its orders by 25%. Managers are considering three options.
Option 1: make 50 workers redundant, paying each Rs 150,000 in redundancy pay.
Option 2: put all 200 workers on a four-day week, cutting the wage bill by 20%.
Option 3: keep all workers and spend Rs 6 million on marketing to win export orders in the Middle East; no orders are guaranteed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which option should AutoParts Pakistan choose? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Option 1: one-off cost 50 × 150,000 = Rs 7.5 million; saves 50 × 45,000 × 12 = Rs 27 million a year, so net Rs 19.5 million in year 1 (less than Option 2's Rs 21.6 million) but more after that; it loses skilled workers who are needed when the recession ends, and morale falls. Option 2: saves 20% × 200 × 45,000 × 12 = Rs 21.6 million a year with no redundancy cost; keeps skills and can return to five days quickly. Option 3: costs Rs 6 million with uncertain return, but tackles the cause (lack of orders) and spreads risk across markets. Judgement e.g.: Option 2, perhaps with some of Option 3, because recessions are temporary.
parts.working: Calculations: 50 × 150,000 = 7,500,000; 50 × 45,000 × 12 = 27,000,000; 200 × 45,000 × 12 = 108,000,000; 20% of that = 21,600,000. Levels: L3 (9–12) a justified recommendation that weighs the options against each other, uses the case data (and calculations where asked) and explains why the rejected option is weaker; L2 (5–8) developed analysis of the options applied to the business, decision only partly supported; L1 (1–4) relevant knowledge with limited application, or a bare decision.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
stem: Clay Craft makes decorative pots in Multan. Fixed costs are $30,000 a year, the variable cost is $12 per pot and each pot sells for $30.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'break-even point'.
parts.answer: The level of output (sales) at which total revenue equals total costs, so the business makes neither a profit nor a loss.
parts.working: 1 mark: output/sales level; 1 mark: total revenue = total costs / no profit, no loss.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate total cost and total revenue if Clay Craft makes and sells 2,000 pots. Show your working.
parts.answer: Total cost $54,000; total revenue $60,000

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
stem: A break-even chart for Lumina Lamps shows: the total cost line starts at $40,000 when output is zero and reaches $100,000 at 3,000 lamps; the total revenue line starts at zero and reaches $120,000 at 3,000 lamps.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the information, calculate (i) the variable cost per lamp, (ii) the selling price and (iii) the break-even output.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what would happen to the break-even output if Lumina Lamps raised its price, and why.
parts.answer: The break-even output would fall, because each lamp now earns more above its variable cost (higher contribution), so fewer lamps are needed to cover the fixed costs of $40,000 – although higher prices may reduce sales.
parts.working: 1 mark: falls; 1 mark: larger gap between price and variable cost; 1 mark: fewer units needed to cover fixed costs / caveat about demand.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
stem:
Spring Water Co. bottles mineral water. Its costs at different levels of output are:
Output (cases per month) | Total cost ($)
1,000 | 50,000
2,000 | 80,000
4,000 | 140,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average cost per case at each level of output.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why average cost falls as Spring Water Co. increases output.
parts.answer: (1) Fixed costs such as the bottling machine and rent are spread over more cases. (2) Economies of scale – e.g. purchasing economies from buying bottles and caps in bulk at a discount, or using faster machinery (technical economies).
parts.working: 2 × (1 mark reason + 1 mark explanation/application).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Costs, scale of production and break-even analysis
stem: Peshawar Leatherworks makes handbags. The price is $25, the variable cost is $14 per bag and fixed costs are $60,000 a year. It sells 8,000 bags a year but could make 11,000. A department store abroad offers to buy 2,000 extra bags at $18 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current annual profit and the extra profit from the order. Show your working.
parts.answer: Current profit $28,000; extra profit $8,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think Peshawar Leatherworks should accept the order? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: uses spare capacity, adds $8,000 profit (+29%), may lead to future orders and a new export market. Against: if existing customers learn of the $18 price they may demand discounts; the order may need overtime or reduce quality; payment and exchange-rate risk from a foreign buyer. Judgement e.g.: accept if the store is in a different market so regular prices are not affected.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Sweet Spot Bakery makes 500 chocolate cakes in the morning, then cleans the equipment and makes 400 lemon cakes in the afternoon.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'batch production'.
parts.answer: Making a quantity (batch) of one identical product, then changing the equipment to make a batch of a different product.
parts.working: 1 mark: a group/quantity of identical products made together; 1 mark: before switching to another product.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two other examples of products often made using batch production.
parts.answer: Any two: bread; biscuits; medicines/tablets; paint in different colours; clothing in different sizes; furniture ranges.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Al-Habib Pharmacy keeps a minimum level of each medicine in stock in case supplies are late.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why a business holds buffer inventory.
parts.answer: Any two: in case deliveries are late; to meet unexpected rises in demand; to avoid stopping production/sales; to avoid losing customers.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two costs of holding inventory.
parts.answer: Any two: storage space/rent; insurance; security; risk of products going out of date or being damaged; money tied up (opportunity cost).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Oak Line Furniture in Gujranwala makes sofas on a long production line. It is changing to cell production, where teams of 6 workers each make complete sofas.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'cell production'.
parts.answer: A form of lean production where the production line is divided into small units (cells), each with a team that makes a complete product or a complete part of it.
parts.working: 1 mark: production divided into cells/units; 1 mark: each team responsible for a whole product or stage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits to Oak Line Furniture of introducing cell production.
parts.answer: (1) Workers feel responsible for a whole sofa, so motivation and quality rise and fewer sofas are returned. (2) Teams can solve problems and change styles quickly without stopping the whole line, increasing flexibility and productivity; workers learn several skills so absence causes fewer delays.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Mega Mugs installed automated filling machines. Before: 20 workers made 2,000 mugs a day. After: 12 workers make 2,400 mugs a day. Each worker is paid Rs 1,200 a day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the labour cost per mug before and after the change. Show your working.
parts.answer: Before Rs 12; after Rs 6

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why higher productivity may not increase Mega Mugs' profit.
parts.answer: (1) The machines are expensive to buy, maintain and power, so total costs may not fall until the investment is paid back. (2) Extra mugs must be sold – if demand does not rise, unsold inventory builds up or prices must be cut; redundancy payments and lower morale may also add costs.
parts.working: 2 × (1 mark reason + 1 mark development).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Heritage Woodworks makes hand-carved furniture to order using job production. The owner is considering also making a standard range of tables using batch production.
Job production: price Rs 120,000 per table; cost Rs 70,000 per table; 300 tables a year.
Batch production: price Rs 60,000 per table; cost Rs 32,000 per table; 1,000 tables a year; needs new machinery costing Rs 10 million.
The workshop can only use one method for tables.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which production method should Heritage Woodworks use? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Job: 300 × (120,000 − 70,000) = Rs 15 million a year. Batch: 1,000 × (60,000 − 32,000) = Rs 28 million a year before machinery; after the Rs 10 million machinery, Rs 18 million in year 1 (more than the Rs 15 million from job production), then Rs 13 million a year more from year 2 onward. Batch also gives lower unit costs, but needs 1,000 sales a year (market research needed), loses the unique hand-carved image and higher margin, and may demotivate skilled carvers. Judgement e.g.: batch production if market research confirms demand for 1,000 standard tables a year; otherwise keep job production, because each hand-carved table earns Rs 50,000 profit and the 300 tables are already made to order.
parts.working: Calculations: 120,000 − 70,000 = 50,000; × 300 = 15,000,000; 60,000 − 32,000 = 28,000; × 1,000 = 28,000,000; 28m − 10m = 18m; 28m − 15m = 13m. Levels: L3 (9–12) a justified recommendation that weighs the options against each other, uses the case data (and calculations where asked) and explains why the rejected option is weaker; L2 (5–8) developed analysis of the options applied to the business, decision only partly supported; L1 (1–4) relevant knowledge with limited application, or a bare decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: First Capital Bank is opening a new branch in Hyderabad.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two factors that affect the location of a service business such as a bank branch.
parts.answer: Any two: near customers/high footfall; security; rent/cost of premises; parking and access; location of competitors; near other businesses.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why a business might relocate.
parts.answer: Any two: lower costs (rent/wages); closer to customers or new markets; more space to expand; government incentives; existing site lease ends; better transport links.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A sugar mill and a bakery are choosing locations in Sindh.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why the sugar mill might locate near its raw materials.
parts.answer: Any two: sugar cane is heavy/bulky and expensive to transport; cane must be crushed soon after cutting; the finished sugar weighs much less than the cane; reliable supply from local farmers.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why the bakery might locate near its market.
parts.answer: Any two: bread is perishable and must be fresh; customers buy daily and want convenience; delivery costs of a bulky finished product; to compete with other bakeries.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: SunStitch Apparel, a European clothing company, is choosing a country for a new factory with 120 workers. In Country P the average wage is $310 a month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two factors SunStitch Apparel should consider when choosing a country for its factory.
parts.answer: Any two: wage costs; skills of the workforce; political stability; tariffs/trade agreements; transport links/ports; government incentives; exchange rates; laws and regulations.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the monthly wage cost for 120 workers in Country P. Show your working.

author: HomiLabs

stem: BookNook sells books only online and delivers across Pakistan from a warehouse.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one location factor that is still important for BookNook's warehouse.
parts.answer: e.g. near good road/motorway links and courier hubs so deliveries are fast; or low rent for a large space.
parts.working: 1 mark factor; 1 mark reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why location is less important for BookNook than for a bookshop on a high street.
parts.answer: (1) Customers order online, so BookNook does not need a site with high footfall – it can use a cheap warehouse away from the city centre, lowering rent. (2) It can serve the whole country from one location using couriers, so it is not limited to customers who live nearby; staff such as web designers can work from anywhere.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Tandoor House is choosing a site for a new restaurant in Lahore. Site A is on a busy main road and costs Rs 350,000 a month to rent. Site B is in a quiet side street and costs Rs 220,000 a month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference in annual rent between the two sites. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline two reasons why Tandoor House might still choose Site A.
parts.answer: e.g. much higher footfall means more walk-in customers and higher revenue that could exceed the extra Rs 1.56 million; better visibility acts as free advertising; easier for customers and delivery riders to find; near offices for lunch trade.
parts.working: 2 × (1 mark reason + 1 mark development).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Pak Shoes plans to move its factory from central Karachi to a special economic zone 60 km away. The zone offers 10 years without tax on profits, cheaper land and reliable electricity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two problems Pak Shoes might face when relocating.
parts.answer: Any two: some workers may not move/need to recruit and train new ones; cost of moving machinery; lost production during the move; further from customers/suppliers; transport for workers.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits to Pak Shoes of locating in the special economic zone.
parts.answer: (1) No tax on profits for 10 years means more retained profit to invest in new machinery or lower prices. (2) Reliable electricity avoids production stoppages caused by power cuts, so output and delivery times improve; cheaper land allows a larger factory and future expansion.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: FreshMart, a supermarket chain, wants to open its first store in Faisalabad. It is looking at sites in the city centre and in a new housing estate on the edge of the city.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two factors FreshMart should consider when choosing the location of its new store.
parts.answer: (1) Customers/footfall: the housing estate has growing numbers of families who need weekly groceries and may have no supermarket nearby, while the centre has many shoppers but also competitors. (2) Cost and space: city-centre land and rent are expensive and parking is limited; an edge-of-city site is cheaper and has space for car parking and deliveries. Also: competitors, transport access, planning permission, availability of workers.
parts.working: For each of two points: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to the case, 2 marks developed analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Rock Cement needs a site for a new plant. Each month 300 lorry trips carry cement to its main market. Site A is 40 km from the market; Site B is 90 km from the market but next to a limestone quarry. Transport costs Rs 150 per km per trip.

parts.label: a
