parts.text: Calculate the monthly cost of transporting cement to the market from each site. Show your working.
parts.answer: Site A Rs 1,800,000; Site B Rs 4,050,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think the cost of transporting cement to the market is the most important factor in choosing the site? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Not necessarily: limestone is the main raw material and is far heavier in total than the finished cement, so Site B saves large costs of transporting raw materials, which could exceed the extra Rs 2.25 million a month. Other factors: availability of workers, power and water, government permission, environmental impact. Judgement: compare total transport costs (raw materials + finished goods), not only delivery costs.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Golden Crust Bakery is choosing between two sites for its next shop. Each shop opens 30 days a month, and gross profit is 60% of revenue.
Site A (shopping mall): 8,000 people pass each day; 3% expected to buy; average spend Rs 400; rent Rs 600,000 a month.
Site B (residential market): 5,000 people pass each day; 5% expected to buy; average spend Rs 350; rent Rs 300,000 a month.
All other costs are the same at both sites.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which site should Golden Crust Bakery choose? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Site A: 240 customers × 400 = Rs 96,000 a day; Rs 2,880,000 a month; gross profit Rs 1,728,000; after rent Rs 1,128,000. Site B: 250 × 350 = Rs 87,500 a day; Rs 2,625,000 a month; gross profit Rs 1,575,000; after rent Rs 1,275,000. B gives about Rs 147,000 more a month despite lower revenue, with regular local customers; A offers more brand exposure and possible growth. Forecast percentages are estimates. Judgement e.g. Site B.
parts.working: Calculations: 8,000 × 0.03 = 240; 240 × 400 = 96,000; × 30 = 2,880,000; × 0.6 = 1,728,000; − 600,000 = 1,128,000. 5,000 × 0.05 = 250; × 350 = 87,500; × 30 = 2,625,000; × 0.6 = 1,575,000; − 300,000 = 1,275,000. Difference 147,000. Levels: L3 (9–12) a justified recommendation that weighs the options against each other, uses the case data (and calculations where asked) and explains why the rejected option is weaker; L2 (5–8) developed analysis of the options applied to the business, decision only partly supported; L1 (1–4) relevant knowledge with limited application, or a bare decision.

author: HomiLabs

stem: CodeWave, a software company in Lahore with 50 staff, is thinking of moving to Dubai to be closer to Gulf clients. Staff in Lahore earn an average of Rs 250,000 a month. In Dubai it would have to pay an average of AED 9,000 a month. The exchange rate is AED 1 = Rs 76.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the increase in the monthly salary bill, in rupees, if CodeWave moves to Dubai. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think CodeWave should relocate to Dubai? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: For: close to clients, easier meetings and trust, possibly higher prices and more contracts; good infrastructure and international image. Against: salary bill rises by Rs 21.7 million a month (174%); higher rent and living costs; existing skilled staff may not move; software can be delivered online from Lahore. Judgement e.g.: open a small sales office in Dubai and keep development in Lahore.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Metro Express runs buses in Lahore. It checks every bus each morning before it leaves the depot.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'quality control'.
parts.answer: Checking the product (or service) for faults, usually by inspecting it at the end of production or at stages, and rejecting faulty items.
parts.working: 1 mark: inspecting/checking for faults; 1 mark: at the end of production / remove faulty items.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways customers might judge the quality of a bus service.
parts.answer: Any two: punctuality/reliability; cleanliness; safety; comfort (e.g. air-conditioning); politeness of staff; value for money.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Silver Line Electronics wants every employee to be responsible for quality.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'total quality management (TQM)'.
parts.answer: An approach in which every employee in every department is responsible for quality at every stage, aiming for zero defects and complete customer satisfaction.
parts.working: 1 mark: all employees responsible for quality; 1 mark: at every stage / aim of no faults / customer satisfaction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two costs to a business of poor quality.
parts.answer: Any two: wasted materials; cost of reworking or replacing faulty goods; refunds; loss of customers/sales; damaged reputation; legal claims.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Bright Bulb makes LED light bulbs. Last week it made 18,000 bulbs, and 270 were faulty.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of bulbs that were faulty. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two ways Bright Bulb could reduce the number of faulty bulbs.
parts.answer: Any two: train workers; maintain/upgrade machines; buy better-quality components; check quality at each stage (quality assurance); involve workers in quality circles/kaizen.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Rehman Water Heaters sells low-priced water heaters to households.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ways a business can show customers that its products are of good quality.
parts.answer: Any two: a recognised quality mark or certification (e.g. ISO); a guarantee/warranty; good reviews and testimonials; quality assurance labels; meeting safety standards.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why quality is important even for a low-priced product such as a water heater.
parts.answer: Customers still expect a cheap heater to work safely and reliably (be fit for purpose); faulty ones lead to returns, complaints and lost sales, and safety problems could cause legal action.
parts.working: 1 mark: quality means meeting customer expectations/fit for purpose; 1 mark: consequence of faults.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Crunchy Biscuits Ltd inspects packs at the end of its production line. Last month it made 500,000 packs and 2% were rejected. Each rejected pack cost Rs 30 to make.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of the rejected packs last month. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to Crunchy Biscuits Ltd of using end-of-line quality control.
parts.answer: Advantage: faulty packs are found before reaching shops, protecting the brand and avoiding complaints or recalls. Disadvantage: faults are found only after all the ingredients and work have been used, so waste is costly (Rs 300,000 a month) and inspectors' wages add further cost; the cause of faults is not prevented.
parts.working: For each point: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to this business, 1 mark developed consequence (analysis).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Indus Autos assembles cars. It now requires its parts suppliers to meet agreed quality standards and checks quality at every stage of assembly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two features of quality assurance.
parts.answer: Any two: quality is checked at every stage of production; aims to prevent faults rather than find them; workers check their own work; suppliers must meet standards; agreed standards are set.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why quality assurance may reduce Indus Autos' costs over time.
parts.answer: Faults are prevented or caught early, so fewer cars need expensive rework or recalls and less material is wasted; fewer inspectors are needed at the end of the line; fewer warranty claims and a better reputation increase sales.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks: prevention not detection (1); less waste/rework (1); fewer inspectors/warranty costs (1); development/application to cars (1).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Biryani Express, a restaurant chain, served 12,000 customers last month and received 84 complaints, mostly about long waiting times and cold food.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of complaints per 1,000 customers. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline two ways Biryani Express could improve the quality of its service.
parts.answer: e.g. train staff and set a target serving time (e.g. 10 minutes), with extra staff at peak times; use heated serving trays/insulated packaging so food stays hot; use customer feedback forms or mystery customers to monitor quality.
parts.working: 2 × (1 mark way + 1 mark link to the complaints).

author: HomiLabs

stem: Surgitech exports surgical instruments from Sialkot to hospitals in Europe and the USA. It is applying for an international quality-management certificate, which requires it to document and follow strict quality procedures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two benefits to Surgitech of gaining an international quality certificate.
parts.answer: (1) Access to markets: many foreign hospitals buy only from certified suppliers, so the certificate allows Surgitech to win new contracts and increase exports. (2) Reputation and fewer faults: documented procedures reduce mistakes, so fewer instruments are rejected or returned, lowering costs and allowing higher prices than uncertified competitors.
parts.working: For each of two points: 1 mark knowledge, 1 mark application to the case, 2 marks developed analysis.

author: HomiLabs

stem: FlyCheap is a low-cost airline. It offers very low fares but charges extra for bags and meals, and its seats have little leg room.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'quality'.
parts.answer: Producing a good or service that meets customers' expectations and is fit for purpose.
parts.working: 1 mark: meets customer expectations/needs; 1 mark: fit for purpose / free from faults.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think FlyCheap should focus on low prices rather than high quality? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Low prices: attract price-sensitive customers and fill seats; low quality in comfort is acceptable because customers expect a basic service. But quality still matters: safety, punctuality and baggage handling must meet expectations, or bad reviews and fines will drive customers away. Judgement: low prices with good basic quality (safety, punctuality) – quality means meeting the expectations of its target market.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Nova Phones assembles 40,000 phone chargers a month. It employs 6 inspectors, each paid Rs 60,000 a month. 3% of chargers are faulty and each faulty charger costs Rs 250 to replace.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total monthly cost of inspectors and faulty chargers. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Do you think introducing total quality management (TQM) would reduce Nova Phones' costs? Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Yes in the long run: every worker checks quality, so faults are prevented, fewer inspectors are needed and waste falls (potentially much of Rs 660,000 a month). But TQM needs training, time and a change of culture; costs rise at first and benefits are slow; workers may resist extra responsibility. Judgement: likely to reduce costs over time if managers fully commit.
parts.working: Marks: knowledge 2, analysis 2, evaluation 2 – evaluation needs a justified judgement that weighs both sides; a bare yes/no or a summary earns no evaluation mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
PowerPlus makes 100,000 power banks a year. At present 5% are made faulty. End-of-line inspection finds one in five faulty units (cost Rs 1,500 each to repair); the rest reach customers and are returned, costing Rs 4,000 each (replacement, delivery and lost goodwill).
Option 1: employ more inspectors at Rs 3 million a year. Faults made stay at 5%, but four in five faulty units would be found before sale.
Option 2: TQM training costing Rs 6 million once plus Rs 1 million a year. Faults made would fall to 2% from the second year; inspection would still find one in five.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which option should PowerPlus choose? Justify your answer using suitable calculations.
parts.answer: Now: 5,000 faulty; 1,000 found × 1,500 = Rs 1.5m; 4,000 returned × 4,000 = Rs 16m; total Rs 17.5m. Option 1: 4,000 found × 1,500 = Rs 6m; 1,000 returned × 4,000 = Rs 4m; + 3m = Rs 13m a year (saves Rs 4.5m). Option 2 (from year 2): 2,000 faulty; 400 × 1,500 = Rs 0.6m; 1,600 × 4,000 = Rs 6.4m; + 1m = Rs 8m a year (saves Rs 9.5m), plus Rs 6m set-up in year 1. Option 2 saves more after the first year and prevents faults, improving reputation; Option 1 acts at once but still lets faults through. Judgement e.g. Option 2 (perhaps with extra inspectors in year 1).
parts.working: Calculations: 0.05 × 100,000 = 5,000; 1,000 × 1,500 = 1.5m; 4,000 × 4,000 = 16m; 4,000 × 1,500 + 1,000 × 4,000 + 3m = 13m; 0.02 × 100,000 = 2,000; 400 × 1,500 + 1,600 × 4,000 + 1m = 8m. Levels: L3 (9–12) a justified recommendation that weighs the options against each other, uses the case data (and calculations where asked) and explains why the rejected option is weaker; L2 (5–8) developed analysis of the options applied to the business, decision only partly supported; L1 (1–4) relevant knowledge with limited application, or a bare decision.
